athenians: A Greek people of Ionic stock dwelling in Attica, whom Croesus identified as the most powerful among the Ionians and sought as allies against Persia; famous for the lawgiver Solon, who traveled to Egypt and Sardis in the early sixth century.
greek: A people inhabiting the lands west of Asia Minor and the Aegean, whom the Persians regarded as enemies separate from their Asiatic domain, and whose oracles at Delphi, Dodona, and elsewhere held great authority in matters of war and destiny.
lacedaemonians: The foremost Greek people of Dorian stock, whose chief city was Sparta in the Peloponnese; Croesus of Lydia sought their friendship as the mightiest of the Greeks, and they later made offerings at Delphi.
hellas: The Greek homeland and its city-states, including Argos, Athens, and the Aegean islands, which the Phoenicians first visited, Helen was abducted from, and which Croesus later sought to subjugate.
libya: A vast region west of Egypt, home to the oracle of Ammon that Croesus consulted.
egypt: A kingdom in northeastern Africa, south of the Mediterranean and east of Libya, to which Io was carried by the Phoenicians, an episode central to Persian and Greek accounts of their mutual enmity.
persian: An Indo-European people from the region east of the Mesopotamian plain who, according to Persian tradition, initiated conflict with the Greeks through the Phoenicians' abduction of Io, and whose growing power under Cyrus later prompted Croesus to seek oracular counsel about war against them.
greeks: Greek-speaking inhabitants of Hellas, regarded by Persians as their enemies since the Trojan War, and Herodotus' own people in the wars he records.
ionians: Greek-speaking people inhabiting the coast and islands of Asia Minor (modern Turkey), who were subjugated and made tributary by Croesus of Lydia, though some Ionian islanders later made peace with him through diplomatic persuasion.
athenian: Greek inhabitants of Athens who, according to Herodotus, created laws through Solon and were bound by oath to uphold them for ten years, and whose city was prosperous enough to honor its war dead with public burial.
spartans: A Greek people living in Laconia in the southern Peloponnese, reformed by Lycurgus into a disciplined warrior society and governed by two kings and ephors; they defeated the Tegeans in war and became powerful allies whom Croesus sought.
egyptian: An ancient people inhabiting the Nile valley and Egypt, who believed themselves the oldest nation until Psammetichus' experiment suggested the Phrygians were older, and who maintained distinctive religious practices such as sacred prostitution in temples of Zeus at Thebes.
nile: The river flowing northward through Egypt that by its annual flood deposits sediment to create arable land, and whose five mouths empty into the Mediterranean sea.
persia: The region comprising the territories of Persian tribes under Median rule, located east of Mesopotamia, whose inhabitants Cyrus rallied to overthrow the Median king Astyages and establish Persian dominance.
scythian: A nomadic people from the steppes north and east of the Black Sea and Caucasus who invaded and ruled upper Asia for twenty-eight years before being expelled, later becoming a target of Darius I's campaign.
argives: A Greek people inhabiting the city and region of Argos in the Peloponnese, who disputed territory with Sparta and were celebrated for athletic prowess and strength.
aeginetans: A Greek island people dwelling in Aegina in the Saronic Gulf, known as skilled sailors and traders who maintained their own sanctuary at Naucratis in Egypt, fought a prolonged naval rivalry with Athens and Samos, and were enlisted by Thebes to raid Attica during conflict with Athens.
attica: The territory of Athens in central Greece, comprising the city-state and its surrounding region; scene of Pisistratus' factional struggles and his return to power.
ionia: A region on the Aegean coast of Asia Minor (modern Turkey) settled by Greek Ionians, divided into twelve cities with four distinct dialects, which fell under Lydian domination under Croesus before being conquered by Persia.
samians: An Ionian people inhabiting the island of Samos off the coast of Lydia (Asia Minor), who spoke their own unique dialect and maintained a sanctuary of Hera in Egypt; they are said to have seized a bronze bowl meant as a gift from Sparta to Croesus.
europe: A continent and geopolitical region to the north and west of Asia and the Mediterranean, identified as the homeland of the Greeks and a territory distinct from Persian Asia in the Persians' geopolitical worldview.
salamis: An island city-kingdom in Cyprus, ruled by Evelthon in the 6th century and later by Onesilus, whose failed revolt against Persian control in 498 BC features prominently in the Ionian Revolt narrative.
hellenes: Greek-speaking peoples of the Aegean and mainland Greece who feature throughout Herodotus' narrative as protagonists in wars against the Persians and as subjects of his ethnographic and historical inquiry.
ister: A major river flowing from the land of the Celts westward through the middle of Europe to empty into the Euxine Sea at Istria, which Herodotus compares in length and course to the Nile.
milesians: An Ionian Greek people inhabiting Miletus on the coast of Asia Minor, who endured an eleven-year war with the Lydian kings Sadyattes and Alyattes before their tyrant Thrasybulus secured peace through a ruse.
lacedaemon: A city-state in southern Greece, the leading Spartan power, which consulted the Delphic oracle about wars against Tegea and sent military aid to Samian exiles against the tyrant Polycrates.
thebans: A people of Upper Egypt whose territory centered on a major city; they feature in Herodotus' accounts of Egyptian religious practices, notably their sacred regard for rams and avoidance of sheep sacrifice, and as witnesses to a miraculous rainfall during the Persian invasion.
thebes: A city in Boeotia in central Greece, on the Ismenus river, famous for its temples and oracle of Apollo Ismenus, where Croesus dedicated golden offerings.
thessaly: A region of northern Greece between the Aegean and the mountains of Macedonia, which paid tribute to the Persian king Darius and through which Lacedaemonian forces passed during their campaigns in Attica.
aegina: An island in the Saronic Gulf off the Peloponnese, celebrated for its naval power and merchants, whose ships defeated the Samians at Cydonia and whose citizens—descendants of Aeacus—were renowned warriors and traders.
ionian: Greek people of Ionic stock inhabiting twelve cities along the coast of Asia Minor (Miletus, Myus, Priene, Ephesus, Colophon, Lebedos, Teos, Clazomenae, Phocaea, Samos, Chios, Erythrae) and their interior hinterland, united by the Panionion sanctuary, whom
corinthians: A Greek city-state whose tyrant Cypselus and his son Periander received dedications at Delphi and patronized the poet Arion.
pelasgians: An ancient pre-Greek people who inhabited parts of Greece (including Thessaly, Attica, and areas near the Hellespont) and other regions, spoke a non-Greek language, and transmitted religious practices and divine names to the early Greeks before being assimilated into the Hellenic stock.
magi: One of the six Median tribes, also functioning as a priestly caste who interpreted dreams for the Median king Astyages and advised him concerning the prophecy about Cyrus.
magus: A priestly caste of the Persians who performed essential ritual functions at sacrifices and played a crucial role in the dynastic upheaval following Cambyses' death, when the Magus Patizeithes orchestrated the usurper Smerdis' seizure of the throne.
carians: An Anatolian people inhabiting the region south of Lydia and Ionia, formerly (according to Cretan tradition) islanders under Minos who invented helmet-crests, shield-devices, and shield-grips before being driven to the mainland by Dorians and Ionians, though they themselves claimed aboriginal mainland origin.
boeotia: A region in central Greece north of Attica, settled in myth by Cadmus and the Phoenicians, and home to Thebes and other cities that figure in Greek religious history.
thessalians: A people inhabiting Thessaly in northern Greece, noted for their cavalry, who allied with the Pisistratid tyrants and offered exiled Hippias the city of Iolcus.
phocians: A Greek people inhabiting the region of central Greece around Mount Parnassus, who contributed one thousand hoplites to the defense of Thermopylae in 480 BC and were posted to guard the mountain path against Persian outflanking.
chersonese: A peninsula on the European side of the Hellespont, containing many cities, settled by the Athenian Miltiades son of Cypselus after he was called by the Dolonci tribe and walled off at its isthmus to secure it against the Apsinthians.
lydian: A wealthy and powerful kingdom in western Asia Minor, ruled by kings including Alyattes and Croesus, which subjugated Greek cities of Ionia and the coast and waged prolonged war against Miletus.
paeonians: A Thracian people dwelling north of the Strymon river, known for their conflict with Perinthus and later forcibly relocated to Asia by Darius after their leaders demonstrated their women's remarkable capability to manage multiple tasks simultaneously.
sicily: A large island in the western Mediterranean, southwest of Italy, known to Herodotus as a destination for Greek colonization attempts and pirate operations.
thrace: A region of southeastern Europe north of the Aegean, bordered by the Danube to the north, inhabited by Thracian tribes, and serving as a refuge for Greek exiles and a route of passage for Persian military campaigns.
peloponnesians: Greeks inhabiting the Peloponnese, who appear throughout the Histories as warriors, settlers, and participants in various conflicts, including Spartan-led invasions of Attica and campaigns in the eastern Mediterranean.
spartan: A Greek warrior people of the Peloponnese whose city-state Lacedaemon (Sparta) reformed its constitution under Lycurgus and later defeated the Tegeans in war, becoming dominant among Hellenic states and eventually clashing with Persia.
libyan: Native inhabitants of the region west of Egypt, consulted through the oracle of Ammon and bordered by mountains to the east where the Nile's flood waters extend seasonally.
dorians: A Greek people inhabiting cities in southwestern Asia Minor (including Halicarnassus, Cnidus, Cos, and the Rhodian cities) and Lacedaemon, who were subjugated by Croesus and known for their participation in shared sanctuaries such as the Triopian temple of Apollo.
tegeans: An Arcadian people inhabiting Tegea in the smooth plain of Arcadia, who initially defeated the Lacedaemonians in war through a misinterpreted oracle, but were later conquered when the Spartans recovered the bones of Orestes and gained the upper hand under kings Anaxandrides and Ariston.
lacedaemonian: A Greek people inhabiting Laconia in the Peloponnese, known for their military prowess and rival to Athens in the classical period; mentioned here in connection with the Trojan War narrative and as recipients of honors at Delphi.
pythian: Title of the priestess of Apollo at Delphi through whom the god's oracles were delivered, including pronouncements to Gyges, Alyattes, and Croesus.
syria: A region east of Egypt and the Mediterranean, extending southeastward toward Arabia and Aethiopia, through which the Scythians passed and where cities like Ascalon were located.
aeolians: Greeks of northwestern Asia Minor who settled twelve cities before losing Smyrna to the Ionians, later subjugated by Croesus and then the Persians.
pontus: A sea bordered by Scythia to the north and Asia Minor and the Hellespont to the south, on whose shores Greek colonists dwell and from whose ports trade and intelligence about the interior peoples are conducted.
milesian: Greek inhabitants of Miletus on the Ionian coast of Asia Minor, who resisted Lydian aggression under Alyattes and later consulted Herodotus about Persian expansion.
euboea: A large island off the east coast of central Greece, wealthy and strategically important as a stepping-stone for Persian expansion into the Aegean and mainland Greece.
chios: An Ionian island city (one of the two Ionian settlements on islands), lying off the coast of Lydia in the Aegean Sea, whose inhabitants spoke the same dialect as Erythrae and who harbored the fugitive Pactyes before surrendering him to the Persians in exchange for the district of Atarneus.
strymon: A river in northern Greece flowing into the Aegean near the Hellespont, forming the boundary of Paeonia and marking the limit of Persian conquest under Megabazus.
arabia: A mountainous region east of Egypt extending from the Mediterranean to the Red Sea, yielding frankincense and bordered by the Nile valley, mentioned by Herodotus as sharing certain burial customs with Babylon and Egypt.
argive: Greeks of the city-state Argos in the Peloponnese, who appear in foundation myths (the abduction of Io) and in historical accounts (Cleobis and Biton; mercenaries hired by Pisistratus).
chians: An Ionian Greek people inhabiting the island of Chios off the coast of Lydia, who aided the Milesians against Lydia and later, under Persian pressure, surrendered the fugitive Pactyes to Cyrus in exchange for the district of Atarneus.
cyprus: An island in the eastern Mediterranean where a temple of Aphrodite existed (said by Cyprians themselves to be founded from the older temple in Syria), and which was conquered and made tributary by the Egyptian king Amasis.
macedonia: A region of northern Greece, bounded by the Prasiad lake to the east and the Dysorum mountain, whose king Amyntas submitted to Persian demands and whose prince Alexander later massacred Persian envoys; later subdued by Mardonius's army during Xerxes' invasion.
boeotians: Boeotians, a people inhabiting the region of Boeotia in central Greece north of Attica, who repeatedly came into military conflict with Athens in the late sixth century, notably expelling the Gephyraeans to Athens and later being defeated by the Athenians at the Euripus.
ethiopia: A region south of Egypt, through which the Nile flows from its mysterious sources; hot, rainless, and inhabited by dark-skinned peoples and nomadic tribes, with the great city of Meroe as its capital.
delphians: The inhabitants of Delphi, keepers of Apollo's oracle, who received lavish dedications from Gyges and Croesus and managed the sanctuary's treasuries.
cyrenaeans: Greek colonists of Cyrene in Libya who, frightened by Cambyses' conquest of Egypt, submitted to Persian rule and sent tribute, though their modest gift of five hundred silver minae displeased the king.
plataeans: A people of Boeotia who, after seeking protection from Theban pressure, placed themselves under Athenian protection and fought alongside the Athenians at Marathon, holding the left wing of their battle line.
babylonians: An ancient Near Eastern people who ruled a major city on the Euphrates; Herodotus notes their king Labynetus was allied with Croesus against Persia, and describes their eventual defeat by Cyrus at their city, which was defended by provisions stored for a long siege.
red-sea: A body of water into which major Mesopotamian rivers (the Euphrates and Tigris) flow, marking the southeastern boundary of the Persian Empire's territory.
lydia: An ancient kingdom in western Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey), ruled by Croesus in Herodotus' account, whose conflict with Persia and consultation of Greek oracles form a major theme of the Histories.
naxos: An Aegean island that Pisistratus conquered and garrisoned with Athenian hostages under the tyrant Lygdamis, later prosperous and troubled by internal faction.
greece: The homeland of the Greeks (Hellenes), who were divided into Dorian and Ionian peoples and whose leading cities were Sparta and Athens, making them a power that the Lydian king Croesus sought as allies.
phoenician: A seafaring people of the eastern Mediterranean coast skilled in trade and maritime commerce, including navigation and craft-work; mentioned by Herodotus chiefly for their religious images (the Pataici), their role as colonists (notably Membliarus' settlement on Calliste/Thera), and Thales of Miletus' descent from them.
asopus: A river in central Greece flowing through Thessaly and Boeotia, rising in the mountains near Trachis and flowing into the sea near Anthele; it figures as a geographical landmark in the Persian Wars, notably at Thermopylae and later as the position of Mardonius' army before Plataea.
assyrians: A people who ruled Upper Asia for five hundred and twenty years before the Medes revolted from them, and whose great cities Ninus and Babylon were eventually conquered by the Medes and then by Cyrus of Persia.
budini: A populous nomadic people inhabiting a densely forested region north of the Sauromatae and east of Scythia, who ate fir-cones, maintained the wooden city of Gelonus (which housed Greek settlers), and joined the anti-Darius coalition of the 510s BC.
mykale: A mountainous promontory on the Ionian coast of Asia Minor opposite Samos, site of the Panionion sanctuary where Ionian Greeks held their federated festival, and where a major Greek naval and land victory against the Persians occurred in 479 BC.
eretrians: An Euboean city-state whose citizens fought alongside the Ionians against Persia in the Ionian Revolt, later fell to the Persian invasion of 490 BC after internal betrayal, and served as a staging point for the Persian assault on Athens.
sicyon: A city-state in the northeast Peloponnese, near Argos, where the tyrant Cleisthenes reorganized religious festivals and later sent ships to aid Aegina against Athens.
araxes: A major river flowing eastward from the Matieni mountains into the Caspian Sea through multiple mouths, forming the boundary between Cyrus' Persian territory and the Massagetae kingdom east of it.
colchians: A people dwelling in Aea near the river Phasis on the eastern shore of the Black Sea, whom Herodotus believed to be of Egyptian origin and who rendered a gift of a hundred boys and a hundred maidens to the Persian king every four years.
corinthian: Greek city-state on the Isthmus of Corinth, known for maritime commerce and tyranny under Cypselus and Periander, whose conflicts with Samos and dedications at Delphi feature prominently in the narrative.
phocaeans: Greek Ionians from Phocaea in Asia Minor, renowned seafarers who pioneered Mediterranean exploration and were eventually displaced by Persian conquest, some of whom colonized Alalia in Corsica.
thera: An island in the Aegean Sea, originally called Calliste, colonized from Lacedaemon by Theras (a Spartan regent and descendant of Cadmus) around the mid-seventh century BC, which then served as the staging point for the Greek colonization of Libya.
naxians: An Aegean island people dwelling in the Cyclades whom banished exiles sought to restore through Persian military aid, but who successfully withstood a four-month siege when warned of the impending attack.
italy: A large peninsula in the Mediterranean, south of Europe, where the musician Arion traveled to make money before his famous encounter with Corinthian sailors.
hellenic: A people who share a common language and originate from Phthia, distinguished by their cleverness and capacity for growth through intermixture with foreign peoples, and whose two chief divisions—the Ionians and Dorians—came to dominate Greece.
borysthenes: A major river of Scythia flowing from the north into the Black Sea, notable for its exceptional fertility and fish; the Greeks of Olbia settled at its mouth and called themselves Borystheneïtae.
sacae: A Scythian people (called Sacae by the Persians) who lived east of the Caspian Sea and served as subjects and soldiers in the Persian Empire, fighting at Marathon and in Xerxes' invasion of Greece.
laconian: The Greek people of Laconia in the southern Peloponnese, notably the Spartans, who by Herodotus' time had subdued most of the Peloponnese and were renowned for military prowess.
syrians: The Cappadocians, called Syrians by Greeks, who lived in central Asia Minor east of the Halys river and were successively subjects of the Medes and Persians under Cyrus, suffering devastation when Croesus invaded their territory at Pteria.
theban: An ancient Egyptian city and region in Upper Egypt, whose inhabitants had distinctive religious practices (notably refusing to sacrifice sheep) and whose priests provided Herodotus with accounts of Egyptian history and mythology.
menelaus: King of Sparta, wronged husband of Helen, who led the Greek expedition against Troy and later, according to Egyptian priests, traveled to Egypt to recover Helen from King Proteus.
carthaginians: A Phoenician people inhabiting the North African coast (modern Tunisia) who, allied with the Tyrrhenians, defeated the Phocaeans in a naval battle near Corsica, and later escaped Persian conquest when the Phoenician crews of Cambyses' fleet refused to attack their kinsmen.
mede: A people of western Asia, subjects of their kings who ruled from Media, involved as allies and advisers in Cyrus the Persian's conquest of Lydia.
barcaeans: A Libyan people dwelling in the city of Barce in Cyrenaica, who collectively killed the tyrant Arcesilaus of Cyrene for his wrongs against them and later withstood a nine-month Persian siege sent to avenge his death.
amazons: A legendary warlike women's nation from the lands beyond the Black Sea, whom the Scythians called the Oiorpata ("killers of men"), said to have intermarried with young Scythian warriors and subsequently settled among the Sauromatae.
samian: A Greek people inhabiting the island of Samos in the Aegean Sea, celebrated by Herodotus for three monumental engineering works: a tunnel through a mountain, a harbor breakwater, and a great temple.
doriscus: A Persian royal fortress in a wide plain of Thrace through which flows the Hebrus river, where Darius had stationed a permanent guard and where Xerxes mustered and numbered his entire invasion force before marching into Greece.
parians: An Aegean island people chosen by the Milesians to arbitrate their civil strife, whom they successfully reconciled by identifying and elevating virtuous landholders to rule the state.
phrygia: A region in western Asia Minor (Anatolia) bounded by Lydia to the west, through which the Persian Royal Road passed for twenty stages on its route eastward to Cappadocia.
aeginetan: An island people of the Saronic Gulf, rivals of Athens in naval power, who supplied a celebrated physician to Polycrates and clashed militarily with Athens in the early classical period.
macedonian: A people inhabiting the territory between the Haliacmon and Lydias rivers in northern Greece, and subjects of King Amyntas who submitted to Persian demands for earth and water under Darius.
arcadians: A Peloponnesian people who alone among the region's inhabitants were not displaced by the Dorian invasion, and thus preserved certain ancient religious rites including the Thesmophoria.
maeander: A river in western Asia Minor (modern Turkey) flowing through the plain near Ephesus, notable to Herodotus as an example of how river deposits create new land, and also (in its winding course) comparable to the upper Nile.
cilicia: A region on the southern coast of Asia Minor, bounded by the Halys river to the north and forming part of the Persian tribute system under Darius, notable for its strategic location and its substantial annual tribute of horses and silver.
arcadia: A region in the central Peloponnese, inland and mountainous, home to various independent tribes; the Spartans initially sought to conquer it but were repelled by Tegea, and later Cleomenes stirred up the Arcadians against Sparta by invoking oaths at the sacred spring of the Styx near Nonacris.
cithaeron: A mountain range in Boeotia, north of the Isthmus, where Greek forces positioned themselves against the Persian army under Mardonius before the battle of Plataea.
babylonian: An inhabitant of Babylon, the great city of Mesopotamia whose king Labynetus mediated peace between the Lydians and Medes, and whose priests (the Chaldaeans) maintained the famous temple of Zeus with its golden furnishings and altar.
cyprians: The inhabitants of Cyprus, who voluntarily joined the Persian forces against Egypt and later (except Amathus) revolted against Persia alongside the Ionians.
ammonians: A Libyan people inhabiting the oasis region of Ammon in the Libyan desert west of Egypt, where they maintained an oracle of Zeus-Ammon and adopted religious practices blending Egyptian and Ethiopian traditions.
phalerum: The chief Athenian port, situated on the coast of Attica south of Athens, where foreign fleets regularly landed and anchored during the campaigns of the 490s and 480s BC.
bosporus: The strait connecting the Pontus (Black Sea) to the Propontis (Sea of Marmara), approximately 120 stades long and 4 stades wide at its narrowest point, which Darius I bridged with a boat-bridge designed by Mandrocles of Samos during his Scythian campaign.
buto: A sacred town in the Nile Delta, site of a major festival and the most honored oracle of Leto in Egypt, and where shrewmice and hawks are brought for burial.
cilicians: A people inhabiting Cilicia (a region in southern Asia Minor), whom Croesus did not subjugate, distinguished by Herodotus as a distinct territorial and ethnic unit like Assyrians or Egyptians.
chalcidians: A people of Euboea who fought against Athens in the early fifth century, defeated by the Athenians after the latter's victory over the Boeotians, and later supplied ships and troops to Xerxes' invasion of Greece.
epidaurians: A city in the Peloponnese that contributed eight ships to the Greek fleet at Artemisium and ten at Salamis during the Persian Wars, and whose land required imported Athenian olive wood to cure its barrenness after consulting the Delphic oracle.
lesbians: An Aegean island people inhabiting Lesbos, who feature in Herodotus as allies of Miletos against Polycrates of Samos and later as subjects of Persian conquest.
mysians: A people inhabiting the region south of the Propontis in northwest Asia Minor, subject to Croesus and later to the Persians, connected by kinship legend to the Lydians and Carians.
halys: A major river of western Asia Minor, flowing north from the Armenian mountains between the Mediterranean and the Euxine Sea, forming the traditional boundary between the Lydian empire (west) and the Median/Persian empire (east).
phrygian: An Anatolian people living in the region of Phrygia, east of Lydia, whose royal house included Gordias and Midas; they appear in the narrative through Adrastus, a Phrygian prince who takes refuge with Croesus.
lycians: An Anatolian people of southwestern Asia Minor (in the region formerly called Milya or Lycia) who traced their origins to Cretan refugees under Sarpedon and were notable for tracing descent through the maternal rather than paternal line; they resisted subjugation by Croesus and later opposed the Persian general Harpagus.
byzantium: A Greek city on the Bosporus (entrance to the Black Sea), which received marbles from Darius' pillars and was later captured by the Persians under Otanes.
megarians: A Greek city-state on the Isthmus of Corinth that contributed twenty ships to the Greek fleet against Persia at Artemisium and Salamis, and whose citizens Gelon of Syracuse later subjugated and divided in Sicily.
phocaea: A Greek city on the Ionian coast of Lydia in Asia Minor, one of the twelve Ionian settlements, which sent an envoy to Sparta for aid against Persian expansion and received a Spartan warning to Cyrus.
trachis: A town in Malis near the coast of the Malian Gulf, about five furlongs south of the Black River, where Xerxes established his camp before the battle of Thermopylae in 480 BC.
eleans: A Greek people inhabiting Elis in the northwestern Peloponnese, famous for organizing the Olympic games, who sent ambassadors to Egypt to seek advice on fair competition rules and who participated late or not at all in the defense of Greece against the Persian invasion.
cretans: An island people inhabiting Crete who, according to Persian account, were among the first Greeks to commit wrongs in the mythical exchanges with Asia, and who during the Persian Wars refused to aid the Greek alliance after consulting the Delphic oracle.
bactrians: A people of central Asia (north of the Pactyic country and south of the Aegli), incorporated into the Persian Empire as a satrapy paying three hundred sixty talents annually, and mustered by Darius for his invasion of Greece under the command of Hystaspes.
phocis: A region in central Greece, north of the Gulf of Corinth and west of Boeotia, whose people fiercely resisted Persian invasion and earlier had defeated Thessalian forces with a famous stratagem involving whitened warriors.
carian: A people inhabiting southwestern Asia Minor (Caria) whose women were married by Ionian colonists after the men killed their male relatives, and whose speech and customs were known to the Greeks of Herodotus' time.
phrygians: An Anatolian people subject to Croesus west of the Halys river, later ruled by the Persians; they were believed by Egyptians, according to a linguistic experiment by Psammetichus, to be the oldest human race.
caria: A region of southwestern Asia Minor (modern Turkey), south of Lydia, that bordered the Ionian cities Miletus, Myus, and Priene, and whose people joined the Ionian Revolt against Persian rule around 500 BC.
maeetian-lake: A large lake north of the Black Sea (Pontus), fed by the Tanaïs river, that bordered Scythia on the south and east and served as a natural boundary for Scythian territory.
achaeans: A Greek people inhabiting Achaea in the Peloponnese, who displaced the Ionians and later supplied troops to Xerxes' Persian invasion force.
issedones: A people dwelling east of Scythia, known to Herodotus chiefly through Aristeas' account and Scythian report; they practiced excarnation and skull-gilding of the dead, granted women equal power with men, and were themselves displaced westward by the Arimaspians.
pelasgian: A pre-Greek, non-Greek-speaking people whom Herodotus says once inhabited much of Greece including Attica and Thessaly, with remnants surviving in his day at Creston above the Tyrrhenians and at Placia and Scylace on the Hellespont.
cyme: An Aeolian city on the mainland coast of Asia Minor, north of Ionia, which became embroiled in the Persian conquest when the fugitive Lydian Pactyes sought refuge there and later produced the tyrant Aristagoras, a leader of the Ionian Revolt.
agathyrsi: A tribe of people dwelling in the region north and west of Scythia, between the Ister river and the lands of the Neuri, noted for their wealth in gold, refined customs, and promiscuous kinship practices.
minyae: Descendants of the Argonauts who were expelled from Lemnos by Pelasgians, initially received by the Lacedaemonians but later imprisoned and forced to escape, after which some settled in the western Peloponnese and others colonized the island of Calliste under Theras.
thracian: A people inhabiting the region north of Greece (south of the Danube and east of Macedonia), known to practice distinctive religious customs and to have produced notable figures like the slave-girl Rhodopis and the sage Salmoxis who learned from Greek teachers.
macedonians: A people inhabiting the region north of Greece who were initially independent but became Persian subjects before Xerxes' invasion of Greece.
euphrates: A wide, deep, and swift river flowing from Armenia through the middle of Babylon and issuing into the Red Sea, which Herodotus describes as dividing the city in two.
delians: Inhabitants of the sacred island of Delos in the Aegean, custodians of a major sanctuary of Apollo and Artemis through which Hyperborean offerings traveled, and recipients of honors paid by Persian commander Datis during Xerxes' invasion.
cimmerians: A nomadic people from north of the Black Sea, driven westward into Asia Minor by the Scythians, where they sacked Sardis and dominated parts of Asia before being expelled by the Lydian king Alyattes.
barce: A Libyan city founded by the exiled brothers of the Cyrenaean king Arcesilaus, where the king was later killed by its citizens and Egyptian forces under Aryandes subsequently conquered it.
assyrian: A people of western Asia whose capital was Babylon, and whose history Herodotus promises to recount separately.
peneus: A river in Thessaly formed by the confluence of several streams, flowing through a narrow pass between Olympus and Ossa into the Aegean Sea, whose mouth Xerxes viewed while considering an inland route into Thessaly.
zancle: A Greek city in Sicily on the strait facing Tyrrhenia (modern Messina), whose tyrant Scythes lost it to invading Samians (aided by the tyrant Anaxilaus of Rhegium) while besieging another town, and subsequently came under the control of Hippocrates of Gela.
hypanis: A river of Scythia rising from a great lake where white horses graze, flowing five days with sweet water before becoming bitter from a spring called Exampaeus on the border of the Alazones' territory, and eventually merging with the Borysthenes near the sea.
sicyonians: Greek people inhabiting the city and territory of Sicyon in the Peloponnese, who honored the hero Adrastus until tyrant Cleisthenes redirected their worship to Melanippus and renamed their Dorian tribes.
arabian: A people inhabiting the region east of Egypt bounded by mountains running north to south toward the Red Sea, whose lands were flooded by the Nile and whose territory yielded frankincense.
theraeans: Greeks from the island of Thera (Santorini) in the Aegean, who founded the colony of Cyrene in Libya after drought forced them to obey a Delphic oracle commanding them to establish a settlement there, with Battus as their leader.
therma: A town on the Thermaic Gulf in Macedonia where Xerxes' Persian fleet assembled and his army encamped during the invasion of Greece in 480 BC.
olympic: Not a distinct people in Herodotus' narrative; "Olympic" refers to the games held at Olympia in Greece, managed by officials called Hellenodicae, where athletes from Greek cities competed in contests including chariot-racing and footraces.
magnesia: A city in Lydia, situated above (inland from) the river Maeander, where the Persian satrap Oroetes resided and where he murdered the Samian tyrant Polycrates.
fisheaters: A people dwelling at Elephantine who spoke the Ethiopian language and served the Persian king Cambyses as interpreters and envoys to the Ethiopian court.
mytilenaeans: Greeks of the island of Lesbos who played significant roles in Persian-era conflicts, including Cöes who advised Darius on the Scythian campaign and was later stoned by his own people, and who disputed control of Sigeum with the Athenians.
epidaurus: A city-state in the Peloponnese, ruled by Procles (Periander's father-in-law), whom Periander attacked and captured after blaming him for turning his son Lycophron against him.
thespians: A Boeotian city-state whose hoplites (700 strong) fought beside the Spartans at Thermopylae, choosing to remain and die rather than abandon Leonidas, and whose city was later burned by Xerxes' army in retaliation for their resistance to Persian medism.
peloponnesian: Inhabitants of the Peloponnese, the peninsula of southern Greece, many of whose peoples fought against Persia and debated strategy at Salamis.
chalcis: A city on Euboea that Athens defeated in battle after the Boeotians, subsequently planting settlers on the lands of its wealthy landowners and ransoming captive nobles.
blackcloaks: A non-Scythian people living north of the Royal Scythians between the Gerrus river and uninhabited marshes, who wore black clothing and were summoned to deliberate on defense against Darius' invasion but refused to aid the Scythians, claiming they bore no prior wrong to the Persians.
potidaea: A town on the peninsula of Pallene in northern Greece, which revolted from the Persians after Xerxes' retreat and endured a siege by Artabazus that was prolonged by treachery from the Scionaean general Timoxenus.
tauri: A people inhabiting the Tauric Peninsula (modern Crimea) in the northern Pontus, renowned for sacrificing shipwrecked sailors and captives to a goddess they identified with Iphigenia, and for taking enemy heads as talismans.
aphetae: A harbor on the coast of Magnesia in Thessaly, at the head of the gulf toward Pagasae, where Xerxes' Persian fleet anchored before attacking the Greeks at Artemisium during the invasion of 480 BC.
troy: A city in Asia Minor (Anatolia) on the Hellespont whose siege by Greeks seeking to recover Helen from Paris/Alexandrus became a foundational episode in Greek-Persian mutual hostilities, though Egyptian priests claimed Helen never reached Troy but remained in Egypt with Proteus.
trojans: An ancient people of Asia Minor (the Troad region near the Hellespont) who, according to Greek legend, were besieged by Greek forces over Helen; by Herodotus' time, their city Ilion had fallen and they survived only in scattered remnants like the Gergithae.
tarentum: A Greek city in southern Italy where the Persian escort of the physician Democedes was detained by its king Aristophilides before Democedes escaped to Croton.
aeolian: Greek-speaking people inhabiting eleven ancient cities on the coast of northwestern Asia Minor (modern Turkey) and nearby islands including Lesbos and Tenedos, who were conquered by Croesus and later came under Persian control.
lycia: A region on the southwestern coast of Asia Minor, notable as the seat of an oracle of Apollo at Patara and homeland of the poet Olen.
branchidae: An oracle sanctuary in the territory of Miletus, consulted by Ionians and Aeolians, to which Croesus sent envoys for divination and where the people of Cyme sought guidance on whether to surrender Pactyes to the Persians.
matieni: A people dwelling in the mountainous regions of Asia where the Gyndes and Araxes rivers originate, subject to Persian tribute under Darius.
corcyraeans: Greek islanders who colonized Corcyra (modern Corfu) off the coast of Epirus, maintained a long-standing feud with their Corinthian mother-city, and later aided Syracuse against Hippocrates of Gela.
thessalian: A Greek people inhabiting Thessaly in central Greece, renowned for their cavalry, who initially sided with Persia during Xerxes' invasion but sought to defend the pass of Olympus and urged other Greeks to do the same.
geloni: A Hellenized people of Greek origin who settled among the Budini in the forest regions north of the Black Sea, spoke a hybrid Greek-Scythian language, and practiced agriculture and Greek religious rites, including the cult of Dionysus.
sestus: A coastal city on the European side of the Hellespont in the Chersonese, strongly fortified and held by Persian forces under Artayctes, which the Athenians under Xanthippus besieged and captured after the battle of Mykale.
troezen: A city in the Peloponnese, the legendary birthplace of Halicarnassian settlers and a refuge where Athenians evacuated their families during the Persian Wars; the Greek fleet gathered at its harbor Pogon before the naval engagements of 480 BC.
orchomenus: A city in Arcadia (Peloponnese) that contributed troops to the Greek defense against Persia and whose notable citizen Thersander recounted an omen of Persian defeat to Herodotus.
parnassus: A mountain in central Greece, sacred to Apollo and the Muses, on whose heights the Phocians and Delphians took refuge during the Persian invasion and whose peaks overlooked the temple of Apollo at Delphi below.
tritonian-lake: A lake in Libya fed by the river Triton, bordering the Machlyes and Auseans, where an oracle told the Lacedaemonians to found a settlement on its island of Phla.
siphnians: An Ionian people of the Aegean island of Siphnus, renowned for gold and silver mines that made them the wealthiest islanders until they were defeated and heavily fined by the Samians, and later contributed a fifty-oared boat to the Greek fleet at Salamis.
sunium: A promontory in southeastern Attica forming the southernmost point of Attica, sacred to Poseidon and important as a landmark for ships rounding it and as a site of Athenian religious observance and sanctuary dedications.
euxine: The Black Sea, bounded by Asia Minor, Scythia, and other lands, its shores inhabited by peoples Herodotus deemed ignorant, save for the Scythians.
cyprian: A people inhabiting the island of Cyprus in the eastern Mediterranean, who revolted against Persian rule under Onesilus but were defeated by the Persian general Artybius, after which their cities were besieged by Persian forces.
palestine: A region of Syria on the eastern Mediterranean coast, south of Phoenicia, extending from Cadytis toward Egypt, whose inhabitants practiced circumcision learned from Egypt and where Sesostris' commemorative pillars were visible.
khemmis: A city in the Theban district of Upper Egypt near the New City, famous as the legendary birthplace of Perseus and site of a sanctuary where he was honored with Greek-style games and contests.
saspires: A nation dwelling between Media and Colchis, north of the Caucasian mountains and south of the Phasis river, who supplied troops (armed like the Colchians) to Xerxes' invasion force under Masistius son of Siromitres.
cnidians: Greek people of Cnidos in southwestern Asia Minor, colonists from Lacedaemon, whose Triopian peninsula was nearly surrounded by sea.
arabian-gulf: A body of water bordering Egypt and Arabia to which the Nile was connected by canal under Darius, serving as a port for Egyptian naval operations and the southern terminus of Egypt's Red Sea access.
melissa: Wife of Periander, tyrant of Corinth, whom he murdered and later consulted as a ghost at the Oracle of the Dead in Thesprotia.
euxine-sea: A sea bounded by Asia Minor, the Caucasus, and Europe, where the river Ister (Danube) terminates and to which Asia Minor's northern coast (Paphlagonia, Sinope) faces.
trojan: A people of Asia Minor who inhabited the region around Ilion (Troy), at the center of the narrative concerning Helen's abduction and the subsequent Greek military expedition.
india: The easternmost land known to the Persians, inhabited by many nations of different languages and customs, whose remoter regions yield abundant gold extracted from sand by giant ants and collected by hardy Indian tribes who trade it to the Persian king.
tarentines: Greek settlers of southern Italy around Tarentum who attempted to destroy settlements founded by displaced Cretans in Iapygia and suffered catastrophic casualties in the resulting conflict.
cyzicus: A Greek city on the southern coast of the Propontis (Sea of Marmara), noted for its worship of the Mother of the Gods and whose tyrant Aristagoras was among the pro-Persian Greek rulers advising Darius.
euripus: A narrow strait between Euboea and the mainland of Greece, passage of which was strategically vital for controlling access to central Greece during the Persian Wars.
perinthians: Greek inhabitants of Perinthus on the Hellespont in Thrace who resisted Persian subjugation under Megabazus but were overcome and subdued as part of Darius' conquest of Thrace.
sigeum: A promontory in the Troad (northwestern Asia Minor) on the Hellespont, where the exiled Pisistratidae tyrants of Athens retreated after their expulsion and where Hippias was later summoned by Sparta.
carystians: An island people of Euboea who participated in the relay of Hyperborean offerings to Delos, initially resisted the Persian demand for hostages and military support but were forced to submit after invasion, and later paid money to Themistocles to avoid Greek attack.
pelion: A mountain in Thessaly on its eastern side, forming part of the ring of mountains enclosing the Thessalian plain; notorious for the rocky headland (the Ovens) where Persian ships were wrecked in a storm during the invasion of Greece.
histiaea: A city in Euboea on the northern coast, whose territory includes Artemisium where the Greek fleet was stationed during the Thermopylae campaign, and which the Persian fleet occupied after the Greeks withdrew.
maneaters: A nomadic people inhabiting the region north of Scythia (inland from the Black Sea coast), known to the Greeks as cannibals and characterized by Herodotus as the most savage nation, lawless and with their own language, who declined to aid the Scythians against Darius' invasion.
laconia: A region of southern Greece (the Peloponnesus) dominated by the city-state of Sparta, which Herodotus portrays as a leading power of Hellas courted by Croesus and known for distinctive customs including elaborate royal funeral rites and the subjugation of neighboring peoples.
cappadocia: A region in central Asia Minor east of Lydia, where Croesus invaded expecting to defeat Cyrus and the Persians, and where the armies first clashed inconclusively at Pteria.
delphian: The inhabitants of Delphi, site of Apollo's oracle, whom Croesus honored above all other oracular shrines after the Pythia correctly identified his secret test of the oracles' truth.
paphlagonians: A people inhabiting the southern coast of the Black Sea (Euxine) between Cappadocia and Bithynia, west of the Halys River; subjects first of Croesus, then of the Medes and Persians, who contributed troops and tribute to the Persian Empire.
locrians: Greek people living in two main divisions (Opuntian Locrians and others) in central Greece who opposed Persian invasion, fighting at Thermopylae and Artemisium, though some Locrian cities also submitted to Xerxes.
tyrrhenians: A people of Italy who, according to Herodotus, were Lydians forced to emigrate by famine under King Atys, sailed to the western Mediterranean under Atys' son Tyrrhenus, and subsequently clashed with Greek colonists (notably the Phocaeans at Cyrnus) around the mid-sixth century BC.
caucasus: A major mountain range forming the western boundary of the Caspian Sea, inhabited by many nations and marking the northern limit of Persian imperial reach.
rhegium: A Greek city in southern Italy (the toe of the peninsula), on the Strait of Messina opposite Sicily, where Phocaean refugees landed after their naval defeat and where the tyrant Anaxilaus ruled during conflicts over Zancle.
gyndes: A river rising in the Matieni mountains that flows through Dardanean territory into the Tigris, which Cyrus divided into 360 channels after it swept away one of his sacred horses during the march to Babylon.
paeonia: A region in Thrace north of the Strymon river near the Hellespont, whose people were deported to Phrygia by the Persian general Megabazus but later escaped during the Ionian Revolt and returned home.
elean: The inhabitants of Elis, a region in the northwestern Peloponnese that controlled the Olympic games and produced seers and contest-directors of renown.
lake-moeris: A large Egyptian lake seven days' journey upstream from the sea, located north of the region that ancient priests claimed was once entirely marsh under the first human king Min, and sacred to crocodiles in the region of Thebes.
cos: One of the Five Dorian cities of the southwestern Aegean, which joined with Lindus, Ialysus, Camirus, and Cnidus in excluding Halicarnassus from the Triopian temple, and whose men were led by the tyrant Artemisia in Xerxes' invasion of Greece.
carchedonians: A Phoenician people inhabiting Carthage in North Africa who, under their king Amilcas, led a major military expedition to Sicily around the time of the Persian Wars and earlier drove Greek colonists from Libya.
cissian: A region of the Persian Empire centered on Susa, which paid three hundred talents in tribute and contained the gates of Babylon through which Zopyrus admitted the Persian forces.
cyrnus: An island in the western Mediterranean where Phocaean Greek colonists settled at Alalia but were expelled after a costly naval defeat by Tyrrhenians and Carthaginians around 540 BC.
thasians: An island people of the northern Aegean, colonized by Phoenicians, who possessed rich gold and silver mines and were subdued without resistance by Darius' fleet, later ordered to demolish their walls and surrender their ships, and subsequently bankrupted by entertaining Xerxes' army.
euboeans: Greeks inhabiting the island of Euboea in central Greece, who bribed Themistocles to keep the Greek fleet at Artemisium rather than allow it to withdraw and leave Euboea undefended.
syracusans: A Greek city-state in Sicily that under Gelon challenged Spartan leadership of the Greek alliance against Persia, and defeated the Carthaginian general Amilcas in Sicily.
sciathus: An island in the Aegean off the coast of Thessalian Magnesia, where a Greek advance guard was stationed and where Xerxes' fleet first encountered Greek ships during the invasion of 480 BC.
pamphylians: A people of southern Asia Minor (Anatolia) who supplied one hundred ships to Xerxes' invasion fleet and are said by Herodotus to descend from Trojan refugees who followed Amphilochus and Calchas.
trachinian: Inhabitants of Trachis, a town in Thessaly at the base of the mountains forming the narrow pass of Thermopylae, notable for Athenades who killed the traitor Epialtes and for providing local intelligence to the Greeks during Xerxes' invasion.
colchian: A people dwelling in Colchis on the eastern shore of the Black Sea, known for their linen-working and close similarity to the Egyptians in customs and language, and figuring in Greek mythology as the home of Medea and her father the king.
clazomenae: An Ionian city in Lydia on the coast of Asia Minor, one of the twelve members of the Ionian league whose citizens shared a common dialect and jointly founded the Hellenion sanctuary at Naucratis in Egypt, later captured by the Persians under Artaphrenes and Otanes.
colophon: An Ionian Greek city on the Lydian coast of Asia Minor, one of the twelve cities of the Ionian League, taken by Gyges of Lydia; Colophonian exiles later seized Smyrna from the Aeolians, and Smyrna itself was originally a colony from Colophon.
achaea: A region of central Greece (Thessaly's southern neighbor) through which Xerxes' army marched toward the pass of Tempe during the Persian invasion, containing the city of Alus and notable for its rivers, especially the Apidanus.
abae: A sanctuary of Apollo in Phocis, central Greece, renowned as an oracle and repository of votive offerings from successful battles, plundered and burned by the Persians during their invasion of 480 BC.
cadmeans: A Hellenic people of Boeotia who at some point were expelled by the Argives, after which they migrated (some to the Encheleis, others remaining and later being driven to Athens by the Boeotians), and whom Herodotus credits with arriving in Boeotia as part of Cadmus' Phoenician retinue.
tigris: A major river of western Asia that flows through Assyria past the city of Ninus and empties into the Red Sea, crucial to irrigation and commerce in Babylon.
caspian: A large inland sea bounded by the Caucasus Mountains to the west and by plains inhabited by the Massagetae to the east, which Cyrus the Great sought to cross in his campaign against the nomadic peoples of Asia.
tmolus: A mountain in Lydia, east of Sardis, noted for gold dust carried down by the river Pactolus and serving as a geographical reference point and refuge during the Ionian attack on Sardis.
ilion: The city of Troy in Asia Minor, besieged by Greeks under Menelaus after the abduction of Helen, though according to Egyptian priests Helen was never there but in Egypt with King Proteus.
erythrae: A town in Boeotia on the mainland, near the Asopus river, where the Greek forces arrayed themselves to face the Persians before the battle of Plataea.
lindus: A Dorian city on the island of Rhodes, one of the "Five Cities" that shared the Triopian temple and received a linen breastplate dedicated by Amasis of Egypt.
pelusium: An important fortress-city on Egypt's northeastern frontier, guarding the eastern approaches and the road to Arabia and Assyria.
dryopians: A people of the Peloponnese who, according to Herodotus, were driven out of the region now called Doris by Heracles and the Malians and subsequently settled at Hermione, Asine, Styra, and Cythnos, providing ships for the Greek fleet against Persia.
nasamonians: A Libyan people inhabiting the region of the Syrtis and eastward, whose young men journeyed into the western desert and reported encountering a city of black people of short stature beside a great river flowing east.
amphictyons: A religious association of Greek states centered at Delphi, responsible for maintaining the sanctuary and its temple, and serving as judges and administrators of pan-Hellenic religious affairs.
samothracian: An Aegean island people inhabiting Samothrace (north of the Aegean between Thrace and the Greek islands), known for practicing mystery rites of the Cabeiri inherited from the Pelasgians, and for their prowess as javelin-throwers in Xerxes' fleet during the Battle of Salamis.
etesian: Seasonal northerly winds that blow regularly across the Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean, invoked by Herodotus both to explain natural phenomena (like the Nile's flooding) and as an excuse by the Corcyraeans for their failure to reach Salamis.
aegean: A sea bordered by Greece to the west and Asia Minor to the east, into which the Hellespont empties and across which maritime traffic between the Greek mainland and the Aegean islands passes.
chorasmians: A people of Central Asia living in a region east of the Caspian Sea, incorporated into the Persian Empire's sixteenth satrapy, from which they paid three hundred talents of tribute and supplied troops equipped like the Bactrians.
thermodon: A river in Anatolia (northern Asia Minor), flowing into the Black Sea, where the Greeks defeated the Amazons according to legend.
propontis: A sea lying between the Bosporus and the Hellespont, roughly 500 stades wide and 1400 stades long, through which Persian forces moved during their campaigns in Anatolia and the Aegean region.
euboic: A unit of weight or currency used as a standard of measurement in tribute calculations, equal to approximately 78 minae and one-thirteenth the value of a Babylonian talent.
arimaspians: A legendary one-eyed people dwelling in the far north beyond the Issedones, said to steal gold from griffins and to press the Issedones westward, though Herodotus himself doubts their existence.
nesaean: A superior breed of large horse native to a wide plain in Media, prized by the Persian king and nobility for riding and drawing chariots.
lampsacus: A Greek city on the Hellespont in Asia Minor, whose citizens imprisoned Miltiades but were forced by Croesus to release him, and were later barred from competing in the athletic contests of the Chersonese.
mantineans: A Greek people of Arcadia in the Peloponnese, who sent Demonax as mediator to Cyrene and later arrived too late for the Battle of Plataea, subsequently banishing their military leaders in shame.
nestus: A river in Thrace that flows into the sea near Abdera and marks the eastern boundary of the region where lions are found in Europe.
ligyes: An Iberian people living inland of Massalia (modern Marseille) in southern Gaul, who served in Xerxes' army and were also mercenaries in Carthaginian forces attacking Sicily.
myrcinus: A place in Edonia (Thrace) on the river Strymon, granted by Darius to Histiaeus as a reward for guarding the bridge over the Hellespont, which Histiaeus began to fortify as a city but was summoned away from by the king, and later became a refuge considered by the rebel Aristagoras before his death at the hands of Thracians
axius: A river in northern Greece forming the boundary between Mygdonian and Bottiaean territory, near which Xerxes' fleet lay at anchor off Therma during the Persian invasion of Greece.
dolonci: A Thracian tribe inhabiting the Chersonese who, after being defeated in war by the Apsinthians, consulted the Delphic oracle and subsequently invited the Athenian Miltiades son of Cypselus to settle and rule their land as tyrant.
satrae: A Thracian mountain tribe dwelling in snow-covered, forested highlands who alone maintained independence from all foreign rule and possessed an oracle of Dionysus administered by the Bessi clan.
cardia: A city in the Thracian Chersonese, near its isthmus, ruled by Miltiades son of Cypselus and his descendant Miltiades son of Cimon, and strategically important as a landmark in Xerxes' campaign and as a Persian outpost under Oeobazus.
sidonian: A Phoenician people of the eastern Mediterranean coast whose ships served as the Persian king's personal vessels and formed a contingent of Xerxes' fleet during the invasion of Greece.
gonnus: A town in the Perrhaebi region of highland Macedonia, located near a mountain pass through which Xerxes' army entered Thessaly, prompting the Greek defenders to abandon the pass of Tempe.
lampsacenes: A Greek city-state on the Asiatic coast of the Hellespont, whose inhabitants captured Miltiades during his campaigns in the Chersonese but released him at the threat of Croesus, and later fell victim to Stesagoras in retaliation.
amathusians: An Cypriot city-state that alone among the Cypriot cities refused to join Onesilus' revolt against Persian rule, subsequently defeated him in siege and later honored him as a hero.
olynthus: A Greek city on the Chalcidic peninsula in the Thermaic gulf region, originally held by Bottiaeans but captured and massacred by the Persian general Artabazus in 479 BC, after which it was given to the Chalcidians.
troezenians: A Greek people of the Peloponnese who contributed five ships to the Greek naval force against Persia and fought as hoplites at Plataea.
delphic: The inhabitants of Delphi, a sanctuary in central Greece sacred to Apollo, whose oracle delivered prophecies on matters of state and personal fate throughout the Greek world.
gargaphian: A spring near Plataea in Boeotia that served as the Greek army's water source before the battle of Plataea, until Persian cavalry blocked it, forcing the Greeks to plan a relocation.
melians: An Aegean island people of Lacedaemonian (Spartan) stock who alone among most islanders refused to submit to Persia and contributed two fifty-oared boats to the Greek fleet at Salamis.
malis: A region of central Greece bounded by mountains and a coastal gulf, lying between Thessaly to the north and the pass of Thermopylae to the south, where Xerxes' army camped before attacking the Greek defenders at Thermopylae.
ossa: A high mountain in Thessaly forming the eastern boundary of the Thessalian plain together with Mount Pelion, through which the Peneus River passes in a narrow gorge.
taenarus: A promontory in the southern Peloponnese (modern Cape Matapan) where, according to legend, the musician Arion was brought ashore by a dolphin after being cast overboard by Corinthian sailors, and where a bronze memorial to this event was erected.
telmessians: Interpreters of omens from Lydia whose prophecy that a foreign army would conquer Croesus' land proved accurate when Cyrus took Sardis.
arcadian: A people of the Peloponnese whose territory included the city of Tegea; they clashed with Sparta when the Spartans, deceived by an oracle, invaded Arcadia hoping to conquer them, but were instead defeated and enslaved.
olympian: Epithet applied to the gods' heavenly abode, and to the immortal Heracles as opposed to the dead hero of the same name.
phocaean: Greeks from Phocaea in Ionia who were allies of other Ionians against Persian expansion, and whose general Dionysius attempted to rally the Ionian fleet at Lade before its defeat.
cymaeans: A Greek city of Aeolia on the coast of Asia Minor, whose people consulted the oracle at Branchidae and chose to send away the fugitive Pactyes rather than surrender him to Persian demand or face siege.
mysia: A region in northwest Asia Minor east of Lesbos, including the district of Atarneus which the Chians received from the Persians in exchange for delivering up Pactyes, and through which Xerxes' army marched on its way to the Hellespont during the invasion of Greece.
phocian: An ancient people of central Greece occupying the Phocian territory between Thessaly and the Corinthian Gulf, remembered by Herodotus chiefly for building the wall and modifying the hot springs at Thermopylae to resist Thessalian invasion, and later for guiding the Persian army against their enemies.
chaldeans: A people of Babylonia, learned in religious practices and astronomy, who served as priests and experts in the temple of Marduk and fought in Xerxes' army against Greece.
sardo: An island in the western Mediterranean, the largest island known to the Greeks, proposed as a refuge and settlement by Bias of Priene and later by the Milesian rebels during the Ionian Revolt.
indian: A numerous eastern people with diverse languages, settlements, and customs—some nomadic, some marsh-dwelling—known for large fierce dogs and gold-dust tributes to the Persian king.
attic: Athenian; of or belonging to Athens and its territory, as in the Attic medimnus and choenix used for measuring grain.
boeotian: A Greek people inhabiting the region of Boeotia north of Attica, including the Thebans, who contested Plataean independence and later fought against the Athenians and their allies.
cretan: Inhabitants of Crete, some of whom ruled Carians and Lycians under Minos in legendary times, and one of whom later guided Theran colonists to Libya.
assuan: A city at the First Cataract of the Nile in southern Egypt, marking the traditional boundary between Egypt proper and Ethiopia.
samothracians: An Aegean island people dwelling on Samothrace who learned the rites of the Cabeiri from the Pelasgians and served in Xerxes' navy during the invasion of Greece, distinguished as skilled javelin-throwers.
illyria: A region in the northwest Balkans, west of Thrace, whose people practiced a distinctive custom of auctioning marriageable maidens and whose territory lay north of the Haemus mountain range where the Angrus river originated.
thesprotia: A region in northwestern Greece where the Oracle of the Dead on the river Acheron was located, consulted by Periander of Corinth concerning a deposit, and formerly called Pelasgia according to Herodotus' account of a Phoenician slave woman.
syrtis: A large gulf on the North African coast west of Egypt, inhabited by the Nasamones and Psylli, notorious for its dangerous shallows and as a boundary region in Herodotus' account of Libyan peoples and territories.
mediterranean: The sea separating Greece and Egypt, and bounding Europe, Asia, and Libya, across which trade and warfare connected the Greek world to the Near East and Egypt.
africa: The continent lying south and west of the Mediterranean, home to Libyan peoples and tribes whom Herodotus describes as nomadic coastal dwellers, interior beast-haunted regions, and desert oases, and from which Carthaginian forces under Amilcas threatened Sicily.
syrian: Inhabitants of Syria and Palestine, between Phoenicia and Egypt, later under Persian rule; Necos II defeated them at Magdolus and took Cadytis.
serbonian: The Serbonian marsh is a coastal wetland on Egypt's northeastern border, near the Casian promontory, said to be where Typho was hidden.
messenia: A region in the Peloponnese, south of Lacedaemon, against which the Lacedaemonians conducted military campaigns and to which they sent aid according to Samian tradition.
macrones: A people of the northeastern coast of Anatolia (near the Thermodon and Parthenius rivers) who learned circumcision from the Colchians and served as the nineteenth Persian satrapy under Xerxes, contributing troops to his invasion of Greece.
parthians: A people of Central Asia east of the Caspian Sea, subject to the Persian king, grouped with Chorasmians, Sogdi, and Arii in the sixteenth satrapy paying three hundred talents of tribute, and mustered under Artabazus in Xerxes' invasion army.
peloponnesus: The large southern peninsula of Greece, homeland of Sparta and other Greek city-states, from which Lacedaemonian and other Peloponnesian forces launched expeditions and campaigns throughout the narrative.
parian: An Aegean island people whose marble was prized for temples and treasuries, and whose city Miltiades besieged after Marathon, demanding tribute on the pretext that they had sent ships to the Persian fleet.
siphnus: An Aegean island famous for its gold and silver mines, whose wealth enabled a magnificent treasury at Delphi, but which was ravaged and forced to pay tribute by the Samians in the late sixth century BC after failing to heed an ambiguous Delphic oracle.
moschi: A people of the Caucasus region who formed the nineteenth satrapy under Persian rule, contributing three hundred talents to tribute and fielding troops equipped with wooden helmets and small long-pointed spears in Xerxes' invasion force.
borysthenites: Greek colonists claiming Milesian origin who inhabited a port city on the Scythian coast and served as a cultural bridge between Greek and Scythian worlds.
crimea: A peninsula in southern Scythia, bounded by the Maeetian lake and the sea, where Cimmerian walls and a ferry survive as monuments to the Cimmerian peoples' flight before the Scythian invasion.
azov: A bay and sea-strait on the north coast of Scythia at the mouth of the Maeetis (Sea of Azov), marking the eastern boundary of the Royal Scythians' territory and serving as a natural landmark in Herodotus' geographical description of Scythia.
perinthus: A Greek city on the European side of the Hellespont in Thrace, subdued by the Persian general Megabazus after resisting Darius' rule and weakened by prior conflict with the Paeonians.
chersonesus: A peninsula in the northeastern Aegean, extending into the Hellespont (modern Gallipoli), where Sestos was the chief city and which Darius left under Persian control under Megabazus, later besieged and captured by the Athenians under Xanthippus after Mykale.
theraean: Greeks from the island of Thera who, according to Herodotus, were instructed by the Delphic oracle to found a colony in Libya, which they eventually did under the leadership of Battus.
tauric: A non-Scythian people inhabiting a peninsular region of southern Scythia (modern Crimea) projecting into the Pontus, bordered by the territory of the Royal Scythians to the north and west.
calliste: An island in the Aegean Sea (later called Thera), originally settled by Phoenician descendants of Membliarus left there by Cadmus, which Theras of Sparta colonized with Lacedaemonian and Minyan settlers in the early archaic period.
alazones: A grain-cultivating people living in Scythia north of the Callippidae, dwelling between the Scythian farmers to their north and the region where the Tyras and Hypanis rivers converge.
cyrenaean: Greek colonists who settled Cyrene in Libya and became engaged in conflicts with neighboring Libyan peoples and internal dynastic struggles.
sybarites: The people of Sybaris, a wealthy Greek city in southern Italy destroyed by Croton, whom the Milesians mourned but who failed to reciprocate when Miletus fell to the Persians.
machlyes: A Libyan people dwelling on the shores of the Tritonian lake west of the Auseans, known for their use of lotus and their long hair worn behind.
armenians: A people rich in flocks living east of Cilicia and west of the Matieni in Asia, according to Aristagoras' description of the Persian Empire to Cleomenes of Sparta.
zanclaeans: Greek inhabitants of Zancle (modern Messina) in Sicily, whose city was seized by Samians in a conflict involving their king Scythes and the tyrant Hippocrates of Gela.
hysiae: A settlement in Boeotia on the border between Attica and Boeotia, near the Asopus river, contested between the Boeotians and Athenians during the early classical period.
caicus: A river of northwestern Asia Minor (Mysia) flowing through a fertile plain, significant as a boundary and route marker in the Ionian campaigns and Xerxes' invasion route.
erasinus: A river flowing from the Stymphalian lake through underground passage to emerge near Argos in the Peloponnese, where Cleomenes received unfavorable omens for crossing during his campaign against Argos.
apsinthians: A Thracian people inhabiting the Chersonese and its northern regions, who warred with the Dolonci and later sacrificed Persian fugitives in their traditional religious rites.
ilium: The region in northwestern Asia Minor (Troad) that was home to Troy and its territory, including the cities of Sigeum and the lands of the Aeolians and Trojans, which lay along the route of Xerxes' invasion and figured in Greek territorial disputes.
salaminians: Inhabitants of Salamis, the chief city of Cyprus, who joined Onesilus's revolt against Persia in 498 BC but later handed the city back to their former king Gorgus.
apidanus: A river of Thessaly in central Greece, flowing from the mountains surrounding the plain and joining the Peneus; notable for being exhausted by Xerxes' army during his invasion in 480 BC.
siris: A town in Paeonia (northern Macedonia) where Xerxes left sick men and the sacred chariot of Zeus during his retreat from Greece after 480 BC.
aphidnae: A deme (or town) of Attica in the territory of Athens, situated in the region where Helen was said to have been hidden during the Tyndarid invasion, and the home of notable Athenians including the polemarch Callimachus at Marathon.
mygdonian: A region in northern Greece east of the Thermaic gulf, bounded by the river Axius, through which Xerxes' Persian army marched and encamped during the invasion of Greece.
hermioneans: Greek people of Dryopian origin inhabiting Hermione in the Peloponnese, driven out of Doris by Herakles and the Malians, who contributed three ships to the Greek fleet against Persia.
ampraciots: A Greek people from Ambracia (in northwestern Greece near the Ambracian Gulf), who contributed seven ships at Artemisium and five hundred hoplites to the Greek force at Plataea.
scione: A town on the peninsula of Pallene (formerly Phlegra) in northern Greece that supplied ships to Xerxes' fleet and was home to the diver Scyllias and the general Timoxenus, who plotted to betray Potidaea to the Persians.
malian: A people inhabiting the region of Malis in central Greece near Thermopylae, notable for the traitor Epialtes of Malis who revealed to Xerxes the mountain path that allowed the Persians to outflank the Greek defenders.
anticyra: A coastal town in Malis at the northern entrance to the gulf of the sea, near the mouth of the river Spercheus, notable as the birthplace of the scout Polyas and the home of Corydallus, whom some accused of betraying the mountain path to Xerxes.
malians: A people of central Greece (Thessaly region) who discovered the mountain path by which the Persians outflanked the Greeks at Thermopylae, and who later fought on the Persian side at Plataea.
decelea: A town in Attica north of Athens, whose people were said to have revealed Helen's hiding place to the sons of Tyndareus, earning them perpetual exemption from dues and chief seats at feasts in Sparta.
leucadians: Dorians from Corinth who contributed three ships to the Greek fleet at Salamis and, together with the Anactorians, eight hundred men to the battle line at Plataea against Mardonius' invasion.
aea: A city of Colchis in the eastern Caucasus region, on the river Phasis, from which Jason sailed to fetch the Golden Fleece and whence Cytissorus traveled to rescue Athamas.
ephesians: Greeks inhabiting Ephesus on the Ionian coast of Asia Minor, who dedicated their city to Artemis when besieged by Croesus, later participated in the Ionian Revolt against Persia, and mistakenly slew Chian refugees during the Persian Wars.
erythraeans: One of the Ionian cities on the mainland coast of Asia Minor, speaking the same dialect as Chios, and contributing eight ships to the Ionian fleet against the Persians at the Battle of Lade.
chian: An Aegean people living on the island of Chios, notable for their seafaring and craftsmanship, and involved in conflicts during the Ionian Revolt and earlier Lydian dealings.
plataean: Inhabitants of Plataea, a city-state in Boeotia near Athens, who fought with the Greek alliance against Persia and helped defeat Mardonius' army at the battle of Plataea in 479 BC.
pindus: A mountain range forming the western boundary of Thessaly and lying in the region from which the Dorian Greeks migrated southward to the Peloponnese.
creston: A city in the region above Tyrrhenia inhabited by Pelasgians who retained their ancient non-Greek language distinct from their neighbors' speech.
hermus: A river of Lydia in western Asia Minor, flowing from Mount Dindymene past Sardis and receiving the Pactolus before emptying into the sea near Phocaea, associated with the battle between Croesus and Cyrus and with the burning of Sardis during the Ionian revolt.
pasargadae: The chief Persian tribe from which the Achaemenid royal house descended; they revolted against the Medes under Cyrus and provided leaders like Badres for later Persian military campaigns.
crathis: A river in Achaea (northwestern Peloponnese), whose name was later taken by a river in Italy, and by which the Achaean city of Aegae was located.
ida: A mountain in northwestern Asia Minor (Mysia/Troas region) near Ilium, notable as a landmark on Xerxes' invasion route and as part of the territory of Aeolian cities.
cilician: An Asiatic people living in the region of southern Asia Minor (modern Turkey) along the Mediterranean coast, whose king Syennesis mediated peace between Lydia and Media, and whose ships participated in Xerxes' invasion fleet.
tyrrhenia: The region in Italy inhabited by the Tyrrhenians (Etruscans), whom Herodotus believed were colonists from Lydia who migrated westward during a famine under the leadership of Tyrrhenus.
gadira: A place near the Pillars of Heracles, by which lay Erythea, the island of Geryones, on the shore of Ocean.
adriatic-sea: A sea in the far northwest of the known world, marking the westernmost limit of the route by which votive offerings travel from the Hyperboreans to Delos, and the approximate eastern boundary of lands beyond the Danube.
termilae: A people of Crete who migrated to Asia Minor under Sarpedon, initially called Termilae, later renamed Lycians after Lycus of Athens joined their settlement.
teians: An Ionian Greek people of Asia Minor who fled Teos to escape Harpagus's forces and settled at Abdera in Thrace, and later fought with seventeen ships at the naval battle of Lade in the Ionian Revolt.
achelous: A large river of northwestern Greece flowing through Acarnania into the sea, notable for its silt-deposition which has converted the Echinades Islands partly into mainland, and marking the western boundary of lion country in Europe.
cadmean: A pyrrhic victory; the term derives from Cadmus and the Theban dynasty (as seen in inscriptions at Thebes), and came to mean a victory gained at ruinous cost.
xanthus: A city in Lycia (southwestern Asia Minor) whose male population perished en masse resisting Harpagus' Persian conquest, leaving it to be repopulated by foreigners.
daphnae: A fortified Egyptian post at the apex of the Nile Delta facing Arabia and Assyria, established by Psammetichus as a defensive garrison and still held by Persian guards in Herodotus' time.
cercasorus: A city on the Nile marking the apex of the Delta, where the river splits into the Pelusian and Canobic branches.
pelusian: The easternmost branch of the Nile in the Delta, near which Ionian and Carian settlers lived under Psammetichus and where Psammenitus later encamped to meet Cambyses.
caunians: A people inhabiting Caunus in southwestern Anatolia, neighbors of the Carians and Lycians, who according to their own tradition came from Crete but whose customs and speech diverged markedly from their neighbors, and who resisted Persian conquest under Harpagus by largely following the Lycian example of mass self-destruction.
cadytis: A major city of Syrian Palestine on the coast between Phoenicia and Egypt, captured by the Egyptian king Necos II and serving as a boundary marker in Herodotus' description of the approach to Egypt.
prosopitis: An island in the Nile Delta, about nine schoeni in circumference, containing multiple towns including Atarbekhis; it supplied boats for collecting the bones of dead cattle for burial, and provided warriors for the Egyptian military class.
celts: A European people living beyond the Pillars of Heracles near the Cynesii/Cynetes, from whose land the Ister (Danube) rises and flows across Europe into the Euxine Sea.
hermotubies: One of two divisions of Egyptian professional warriors, numbering up to 160,000 at peak strength, recruited from the districts of Busiris, Saïs, Khemmis, Papremis, Prosopitis, and half of Natho, exempt from all trades and taxation, with a thousand annually serving as the king's bodyguard.
cydonia: A city on the northwestern coast of Crete, founded by Samian exiles fleeing Polycrates' tyranny, where they prospered for five years before being defeated and enslaved by Aeginetans and Cretans.
achaean: Greek people of the Peloponnese who never left that peninsula but migrated within it to occupy another people's land.
kalasiries: One of two divisions of Egyptian warriors, the Kalasiries were stationed in twelve districts of the Nile Valley and at their peak numbered 250,000 men, holding hereditary military service and tax-exempt farmland as their privilege.
ienysus: A coastal city in Palestine marking the boundary between Arabian and Syrian territory, situated west of the Serbonian marsh on the approach to Egypt.
magnesians: Greek people of Magnesia in Thessaly who paid tribute to the Persians and contributed forces to Xerxes' invasion of Greece.
paricanians: A people of the Persian empire, dwelling in Media, who served as mounted troops in Xerxes' invasion army and paid tribute to Darius.
caspatyrus: A town in the Pactyic region of northwestern India near the Indus River, from which Darius I sent Scylax to sail down the Indus and around to Egypt.
tibareni: A people of the eastern Black Sea coast who, together with the Moschi and others, formed the nineteenth Persian satrapy and contributed contingents to Xerxes' invasion army.
dnieper: A major river of southern Scythia, also called the Borysthenes, whose daughter in Scythian legend mothered Targitaüs, the supposed ancestor of the Scythian people.
metapontines: Greeks inhabiting Metapontum in southern Italy, who according to legend received a visitation from the apotheosized Aristeas and erected a shrine to Apollo on his instruction.
crotoniats: Greeks of the Italian city Croton who resisted Persian attempts to recapture the escaped physician Democedes and later disputed whether they received aid from the Spartan Dorieus or only the Elean diviner Callias in their war against Sybaris.
mossynoeci: A people of the Black Sea coast (modern Georgia/Turkey region) who formed the nineteenth Persian tax province with the Moschi, Tibareni, Macrones, and Mares, contributing three hundred talents annually and serving in Xerxes' invasion army with wooden helmets and spear-armed equipment.
pactyic: A people inhabiting a region in northwestern India near Caspatyrus, noted for their martial prowess and their role in collecting gold-bearing sand from desert ants during the Persian imperial period.
