iapygia: A region in southern Italy (the heel of the peninsula) where Persian sailors were wrecked and enslaved, and where Cretans driven ashore by storm founded the town of Hyria and became the Messapians.
hyperborean: A legendary people said by poets to live beyond the north wind, known to Greeks chiefly through cult practices at Delos where maidens from that land allegedly died and received ritual honors from Delian girls.
delian: A Greek people inhabiting the sacred island of Delos, who maintained that Hyperborean offerings passed through their island on a long relay journey from the far north and honored two Hyperborean maidens who died there with a commemorative hair-cutting custom.
tenians: An Aegean island-people whose trireme deserted the Persian fleet at Salamis with news that enabled the Greeks to fight the decisive naval battle, and were subsequently honored at Delphi alongside other victors over the barbarian.
calchedon: A Greek city on the Asiatic shore of the Bosporus, opposite Byzantium, founded seventeen years before Byzantium and notable for its inferior location relative to its rival.
gerrhus: A river of Scythia that branches from the Borysthenes and flows southeast through the lands of the Nomads and Royal Scythians before joining the Hypacuris.
troad: A region of northwestern Asia Minor along the Hellespont, containing the city of Sigeum and formerly inhabited by Aeolians and remnants of Trojans, which the Persians conquered under Otanes and Hymaees.
carystus: A city of Euboea that received and forwarded sacred offerings from the Hyperboreans to Delos, and was later ravaged by the Greeks after their victory at Salamis.
exampaeus: A region in Scythia between the Borysthenes and Hypanis rivers, notable for a bitter salt spring that spoils the Hypanis and for a colossal bronze vessel supposedly forged from arrowheads by King Ariantas as a population census memorial.
ceos: An Aegean island off the coast of Attica, positioned near Salamis and Cynosura, from which Persian forces operated during the naval battle of Salamis (480 BC).
byzantines: Greek colonists dwelling on the European side of the Bosporus who founded their city and faced Persian domination; they later fled to Mesambria during the Phoenician campaign and repurposed Darius' marble pillars for their temple of Artemis.
cyzicenes: A Greek city on the southern coast of the Propontis (Sea of Marmara), whose inhabitants voluntarily submitted to Persian rule before the Phoenician attacks of 492 BC and thus were spared destruction.
sestos: A city on the European side of the Hellespont in the Chersonese, strategically important as a crossing point between Europe and Asia and later captured by the Athenians under Xanthippus.
tearus: A river in Thrace with thirty-eight medicinal springs renowned for healing, flowing through a tributary system into the Hebrus and ultimately the sea near Aenus, where Darius I camped and erected a commemorative pillar during his Scythian campaign.
auschisae: A Libyan people dwelling inland of Barce and extending to the coast at Euhesperidae, living west of the Asbystae in the region of Cyrenaica.
aziris: A place in Libya with groves and a river, where early Greek colonists from Thera first settled for six years before being persuaded by local Libyans to move westward.
lepreum: A city in the Peloponnese, established by Minyae who were driven out of Laconia, later conquered by the Eleans, and contributed two hundred men to the Greek force at Plataea.
teugetum: A mountain or high place in Laconia where the Minyae (descendants of the Argonauts) twice encamped after being expelled from Lemnos and before their eventual dispersal to various colonies.
augila: An oasis in the Libyan desert southeast of the Nasamones' coastal territory, known for its salt hill, springs, and abundant date palms, which the Nasamones visited seasonally to harvest fruit.
mantinea: A city-state in Arcadia in the Peloponnese, known for producing the mediator Demonax who reformed Cyrene's government, and whose hoplites fought at Plataea though they arrived after the main battle.
lotus-eaters: A people living on a headland in Libya west of Egypt, subsisting on the lotus fruit which they also ferment into wine.
macae: A Libyan people inhabiting the coastal region west of the Nasamones in North Africa, known for their distinctive crested hairstyles and ostrich-skin shields, who expelled the Spartan colonist Dorieus from the Cinyps river valley.
cynosarges: A sanctuary of Heracles in Attica near Athens, where the Athenian army encamped after the Battle of Marathon.
memnonian: Memnonian is an epithet applied to Susa, the Persian king's residence, rather than a people.
teucrians: A people of Asia Minor (Mysia region) who, along with the Mysians, crossed the Bosporus into Europe in ancient times, subdued the Thracians, and drove them southward until they themselves were displaced back across the Strymon by Thracian pressure.
pylos: A coastal region in the Peloponnese in Lacedaemonian (Spartan) territory, where the Corcyraeans anchored their ships during the Persian Wars, and the legendary home of Melampus before he traveled to Argos.
lemnians: An Aegean people who inhabited the island of Lemnos and also settled in the Peloponnese (specifically the Paroreatae region); they resisted Persian conquest under Darius but were eventually subdued, and some migrated to mainland Greece.
prasiad-lake: A lake in Paeonia near the Pangaean mountains whose pile-dwelling inhabitants resisted Persian subjugation under Megabazus.
pieria: A coastal region of Macedonia in northern Greece where Xerxes' army encamped before advancing, prompting the Greeks to move to defend Thermopylae and Artemisium.
gephyraeans: A Phoenician people who settled in Tanagra in Boeotia with Cadmus, were expelled by the Boeotians, and migrated to Athens where they became citizens under restrictions and introduced the alphabet to Greece.
petra: A township in the territory of Corinth, where Eetion dwelt and where the Bacchiadae sent men to kill the infant who would become the tyrant Cypselus.
pythians: Ambassadors appointed by the Spartan kings to represent Lacedaemon at the oracle of Delphi, who dined at public expense and had access to all oracular pronouncements.
amathus: A city in Cyprus that resisted the Ionian Revolt and refused to join Onesilus' uprising against Persian rule, successfully defending itself against his siege.
brygi: A Thracian people who inhabited the regions of Macedonia and Thrace, notable for attacking and wounding Mardonius and his Persian army by night, though they were subsequently subjugated by the Persians and later forced to supply troops to Xerxes' invasion of Greece.
fair-coast: A coastal region in Sicily facing the Tyrrhenian Sea, which the Zanclaeans invited Ionian settlers to colonize, though the Samians were diverted from settling there and instead seized Zancle itself.
asopus-river: A river in Boeotia forming the boundary between Theban and Plataean territory, and later the position of Mardonius' Persian army camp during the invasion of Greece.
styx: A river in Arcadia in the Peloponnese, near the city of Nonacris, whose water was held sacred for oath-taking and was believed to have supernatural power, as Cleomenes used it to bind Arcadian leaders to his cause.
styrians: An Aegean island people of Dryopian stock who contributed two ships to the Greek fleet at Artemisium and Salamis during the Persian Wars.
caspians: A people of the Caspian region whose infantry carried reed bows and short swords, and whose cavalry were equipped identically to their foot soldiers; they served in Xerxes' invasion army under the command of Ariomardus.
black-river: A river in Malis (central Greece), flowing into the sea near Trachis, about twenty furlongs south of the river Dyras; Xerxes' army crossed it during their march through Greece.
crestonaean: A people of inland Thrace whose territory lay between the Paeonian lands and the Mygdonian plain, through which the river Cheidorus rose and flowed.
arians: A people of Central Asia who formerly bore the name "Arians" before being renamed "Medes" according to their own tradition; they served in Xerxes' invasion army equipped with Median bows under the command of Sisamnes son of Hydarnes.
cissians: A people of the Persian Empire who wore turbans, were commanded by Anaphes son of Otanes, and fought alongside the Medes against the Greeks at Thermopylae.
bermius: A mountain in Macedonia, rising above the legendary garden of Midas, too high and cold to be climbed, from which the sons of Temenus descended after settling there and subsequently conquered the rest of Macedonia.
pangaean-range: A high mountain range in Thrace between the territories of the Pierians, Odomanti, and Satrae to the south and the Paeonians, Doberes, and Paeoplae to the north, rich in gold and silver mines, through which Xerxes' army marched westward during his invasion of Greece.
pierians: A Thracian people near Mount Pangaeum whose territory Xerxes passed through, and who contributed land forces to his invasion of Greece; the gold and silver mines of the region belonged to the Pierians, Odomanti, and Satrae.
enipeus: A river of Thessaly, flowing from the surrounding mountains into the central vale and eventually joining the Peneus, the main river draining Thessaly to the sea.
tempe: A narrow mountain pass in Thessaly between the peaks Olympus and Ossa, through which the river Peneus flows, forming the main gateway from Macedonia into Thessaly and strategically vital to the defence against Xerxes' invasion in 480 BC.
perrhaebi: A people of Thessaly near Gonnus, through whose territory Xerxes' army passed on the upper route into Thessaly.
sepiad: A headland in Magnesia on the Thessalian (Magnesian) coast where Xerxes' Persian fleet anchored before a storm wrecked many of his ships.
andrians: An Aegean island people who initially sided with Persia against the Greeks and later refused Themistocles' demand for money, resulting in their island's siege by the Greek fleet.
casthanaea: A coastal city in Magnesia on the eastern shore of Thessaly, between which and the Sepiad headland the Persian fleet beached and was partially destroyed by storm in 480 BC.
seriphians: A small Ionian people from Athens living on the island of Seriphos, who alone among islanders refused to submit to Xerxes and fought at Salamis with a single fifty-oared boat.
alpeni: A village near Thermopylae in Locris, at the narrowest part of the pass into central Greece, where the Greek forces expected to obtain supplies during the Persian Wars.
phlius: A Greek city-state of the Peloponnese that contributed two hundred hoplites to the Greek force at Thermopylae and one thousand men at Plataea, stationed opposite the Bactrians.
potidaeans: A Greek city-state in Pallene (peninsula of northern Greece) that contributed three hundred hoplites to the Greek alliance at Plataea and defended itself against the Persian siege under Artabazus, claiming divine aid from Poseidon in drowning the invaders.
psyttalea: A small island lying between Salamis and the Greek mainland where Xerxes stationed Persian troops to rescue survivors and kill enemies during the naval battle, until Aristides led Athenian hoplites across to massacre them.
europus: A town in Macedonia, home to Mys, whom Mardonius sent to consult Greek oracles during his winter quarters in Thessaly after the Persian invasion of 480 BC.
oeroe: A river in Boeotia near Plataea that divides into two channels around a dry-land island, named (by local tradition) after a daughter of Asopus, where the Greek allied forces planned to reposition during the Persian Wars to secure water and avoid Persian cavalry.
persian-gulf: A body of water bordering Persia to the south, sometimes called the Red Sea by Herodotus.
bithynians: A Thracian people who crossed into Asia Minor (where they became known as Bithynians), formerly called Strymonians when they dwelt by the Strymon river, subsequently subjugated by Croesus and later commanded by Bassaces in Xerxes' invasion of Greece.
mariandynians: A people of northern Asia Minor (Paphlagonia region) who paid tribute to Croesus and later to Darius I as part of the Persian empire.
asiatic: A geographical designation for the peoples and lands of western Asia Minor and the Near East, including the Lydians and other kingdoms east of the Aegean, distinguished from Libya and Europe by the rivers Nile and Phasis.
phthia: A region in Thessaly in northern Greece, legendary home of the Hellenic people in the time of Deucalion and later inhabited by the Achaeans, who submitted to Persia during the Persian Wars.
ionic: Greek peoples of Ionian stock, chiefly the Athenians, whom Herodotus counts among the foremost Greek races, originally of Pelasgian descent.
pelasgic: An ancient pre-Greek people of the Aegean region whose language differed from Greek, many of whom merged with early Hellenic populations, and whose defensive walls were later used in Athens during conflicts.
histiaean: An ancient Greek people of Thessaly who inhabited the region under Mount Ossa and Olympus before the Hellenic Dorians were driven out by the Cadmeans and migrated southward.
dryopia: A region in central Greece from which the Hellenic (later Dorian) people migrated southward into the Peloponnese.
acarnanian: A people inhabiting the region of Acarnania in northwestern Greece, represented in Herodotus' narrative by individuals such as the diviner Amphilytus (who prophesied to Pisistratus) and the seer Megistias (who served at Thermopylae).
placia: A city on the Hellespont (Dardanelles) originally inhabited by Pelasgians, whose inhabitants later migrated to Athens and retained a non-Greek language distinct from their neighbors.
pterian: A people inhabiting the region of Pteria in Cappadocia (the strongest part of that country, near Sinope on the Euxine), whom Croesus conquered and enslaved during his campaign against Cyrus.
cappadocians: An inland people of central Asia Minor called Syrians by the Greeks, subjects first of the Medes and then of Cyrus, dwelling east of Paphlagonia beyond the river Halys and noted for their wealth in flocks and produce.
thyreae: A contested border territory between Argos and Sparta that the Lacedaemonians seized and held, site of the famous battle of the three hundred where Sparta's victory established their control over it.
greeks-syrians: A people dwelling in Cappadocia (inland Asia Minor east of the Halys river), called Syrians by Greeks but Cappadocians by themselves, subjects first of the Medes and then of Cyrus and the Persians.
mardian: A Persian tribe; one of its members, Hyroeades, first scaled the unguarded acropolis of Sardis, enabling the city's capture by Cyrus.
ombrici: An Italian people dwelling inland north of the Adriatic, through whose country rivers including the Carpis and Alpis flowed northward to the Danube, and among whom the Lydian emigrants (later called Tyrrhenians) settled after fleeing famine.
mardi: A Persian tribe of wandering herdsmen who inhabited regions of central or eastern Persia.
myus: An Ionian city in Caria, situated between Miletus and Priene, speaking the same dialect as those two cities and participating in the Ionian revolt against Persian rule.
median: A people of the Iranian plateau unified by Deioces into a single nation, comprising six tribes (Busae, Paretaceni, Struchates, Arizanti, Budii, and Magi), who served as major cavalry and infantry forces in the Persian armies of Xerxes.
colchi: A people inhabiting the land at the eastern end of the Black Sea near the river Phasis, located between the Maeetian lake and Media, whom Herodotus places on the route of Scythian expansion into Asia.
roman: A people of Italy (the Tyrrhenians, formerly Lydians who emigrated under Tyrrhenus) who, according to Herodotus, were encountered by the Phocaeans and participated in drawing lots for prisoners of war.
triopian: Dorian Greeks of the southwestern coast of Asia Minor (the "Five Cities" of Lindus, Ialysus, Camirus, Cos, and Cnidus) who shared a sanctuary of Apollo and enforced strict rules against misuse of sacred offerings.
sea-of-azov: A large shallow sea north of the Black Sea, bounded by the Tauric (Crimean) peninsula and the Caucasus, which served as a geographical reference point for Scythian movements and migrations.
sagartii: A Persian tribe of wandering herdsmen who, along with the Dai, Mardi, and Dropici, formed part of the Persian tribal confederacy subject to the Pasargadae, and were later incorporated into the fourteenth satrapy of the Persian Empire paying six hundred talents in tribute.
halicarnassians: Dorian inhabitants of Halicarnassus in Asia Minor, expelled from the Triopian temple alliance for sacrilege, whose ranks included the naval commander Artemisia in Xerxes' fleet.
molossians: An Epirote tribe of northwestern Greece whose representative Alcon competed in the bride-contest of Agariste at Athens.
aegiroessa: An Aeolian city on the coast of Asia Minor, one of eleven ancient settlements of the Aeolians in the region.
lycian: An Anatolian people of the southwestern coast (modern-day Turkey), some of whose kings among certain Ionian cities claimed descent from Glaucus son of Hippolochus, and whose bow type was used by other contingents in Xerxes' army.
oenussae: Small islands near Chios in the Aegean, which the Chians refused to sell the Phocaeans, who then departed from there for Cyrnus.
cadiz: A port city on the coast of Iberia near the Strait of Heracles (Pillars of Heracles), known to the Greeks as Gadira and associated in mythology with Heracles' labour to fetch the cattle of Geryones.
caucones: A people of the Peloponnese (in the region of Pylos) who were driven out of their homeland by Minyae refugees and subsequently displaced to other territories.
alalia: A city on the island of Cyrnus (Corsica) founded by Phocaean Greeks under divine command, which they abandoned after a costly naval victory against Tyrrhenians and Carthaginians.
agyllaioi: An Etruscan people inhabiting the city of Agylla in Italy, who stoned Phocaean Greek sailors and subsequently honored them with religious rites and games in expiation of the deed.
agylla: A city in Tyrrhenian (Etruscan) territory in Italy, whose inhabitants stoned Phocaean Greek sailors and were thereafter cursed until they instituted perpetual religious honors for their victims.
milyan: The Milyans were the earlier inhabitants (also called Solymi) of the land later held by the Lycians, whom Sarpedon and his followers, exiles from Crete, came to rule.
cnidian: Greek colonists from Lacedaemon who inhabited the Triopion peninsula in southwestern Asia Minor and attempted to fortify themselves by digging a trench across the isthmus to make their territory an island when Harpagus invaded Ionia, but abandoned the effort after a Delphic oracle's warning and subsequently submitted to him without resistance.
milyans: An Anatolian people inhabiting the region later called Lycia in southwestern Asia Minor, who were ultimately absorbed into or became known as the Lycians after the arrival of Sarpedon from Crete and later Lycus from Athens, and who paid tribute to Darius as part of the first satrapy of the Persian empire.
caunus: A city in Caria (southwestern Asia Minor) that submitted to Harpagus during the Persian conquest but later joined the Ionian Revolt after the burning of Sardis.
pedaseans: An inland Carian people dwelling above Halicarnassus who resisted Harpagus' conquest longer than any other nearby group, fortifying the hill of Lide until finally overcome.
baal: Babylonian deity identified by Herodotus with Zeus, called "Belus" in the Histories, worshipped in a great shrine atop an eight-towered ziggurat where a chosen woman spent the night.
chaldaeans: Priests of Zeus Belus in Babylon who maintained the great temple and its rituals, including the selection of a native woman to sleep in the shrine.
ardericca: An Assyrian village on the Euphrates, made notable by Queen Nitocris's diversion of the river so that it passed the village three times; later also a domain in the Cissian land where King Darius settled captive Eretrians.
acarnania: A region of northwestern Greece through which the Achelous river flows and deposits sediment to form islands, marking the western boundary of the range of lions in Europe.
casian-mountain: A mountain near the Serbonian marsh on the northeastern coast of Egypt, marking the border between Syria-Palestine and Egypt.
caspian-sea: A vast inland sea bounded to the north by the lands of the Medes and Saspires, into which the Araxes river flows, and not connected to the outer ocean that surrounds the world.
nile-valley: The river valley of the Nile in Egypt, extending from Heliopolis southward for fourteen days' journey and bounded by Arabian mountains to the east and Libyan mountains to the west, which forms the narrow habitable core of Egypt and depends entirely on the river's annual flooding for agriculture.
arabian-mountains: A mountain range running north–south along Egypt's eastern border, yielding frankincense at its eastern edge and quarried for stone to build the pyramids.
syene: A city in the Thebaid (Upper Egypt), located between the Cataracts and Elephantine, serving as a reference point for the southern boundary of Egypt proper.
eneti: An Illyrian people known for an annual marriage-market custom where maidens were publicly sold to prospective husbands, with proceeds from selling the beautiful subsidizing dowries for the plain or disabled; also mentioned as dwelling on the Adriatic Sea, their territory lying beyond the Ister River in the north.
marea: A fortified Egyptian settlement on the western border near Libya, garrisoned as a watchpost against Libyan incursion in the reign of Psammetichus and still held by the Persians in Herodotus' time.
canobus: A town at the Canobic mouth of the Nile in the Delta, on the route by which ships from the sea sailed inland to Naucratis.
canobic-mouth: The westernmost natural mouth of the Nile Delta, to which traders unable to sail directly to Naucratis were required to divert.
deserters: Egyptian soldiers who revolted from Psammetichus after three years of unreturned garrison duty at Elephantine, migrated to Ethiopia with their leader's army (numbering 240,000 fighting men), and settled there at the king's invitation, subsequently adopting Egyptian customs and intermarrying with the local population.
ammonian: A Libyan people inhabiting an oasis in the Libyan desert (the site of the oracle of Ammon) who reported to Herodotus that a Persian army sent by Cambyses was buried by a sandstorm while marching against them from Oasis.
istria: A city at the mouth of the Ister (Danube) river on the Euxine (Black) Sea, founded by Milesian colonists.
mendesian-district: An administrative district in Lower Egypt whose inhabitants held goats sacred, especially the he-goat associated with Pan, and sacrificed sheep rather than goats, in contrast to the Theban district.
mendesians: An Egyptian people of the Mendesian district in the Nile Delta who revered Pan and sacred goats, particularly one sacred he-goat, and held goatherds in high regard.
samothrace: An island in the northern Aegean Sea off Thrace, formerly inhabited by Pelasgians who transmitted to its inhabitants the mystery rites of the Cabeiri.
phasis-river: A river flowing into the northern (Black) sea that forms the boundary of Colchis in the far northeast, mentioned as a landmark of Sesostris' Egyptian campaign and as the limit of Persian-dominated territories toward the north.
nysa: An Ethiopian region beyond Egypt, sacred to Dionysus, whose inhabitants gave periodic gifts rather than tribute to the Persian king.
cabeiri: A mystery cult practiced by the Samothracians (who learned it from the Pelasgians), whose rites and sacred images were kept secret and known only to initiates.
tyrian: Inhabitants of Tyre in Phoenicia, whose priests preserved ancient temple records and whose ancestors settled colonies (notably in Thasos) in search of the mythical Europa, after whom the continent came to be named.
magdolus: A town in Syria where Pharaoh Neco II defeated the Syrian army before capturing Cadytis.
casian: A promontory marking the boundary between Egypt and Syria, near the Serbonian marsh.
azotus: A major city in Syria that withstood Psammetichus' siege for twenty-nine years, the longest recorded siege known to Herodotus.
barca: A Libyan city west of Cyrene that, along with Cyrene, submitted to Cambyses after his conquest of Egypt and was incorporated into the Persian tax-province of Egypt.
dadicae: A people of Central Asia, grouped with the Gandarians and others in Persia's seventh satrapy and in Xerxes' invasion force, equipped after the Bactrian fashion.
pitana: A district or subdivision of Sparta, whose battalion was commanded by Amompharetus at the Battle of Plataea.
caspii: A people of the Caspian region who, along with the Pausicae, Pantimathi, and Daritae, formed the eleventh satrapy under Darius, contributing two hundred talents in tribute.
zacynthians: Greeks of the island Zacynthus off the west coast of the Peloponnesus, who harbored the exiled Spartan king Demaratus when Lacedaemon pursued him, refusing to surrender him to his pursuers.
thamanaei: A people of inland Asia who lived at the boundaries of Chorasmia, Hyrcania, and Parthia, grouped in the Persian fourteenth tax-district and subject to Persian control of water from the river Aces.
halicarnassian: Greeks of Dorian stock inhabiting the city of Halicarnassus on the coast of Caria in Asia Minor, who supplied ships and fighters to both Egyptian and Persian forces in Herodotus' narrative.
eridanus: A river supposedly flowing into the northern sea, from which amber was believed to come, but which Herodotus doubts exists and suspects is merely a Greek poetic invention.
hyrcanians: A people living in Asia near the Chorasmians, Parthians, and Sarangians, dependent on the river Aces for irrigation until Persian kings controlled its water-gates; later they provided troops for Xerxes' invasion of Greece under the command of Megapanus.
dascyleium: A Persian provincial capital located in northwestern Asia Minor (the Hellespont region), whose governor Mitrobates was killed by Oroetes during the confusion after Cambyses' death.
heraeum: A sanctuary of Hera in Samos, where Polycrates' scribe Maeandrius later dedicated the furnishings of his master's house.
borysthenes-river: A major river of Scythia flowing from the north through pastoral and farming lands toward the Black Sea, second only to the Nile in productivity and abundance of fish and sturgeon.
geryones: A mythical monster who dwelt on the island of Erythea beyond the Pillars of Heracles, whose cattle Heracles drove away, an episode Pontic Greeks linked to the origin of the Scythians.
artace: A town in the region of Proconnesus in the Hellespont, burnt by the Phoenician fleet during Darius' European campaign.
italian: A people inhabiting the Italian peninsula, mentioned by Herodotus only in the context of the Metapontines and in geographical comparisons with Scythian and Calabrian territories.
panticapes: A river in Scythia east of the Borysthenes, forming the eastern boundary of the Scythian farmers' territory, and counted among the major rivers of the region.
callippidae: Hellenized Scythians inhabiting the region north of the Borysthenes' midpoint on the Scythian coast, distinguished from pastoral Scythians by their cultivation and consumption of grain and vegetables.
paeonian: A people dwelling in the interior regions north of Greece (between Thrace and Macedon), through whose territory Xerxes' army marched en route to Thermae during the Persian invasion.
thyssagetae: A numerous nation of hunters living north of the Budini in the steppes beyond a seven-day desolate zone, through whose territory four major rivers flow toward the Maeetian Lake.
olen: Olen of Lycia was a man, not a place, who composed hymns sung at Delos, including those invoking the goddesses Opis and Arge.
indus: A major river in Asia, second only to the Nile in producing crocodiles, whose mouth and course Darius explored by sending Scylax downriver to the sea, after which he subjugated the Indians and used the sea for navigation.
black-sea: A vast northern sea bounded by the Bosporus to the south, extending to Colchis in the east, measuring roughly 11,100 stades in length and 3,300 in breadth at its widest point, which Darius I inspected during his Scythian campaign.
borystheneitae: Greek colonists settled at Olbia on the Hypanis river in Scythia, who called themselves Borystheneïtae after the nearby Borysthenes river.
hypacuris: A river of southern Scythia that flows into the sea, into which the Gerrhus also empties; one of the major waterways of the Scythian land.
cimmerian-bosporus: A strait in the far north connecting the Maeetian lake to the Black Sea, which freezes solid in winter and lies west of Scythian territory.
naparis: A Scythian river that flows into the Danube (Ister), one of five major tributaries from the Scythian lands that increase the river's volume.
tauric-chersonese: A mountainous peninsula in Scythia inhabited by the Tauric people, projecting into the Pontus east of the city of Carcinitis, comparable in shape to Attica's Sunium or Calabria's promontory between Brundisium and Tarentum.
ararus: A Scythian river, one of five tributaries flowing between the Porata and Tiarantus to join the Ister (Danube).
carcine: A city in Scythia near the mouth of the Hypacuris river, marking the boundary between the Woodland region and the Racecourse of Achilles.
tiarantus: A river of Scythia, the second of five major tributaries flowing into the Ister from the east, smaller than the Pyretus and located west of it.
haemus: A mountain range in Thrace and the Balkans, running east-west and forming a major watershed from which several tributaries of the Danube flow northward.
racecourse-of-achilles: A coastal region of Scythia along the Black Sea, named after the legendary hero Achilles and located near the mouth of the Hypacuris river.
rhodope: A mountain range in Thrace, source of the Cius river which flows through Haemus into the Ister.
ordessus: A river in Scythia, one of five tributaries that join the Ister and help maintain its volume year-round.
hebrus: A river of Thrace that flows through the plain of Doriscus and empties into the sea near the city of Aenus, significant as a landmark of the region through which Xerxes' army passed during his invasion of Greece.
syrgis: A river flowing through the territory of the Thyssagetae into the Maeetian Lake, in the region north of the Budini and east of Scythia.
gerrhi: A Scythian tribe dwelling at the farthest navigable point of the Borysthenes river, where Scythian kings were buried in elaborate tombs.
thracian-bosporus: The straits separating Europe and Asia Minor (modern Bosporus), which Darius bridged to cross into Thrace during his Scythian campaign.
agrianes: A Thracian people dwelling in the region east of the Strymon river and near the Pangaean mountains, who resisted subjugation by the Persian general Megabazus.
dark-rocks: A pair of rocky formations at the entrance to the Pontus (Black Sea), traditionally believed by Greeks to have once moved, which Darius viewed during his crossing into Europe.
maeetian: A people inhabiting the region around the Maeetian Lake (also called the Maeetian Sea), north of the Black Sea and east of the Scythians, through whose territory four major rivers flowed.
aenus: A city on the coast of Thrace where the Hebrus river empties into the sea, situated on the route of Xerxes' invasion force marching westward through the region.
brauron: A coastal sanctuary in Attica sacred to Artemis, where Athenian women gathered for a festival and were seized by Pelasgians from Lemnos seeking vengeance on Athens.
calchedonians: A Greek city-state on the Asiatic shore of the Bosporus, founded seventeen years before Byzantium, whose inhabitants fled to Mesambria when the Phoenician fleet attacked during Xerxes' invasion.
tyndaridae: Sons of Tyndareus, the Dioscuri (Castor and Pollux), whose crew membership on the Argo won Sparta's welcome for the Minyae and whose invasion of Attica to recover Helen is linked to Decelea's privileges at Sparta.
adyrmachidae: A Libyan tribe inhabiting the coast immediately west of Egypt, as far as the harbor of Plynus, noted for following Egyptian customs while adopting Libyan dress and for their unique practice of presenting unmarried girls to the king.
oaxus: A town in Crete ruled by Etearchus, where the stepmother of Phronime resided and where the Theraean trader Themison encountered Etearchus before sailing away with Phronime.
aegidae: A prominent Spartan clan descended from Aegeus, son of Oeolycus, who suffered childlessness until they erected a shrine to the avenging spirits of Laïus and Oedipus on divine instruction, after which their children survived.
irasa: A fertile region in Libya west of Aziris, which the Libyans concealed from Greek settlers but later became the site of a battle between Cyrenaeans and Egyptians under Apries.
giligamae: A Libyan people whose territory stretched west from near Cyrene to the island of Aphrodisias, encompassing Platea, Aziris, and the start of the silphium country, with customs like other Libyans.
asbystae: A Libyan people living inland south of Cyrene, known for their extensive use of four-horse chariots and their imitation of Cyrenaean customs.
paroreatae: A Peloponnesian people whose territory was in the southwestern Peloponnese and was settled by Lemnian colonists who drove out the aboriginal inhabitants.
cinyps-river: A river in Libya that flows from the wooded Hill of the Graces into the sea through the territory of the Macae, near which the Spartan Dorieus attempted to establish a colony.
euhesperidae: A coastal town in Libya west of Barce, marking the western limit of Persian expansion under Darius into North Africa.
auseans: A Libyan people living on the shores of the Tritonian lake west of the Machlyes, known for their annual festival to Athena where maidens fight with stones and sticks, and for their practice of promiscuous intercourse with paternity determined by resemblance.
barcaean: A Libyan people living in the region around the city of Barce in northeastern Libya, who shared dietary customs with the nearby Cyreneans, particularly abstaining from pork and beef.
atarantes: A Saharan people living inland south of the Mediterranean coast, ten days' journey beyond the Garamantes, distinguished by having no individual names but only a collective tribal designation, and notable for cursing the sun during the heat of day.
gindanes: A Libyan people dwelling on the coast west of Egypt, known for women who wear leather anklets as marks of their sexual liaisons.
triton-river: A river in Libya marking the boundary between the nomadic eastern regions and the cultivated, mountainous western lands inhabited by settled peoples like the Maxyes.
bactria: A region of inland Asia under Persian rule, where Darius settled exiled Barcaeans who founded a town named after their homeland.
maxyes: An agricultural Libyan people dwelling west of the Triton river, distinguished by long hair on the right side of their heads and shaved left side, who claimed Trojan descent.
atlantes: A Libyan people living near Mount Atlas in the interior desert, named after the mountain; they reportedly eat no living creatures and experience no dreams.
crestonaeans: A Thracian people above whom dwelt tribes practicing suttee (wife-immolation at a husband's death), distinguishing those tribes from other Thracians.
trausi: A Thracian tribe distinguished from other Thracians by their unique customs regarding birth and death, mourning newborns for the sufferings they must endure and celebrating the dead as liberated from worldly sorrows.
edonian: A Thracian people dwelling in the region around the Strymon river, where Histiaeus sought to found Myrcinus and through whose territory Xerxes' army crossed during the invasion of Greece.
antandrus: A city in the Troad (northwestern Asia Minor), captured by the Persian general Otanes and later passed through by Xerxes' invading army en route to Ilium.
paeoplae: A Paeo­nian tribe dwelling north of the Pangaean mountains and east of the Strymon river, deported to Asia by Megabazus during the Persian conquest of the Balkans.
greek-sea: The Aegean Sea, or more broadly the waters off the coast of western Asia Minor and Greece, which serves as the starting point for measuring distances inland to Persian territory.
doberes: A people dwelling north of the Pangaean mountains and east of the Strymon river in Thrace, notable for their lake-dwelling settlements built on platforms supported by piles.
odomanti: A people living near the Pangaean mountains and Prasiad lake in Thrace, dwelling on platforms built over the lake and resisting Persian conquest, known for abundant fish and skilled in lacustrine construction.
egestans: A Sicilian people inhabiting the region around Egesta in northwestern Sicily, who fought alongside the Phoenicians against the Spartan colonist Dorieus and his followers, and subsequently honored the fallen Greek Philippus of Croton as a hero.
messenians: A Greek people of the Peloponnese whose conflict with Sparta, along with struggles against Arcadians and Argives, exemplifies wars of little material worth that Aristagoras urged Cleomenes to abandon in favor of conquering Asia.
alopecae: A locality in Attica near Athens where the tomb of the Spartan general Anchimolius, slain by Pisistratid cavalry at Phalerum, was situated.
gephyraean: An Athenian clan claiming Eretrian origin but descended from Phoenicians who came with Cadmus to Boeotia, settling at Tanagra before being expelled to Athens, where they were received as citizens with restricted privileges; they produced the slayers of the tyrant Hipparchus.
coronea: A city in Boeotia near Thebes, mentioned as one of Thebes' neighboring allies in their appeal to Delphi for aid against Athens.
ilissus: A stream in Attica near Athens, marking a boundary of the plain of Phalerum where Lacedaemonian forces under Anchimolius were defeated by the Pisistratid tyrants' Thessalian allies.
scamander: A river in the Troad (northwestern Asia Minor) flowing past the citadel of Priam (Troy), significant as the first water-source inadequate for Xerxes' invading army and as the location where Sigeum, where the exiled Pisistratidae withdrew, lay on its banks.
pactolus: A river flowing through the marketplace of Sardis, carrying gold dust from Mount Tmolus and joining the Hermus, where Lydians and Persians made their final stand during the Ionian burning of the city.
paesus: A city on the Hellespont (northern Aegean coast) captured by the Persian general Daurises during his campaign against the Ionian revolt.
solians: A Cypriot people whose king Aristocyprus fought against the Persians in the Ionian Revolt, dying at the battle of Salamis in Cyprus.
ephesian: Greeks inhabiting the city of Ephesus in Ionia (western Asia Minor), who participated in the Ionian Revolt against Persian rule and were reportedly involved in the aftermath of the Persian Wars.
thespiae: A Boeotian city neighboring Thebes, which refused to submit to Persia during the invasion of Xerxes and was considered by the Thebans as one of their closest allies.
aeolia: A region on the coast of Asia Minor north of Ionia, whose cities (notably Cyme) were conquered and subject to Persian rule during the wars described by Herodotus.
dardanus: A city on the Hellespont in the Troad, near Abydos, taken by Daurises during the Ionian Revolt and later passed by Xerxes' army en route to Greece.
messene: A city in Sicily on the strait between Sicily and Italy, originally called Zancle and renamed Messene by Cadmus of Cos, who colonized it with Samian settlers.
inyx: A city in Sicily where Hippocrates, tyrant of Gela, imprisoned Scythes and Pythogenes after seizing Zancle.
myesians: A people of Ionia in Asia Minor who contributed three ships to the Ionian fleet at the Battle of Lade against the Persians.
didyma: A sanctuary in Ionia near Miletus, sacred to Apollo, whose temple and oracle were plundered and burned by the Persians after the fall of Miletus.
black-bay: A body of water in the Chersonese (Thrace), between the Hellespont and the mainland, through which armies and fleets passed en route westward.
gallipoli: A peninsula in the Hellespont region (the Chersonese), whose isthmus Miltiades fortified against the Apsinthians and through which Xerxes' army marched during the Persian invasion.
chalcidian: Greeks inhabiting the region of Chalcidice in northern Greece, who received control of Olynthus from the Persian general Artabazus after he expelled the Bottiaeans.
sacred-way: A road from Delphi through Phocis and Boeotia toward Athens, traveled by the Dolonci after consulting the Delphic Oracle.
icarian-sea: The sea between Samos and the Cyclades, sailed through by the Persian fleet under Datis and Artaphrenes en route to attack Naxos in 490 BC.
messenian: A people inhabiting the region southwest of Laconia (Sparta), whom the Lacedaemonians fought repeatedly and whose territory was a subject of Peloponnesian conflict; one Messenian named Panites is credited with advising the Spartans on a matter of succession.
hymettus: A mountain in Attica near Athens, at the foot of which the Pelasgians once settled before being expelled by the Athenians.
ionian-gulf: A body of water in northwestern Greece, bounded by Epirus and Aetolia to the east and Italy to the west, from which the Epidamnian Amphimnestus traveled to compete for the hand of Agariste.
nonacris: A city of Arcadia in the Peloponnese, notable as the site of a spring said to be the water of the Styx, by which Cleomenes swore the Arcadians to oath against Sparta.
celaenae: A city in Phrygia where the Maeander and Cataracts rivers originate, notable as a landmark on Xerxes' march to Sardis.
eretrian: Inhabitants of Eretria on Euboea who resisted the Persian invasion of 490 BC but were betrayed after a six-day siege and enslaved by Darius' forces.
lemnian: An island people in the Aegean who inhabited Lemnos and became notorious for committing atrocities—the massacre of Athenian women and their children—which gave rise to the proverbial expression "Lemnian crime" for acts of cruelty, and later a Lemnian trireme deserted to the Greeks at Artemisium during the Persian Wars.
colossae: A great city of Phrygia through which the river Lycus passes before disappearing underground and reappearing to join the Maeander; a landmark on Xerxes' route to Lydia.
gandarians: A Central Asian people levied by Xerxes, equipped like the Bactrians, and commanded by Artyphius son of Artabanus in the invasion of Greece.
lacedaemonia: The region of southern Greece ruled by Sparta, which features prominently in the narrative as a major Greek power whose customs (regarding royal succession) Demaratus invokes at the Persian court, and whose military conflicts with Argos and role in the Greek alliance against Persia shape the wider strategic context.
utians: An eastern Iranian people who, equipped like the Pactyes, were commanded by Arsamenes son of Darius in Xerxes' invasion army.
cicones: A Thracian people whose territory lay on the coast of the Aegean Sea near the city of Sane, through which Xerxes' army marched during the invasion of Greece.
madytus: A city on the Chersonese (Gallipoli peninsula) on the Hellespont, between Sestus and a headland opposite Abydos, where Artayctes the Persian governor was executed by the Athenians under Xanthippus.
mariandyni: A people of Anatolia living near the Black Sea coast, equipped like the Paphlagonians and commanded by Gobryas in Xerxes' invasion army of 480 BC.
mycians: A Persian subject people who, along with the Utians and Paricanians, served in Xerxes' invasion force of 480 BC, equipped in the style of the Pactyes and led by Arsamenes son of Darius.
cythnus: An Aegean island where the Parians stationed a watch-force during the Persian Wars to monitor the campaign's outcome.
meiones: An Anatolian people formerly inhabiting the region later called Lydia, who changed their name to Lydians after Lydus son of Atys.
achaia: A region of the northwestern Peloponnese, anciently inhabited by Ionians before their migration to Asia Minor, to which Delphians fled their town during the Persian invasion.
lisus: A river in Thrace between the Samothracian city of Mesambria and the Thasian city of Stryme, which was drained dry by Xerxes' army during the Persian invasion of Hellas.
maronea: A Greek city on the coast of Thrace, lying between the river Lisus and the Ismarid lake, which Xerxes' army passed during its advance into Greece.
dicaea: A Greek city on the Thracian coast between Maronea and Abdera, near the Bistonian lake, through which Xerxes' army passed during his invasion of Greece.
aenea: A town on the coast of Thermaic gulf near the Mygdonian territory in northern Greece, from which Xerxes' fleet proceeded toward Therma.
nine-ways: A crossing point on the Strymon river in Edonian territory where Xerxes' army crossed during the invasion of Greece, notable as the site of a Persian human sacrifice of nine children.
acanthians: Inhabitants of Acanthus in Thrace, who supported Xerxes' invasion by aiding the canal-digging project and were honored with Median dress.
ampelus: A headland at the tip of Sithonia (not Torone) in northern Greece, rounded by Xerxes' fleet in 480 BC while sailing toward the Thermaic gulf.
bessi: A clan of the Satrae dwelling in the Thracian mountains, who served as priests and keepers of a shrine of Dionysus with an oracle-priestess.
onochonus: A river of Thessaly that flows from the surrounding mountains into the vale and joins the Peneus, notable for being unable to supply enough water for Xerxes' invading army.
peneus-valley: A valley in Thessaly through which the river Peneus flows in a narrow pass between Mounts Olympus and Ossa, forming a strategic gateway into Thessaly that Xerxes examined before choosing an alternative northern route through Macedonia.
haliacmon: A river in northern Greece forming part of the boundary between Bottiaean and Macedonian territory, whose waters unite with the Lydias before reaching the sea near Therma.
cheidorus: A river of Crestonaean origin flowing through Mygdonia into the marshes of the Axius, which was drained entirely by Xerxes' invading army in 480 BC.
dolopes: A Greek people who submitted to Persia and supplied troops to Xerxes' land army.
halia: A coastal settlement in the Argolid under Tiryns' control, where Aneristus son of Sperthias landed merchant ships.
bottiaean: An ethnic group inhabiting the territory between the Axius and Haliacmon rivers in Macedonia, bounded by Mygdonian lands to the east and Macedonia proper to the west, with settlements including Ichnae and Pella.
enienes: A Greek people of Thessaly who furnished troops to the Persian invasion force under Xerxes and were later subject to the Greek oath at Delphi to punish those who had medized.
elisyci: A people of uncertain location listed among the diverse forces recruited by the Carthaginian king Amilcas for his invasion of Sicily in support of the tyrant Terillus.
syracusan: Greeks inhabiting Syracuse in Sicily who submitted to Gelon's rule and were led by him against the Carthaginian Amilcas.
acragas: A Greek city in Sicily, ruled by Theron in Herodotus' time, and later inhabited by Cretans who had unsuccessfully besieged Camicus.
laurium: A silver-mining district near Athens whose revenues Themistocles persuaded the Athenians to use for building two hundred triremes, originally for war with Aegina, which later proved decisive against Persia.
cyrnians: An island people living off the western coast of Italy who were enlisted by the Carthaginian king Amilcas in his invasion force against Sicily around 480 BC.
carchedon: A Phoenician city in North Africa (modern Tunisia) whose general Amilcas led forces against the Greeks in Sicily and was defeated by Gelon and Theron.
sicania: An island in the western Mediterranean, formerly called by that name and later known as Sicily, where Minos died and where Cretans besieged Camicus before being scattered by storm to Iapygia.
hybla: A town in Sicily near which Hippocrates, tyrant of Gela, died while campaigning against the Sicels.
carchedonian: A North African people inhabiting Carthage (Carchedon), who fought Greek forces in Sicily under their king Amilcas during the Persian Wars.
thyia: A sanctuary in the territory of Delphi dedicated to Thyia daughter of Cephisus, where the Delphians instituted wind-sacrifices after consulting Apollo's oracle during the Persian invasion.
rhegians: A Greek city in southern Italy whose three thousand citizens, conscripted by Micythus to aid Tarentum against Hyrian settlers from Crete, were slaughtered in a catastrophic battle that became legendary for its scale of Greek losses.
cephisus: A figure of mythology whose daughter Thyia gave her name to a sacred precinct at Delphi where the Greeks subsequently honored the winds.
alus: A town in Achaea (southern Thessaly) where the Greek allied force disembarked to guard the pass of Tempe against Xerxes' invasion, and where Xerxes later halted to learn of local religious practices concerning the cult of Laphystian Zeus.
colchis: A region on the eastern coast of the Black Sea, legendary destination of Jason and the Argonauts' quest for the Golden Fleece, and home of Cytissorus, son of Phrixus, who came to rescue Athamas.
opuntian-locrians: A Greek people inhabiting the region around Opus in Locris (central Greece), who contributed seven fifty-oared barks to the Greek naval alliance against Xerxes' invasion.
mycenaeans: A Greek people who inhabited part of the Peloponnese and fielded eighty hoplites at Plataea in 479 BC, notable chiefly as antagonists whom the Athenians claim to have defeated in ancient times.
pylae: A narrow pass in Malis (Thessaly) between Mount Oeta and the sea, also called Thermopylae, where Greeks held off the Persian army in 480 BC until outflanked via a mountain path.
hellespontian: A people or ethnic group dwelling in the region of the Hellespont (the narrow strait between Europe and Asia Minor), known to the Greeks for the distinctive easterly wind they called by that name.
anopaea: A mountain path in Locris that runs along a ridge from the Asopus river gorge to Alpenus, used by the Persians to encircle the Greek forces at Thermopylae.
ceans: Ionians from the Aegean island of Ceos who contributed two ships to the Greek fleet at Salamis.
geraestus: A promontory at the southern tip of Euboea, where the Persian fleet planned to cut off the Greek retreat during the naval campaign of 480 BC.
thespian: A native or citizen of Thespiae, a Boeotian city that fought at Thermopylae and later granted citizenship to Sicinnus, Themistocles' servant.
parapotamii: A town in Phocis in central Greece, destroyed by the Persian army under Xerxes while marching down the Cephisus river toward Athens.
dryopian: An ancient people who formerly inhabited the region later called Doris (between Malis and Phocis), from which they were displaced by Heracles and the Malians, with some settling in Hermione in the Peloponnese.
thriasian: The Thriasian plain, a plain in Attica near Eleusis where the Athenians proposed to make a stand against Xerxes' invading army.
crotonians: Greeks of Achaean descent from Crotona in southern Italy who contributed a single ship under Phayllus to the Greek resistance against Xerxes' invasion.
cynurians: An aboriginal Peloponnesian people of Ionian stock living in the region of Argos who had become Dorianized through time and Argive rule, comprising the Orneatae and perioikoi.
aetolians: One of four immigrant nations inhabiting the Peloponnese, the Aetolians held only the city of Elis and remained neutral during the Persian Wars.
calyndian: An Anatolian people whose king Damasithymus commanded a ship in Xerxes' fleet at Salamis, where Artemisia of Halicarnassus rammed and sank their vessel.
calyndians: An allied people of the Persians, dwelling in Caria, whose king Damasithymus fought at Salamis and was killed when Artemisia rammed his ship.
cynosura: A headland on Salamis where the Persian fleet stationed ships, together with those at Ceos, to help encircle the Greek fleet before the battle of Salamis.
phliasians: A Greek city-state of the northeastern Peloponnese that sent hoplites to defend Hellas during the Persian Wars and lost men to Persian cavalry at Plataea.
orestheum: A town in Arcadia through which the Spartan army under Pausanias marched against the Persians in 479 BC.
dipaea: A place in Arcadia where the Spartans defeated the Arcadians (except Mantineans) in one of the five great victories that Tisamenus helped them win.
philasians: A Greek people who fought at Plataea in 479 BC, stationed near Megara and routed by Theban cavalry while advancing across the plain.
anactorians: Greek allies from the Ionian islands who fought at Plataea in 479 BC, positioned in the battle line between the Sacae and the Leucadians.
datus: A gold-mining region in Thrace, controlled by the Edonians, where the Athenian general Sophanes was killed in battle.
meii: An ancient people of Anatolia whose territory in what is now western Turkey was subsequently called Lydia after the rule of Lydus, son of Atys.
heraclid: Descendants of Heracles who ruled Sardis for twenty-two generations (505 years) until Candaules, the last of their line, was overthrown by Gyges and the Mermnadae dynasty.
gaeson: A coastal area near Mykale in Ionia, past which the Persian fleet sailed before beaching their ships and fortifying a camp ahead of the battle of Mykale.
deceleans: A deme of Attica whose inhabitants claimed that their ancestors revealed Helen's location to the Dioscuri during their invasion, earning them perpetual privileges and exemption from Spartan ravaging.
pitanate: A battalion of Spartan hoplites under the command of Amompharetus, present at Plataea in 479 BC and notable for their initial refusal to withdraw when Pausanias ordered the Greek forces to reposition.
paphlagonia: A region in northern Asia Minor between the Halys river and the Euxine (Black) Sea, lying east of Bithynia and south of the Pontic coast.
scolopois: A place near Mykale on the Asiatic shore, by the Gaeson, where there is a temple of Eleusinian Demeter, past which the Greek fleet sailed before beaching and fortifying their ships ahead of the battle of Mykale (479 BC).
limeneion: A battle site in Milesian territory where the Milesians suffered a major defeat during the eleven-year Lydian war under Sadyattes and Alyattes.
asiatic-greeks: Greek cities and peoples of the Ionian coast and mainland of Asia Minor, whom Croesus of Lydia (r. 560-546 BC) conquered and made tributary before abandoning plans to attack the Greek islands.
mysian-olympus: A mountain in Mysia (northwestern Asia Minor) where a monstrous boar appeared and devastated the Mysian fields, prompting them to seek aid from Croesus.
parus: An island in the Aegean Sea, home of the poet Archilochus, who mentioned Gyges in his verses.
gygian: Term used by the Delphians for the gold and silver offerings dedicated at Delphi by Gyges, king of Lydia.
terentum: A port city in southern Italy (modern Taranto) where the musician Arion reportedly accumulated wealth before his dramatic sea rescue.
phocia: A region in central Greece, home to the oracle at Abae, which Croesus consulted regarding his Persian campaign.
mount-olympus: A mountain in the region of Phrygia or Mysia in Asia Minor, where Croesus's son Atys was killed by a spear while hunting a supernatural boar.
chalybes: An Anatolian people living east of the Paphlagonian coast, subjugated by Croesus of Lydia and famous in antiquity for their skill in working iron.
thracian-thynians: A Thracian tribe inhabiting the region south of Thrace (near the Propontis), conquered and held subject by Croesus of Lydia.
pytho: Pytho is the sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi in central Greece, famous for its oracle, to which Croesus sent lavish gifts in gratitude for favorable prophetic responses.
doric: A Hellenic people whose chief representatives were the Lacedaemonians, distinguished from the Ionic Greeks and said to have migrated from northern Greece (Phthia, Histiae, Pindus, Dryopia) into the Peloponnese, where they took their name.
tyrrheni: An Etruscan people of Italy, north of whose territory certain non-Greek-speaking Pelasgian communities (notably at Creston) were located in historical times.
clazomenians: Inhabitants of Clazomenae, a Greek city in Ionia (on the coast of Asia Minor), who received the golden bowl dedicated by Croesus at Delphi as part of their treasury.
scylace: A town on the Hellespont (Dardanelles strait) formerly inhabited by Pelasgians, cited by Herodotus as evidence that pre-Greek populations of the region spoke a non-Greek language.
etruscans: An Italic people dwelling in the region north of Latium (called Tyrrhenia/Tyrrhenian territory by Greeks), mentioned by Herodotus only in passing as neighbors of the Pelasgians.
thornax: A mountain or hill in Laconia where a statue of Apollo dedicated by the Lacedaemonians stood.
tegean: A people of Arcadia whose plain the Spartans, misled by a Delphic oracle, tried to conquer but were instead defeated and put in their own chains.
nisaea: A harbor town on the Saronic coast near Megara, captured by Pisistratus in a military campaign that enhanced his reputation among the Athenians.
paeanian: A deme of Attica, home of Phya, the woman dressed as Athena to help restore Pisistratus to power.
eurotas-valley: A valley in Laconia (southern Greece) containing Sparta, the leading Greek city-state and chief ally sought by Croesus of Lydia.
armenian-mountains: A mountain range in Asia Minor from which the Halys river originates, forming part of the boundary between Median and Lydian empires.
cappadocian-syrians: An Anatolian people dwelling east of the river Halys, formerly subjects of the Medes and then of Cyrus, whose territory lay between the Paphlagonians to the northwest and other regions to the south and east.
kizil-irmak: A major river of Asia Minor flowing from the Armenian mountains northward through Cilicia and Cappadocia, forming the historical boundary between the Median and Lydian empires and separating Cappadocian Syrians from Paphlagonians.
asia-minor: The peninsula of western Asia (modern Turkey), home to Lydia and the Greek Ionian cities, whose conflicts with Near Eastern and Greek powers feature prominently in Herodotus' account.
pterians: Inhabitants of Pteria in Cappadocia, who were conquered and enslaved by Croesus before his armies clashed with Cyrus's forces in their territory.
sardian: Citizens or subjects of Sardis, the capital of Lydia, who appealed to the Spartans for military aid against the Persian siege during Croesus' reign.
ismenus: A sanctuary of Apollo in Boeotia near Thebes, where Croesus dedicated a golden tripod.
telmissus: A city in Lycia famous for its diviners and dream-interpreters, whom Croesus consulted about an ominous portent of snakes swarming in Sardis.
telmessian: A people of Telmessus in Lycia renowned for divination, whom Croesus consulted to interpret a portent of snakes devoured by horses before Sardis fell to the Persians.
gygaean-lake: A lake in Lydia near the tomb of Alyattes, fed by perpetual springs and notable for its proximity to this monumental burial structure.
paretaceni: A Median tribe enumerated among the peoples united by Deioces under Median rule.
umbria: A region of Italy where, per Herodotus, Lydian colonists led by Tyrrhenus settled and founded cities after fleeing famine, becoming the Tyrrhenians.
telmessus: A city in Lydia famous for its seers and diviners, whom Croesus consulted to interpret the portent of snakes and horses at Sardis before his capture by Cyrus.
hamadan: The ancient city of Ecbatana (modern Hamadan), capital of Media built by King Deioces in a series of seven concentric walled circles on a hill in the plain, serving as the royal fortress and treasury of the Median realm.
arizanti: A Median tribe dwelling in the region that became Media (northwest Iran).
busae: One of the six Median tribes united under Deioces.
struchates: A Median tribe among those united by Deioces in the formation of the Median nation.
budii: A Median tribe dwelling in the region of Media (in what is now Iran), enumerated among the six principal divisions of the Median nation under Deioces.
caucasian-mountains: A major mountain range forming the northeastern boundary of the known world to Herodotus, lying to the right (east) of the upper route by which Scythians invaded Asia and defeated the Medes.
ascalon: A city in Syria (Palestine) that housed an ancient sanctuary of Aphrodite, which the Scythians partially plundered during their invasion of Egypt, incurring divine punishment.
derusiaei: One of the Persian tribes, characterized as tillers of the soil rather than nomadic herders.
germanii: A Persian tribe of tillers of the soil, listed among the non-nomadic peoples of the Persian interior.
panthialaei: A Persian tribe of tillers of the soil, mentioned among the peoples ruled by the Achaemenid dynasty but not among those first persuaded by Cyrus to revolt from Media.
maspii: One of the three principal Persian tribes that Cyrus assembled to revolt against the Medes, dwelling in Persia.
maraphii: One of the three principal Persian tribes assembled by Cyrus to revolt against Median rule, on whom the other Persian tribes depended.
dai: A Persian tribe of wandering herdsmen who, along with the Mardi, Dropici, and Sagartii, formed part of the Persian tribal confederacy subordinate to the Pasargadae.
azerbaijan: A mountainous region north of Ecbatana in Media, bordering the territory of the Saspires and marked by wild forests, where Astyages ordered the infant Cyrus to be exposed.
dropici: A nomadic Persian tribe of herdsmen who inhabited regions of Persia and were distinguished from the settled agricultural tribes by their pastoral way of life.
five-cities: Five Dorian cities of the southwestern coast of Asia Minor (Lindus, Ialysus, Camirus, Cos, and Cnidus) that jointly excluded Halicarnassus from their shared sanctuary of Triopian Apollo after a Halicarnassian violated the temple's law forbidding removal of victory tripods.
camirus: One of the Five Cities of the Dorians in the southwestern Aegean (southwestern Asia Minor), which collectively maintained the sanctuary of Triopian Apollo and expelled Halicarnassus from its use.
aegae: An Achaean city in the Peloponnese, located along the coast near the river Crathis, one of twelve divisions that displaced the Ionians from the region.
bura: One of twelve Achaean cities in the Peloponnese, in the region that the Ionians had formerly inhabited before being driven out by the Achaeans.
six-cities: A group of six Dorian cities on and near the southwest coast of Asia Minor (Lindus, Ialysus, Camirus, Cos, Cnidus, and Halicarnassus), which shared a sanctuary of Triopian Apollo until Halicarnassus was expelled for violating the temple's rules about dedication of votive tripods.
helice: An Achaean city in the northern Peloponnese where Ionians took refuge after being defeated in battle by the Achaeans.
aegion: One of the twelve Achaean cities on the northern coast of the Peloponnese, formerly held by the Ionians before the Achaeans drove them out.
ialysus: One of the five Dorian cities of the southwestern coast of Asia Minor (Rhodes), excluded with Lindus and Camirus from the Triopian temple of Apollo after Halicarnassus broke the sacred law.
rhype: An Achaean city in the Peloponnese, one of the twelve divisions that the Achaeans occupied after displacing the Ionians.
aegira: An Achaean city in the Peloponnese, located between Pellene and Aegae, whose territory the Achaeans held after displacing the Ionians who had previously dwelt there.
pirus: A river in Achaea in the northwestern Peloponnese, located near the city of Olenus.
olenus: An Achaean city in the Peloponnese, one of the twelve Achaean divisions that displaced the Ionians, near the great river Pirus.
patrae: An Achaean city in the northwestern Peloponnese, one of twelve divisions that replaced the Ionian settlements after the Achaeans drove out the Ionians.
tritaeae: An inland city of Achaea in the northwestern Peloponnese, one of the twelve Achaean divisions that occupied territory formerly held by the Ionians.
phareae: An Achaean city in the Peloponnese, one of the twelve divisions that the Achaeans occupied after driving out the Ionians.
pelasgian-arcadians: A people of Arcadian origin who were incorporated into the Ionian colonies of Asia Minor, particularly at Miletus, where they mixed with other non-Ionian groups in the population.
minyans: A Greek people from Orchomenus in Boeotia who, along with other non-Ionian groups, mingled with the Ionians who settled the twelve Ionian cities of Asia Minor.
abantes: A people of Euboea who, though not Ionians by name, became mixed among the Ionian colonists who founded the twelve cities of Ionia.
lerisae: An ancient Aeolian city on the coast of Asia Minor, one of eleven original Aeolian mainland settlements before Smyrna was taken by the Ionians.
pylus: A city in Anatolia whose inhabitants (the Caucones) were among those claiming descent from Codrus and serving as kings for certain Ionian communities.
helicon: A mountain in Boeotia, in mainland Greece, sacred to Poseidon and associated with Ionian religious festivals.
aeolis: A region on the coast of Asia Minor (modern Turkey) where twelve Aeolian cities were established on more fertile land than the Ionian settlements, though with inferior climate.
phriconian: An epithet applied to Cyme, one of the eleven (originally twelve) Aeolian cities on the mainland of Asia Minor.
gryneia: An ancient Aeolian city on the mainland coast of Asia Minor, one of the eleven surviving Aeolian settlements after Smyrna was taken by the Ionians.
cilla: A city in Aeolia on the mainland of Asia Minor, one of the eleven (originally twelve) ancient Aeolian settlements, whose land was better than Ionia's but whose climate was worse.
neon-teichos: An ancient Aeolian city on the mainland coast of Asia Minor, one of twelve original Aeolian settlements before the Ionians seized Smyrna.
phricion: A city on the mainland coast of Asia Minor in the Aeolian region, identified as an alternative name for Cyme.
panormus: A harbor in the territory of Miletus on the Ionian coast of Asia Minor.
bactrian: An Iranian people inhabiting the region of Bactria (in Central Asia), whom Cyrus the Great had to subdue and hold in his empire before turning his attention to Ionian Greeks.
hundred-isles: An island or group of islands in the Aegean Sea where one Aeolian city was situated, joining the Ionian revolt against Persian rule.
maeandrus: A river in western Asia Minor (modern Turkey) whose plain was plundered by the Persian general Mazares after the fall of Tabalus.
pergamum: A city in the Aeolian region of Asia Minor on the mainland coast, not mentioned by name in the extant Herodotean passages provided.
iberia: Iberia is the Iberian peninsula, reached by Phocaean Greeks in their early sea-voyages beyond Tyrrhenia.
tartessians: A wealthy maritime people of southern Iberia (Spain) whose king Arganthonius befriended Phocaean Greek traders and helped them fortify their city in response to growing Median power.
smyrnaeans: An Ionian city on the coast of Asia Minor whose inhabitants were scattered among other Ionian cities after Colophonian exiles seized their town and the Aeolians subsequently recovered and depopulated it.
colophonian: Greeks from Colophon in Ionia who, as political exiles, seized Smyrna from the Aeolians by treachery during a Dionysian festival, but were subsequently expelled and their city dispersed among other Ionian settlements.
caere: An Etruscan city in Italy (modern Cerveteri) whose people, the Agyllaeans, stoned Phocaean survivors and were thereafter cursed until they instituted religious honors for the dead.
corsica: An island in the western Mediterranean where Greek Phocaeans had established a colony called Alalia about twenty years before their final evacuation from Phocaea.
sardonian: A sea between Corsica and Sardinia where the Phocaeans fought the Tyrrhenians and Carthaginians in a costly naval victory.
oenotrian: An ancient people of southern Italy whose territory included the region where Greek Phocaean refugees later founded the city of Hyele.
etruria: A region in central Italy inhabited by the Tyrrhenians, who joined the Carthaginians in a naval battle against Phocaean Greeks and stoned captive Phocaean sailors, an act for which the Tyrrhenian city of Agylla incurred divine anger.
hyele: A city in the Oenotrian country (southern Italy) founded by Phocaeans fleeing from Tyrrhenian attack, after they learned from an oracle that they should establish a settlement named after the hero Cyrnus rather than the island.
agyllaeans: Tyrrhenian people inhabiting the town of Agylla in Italy, who stoned to death captured Phocaean sailors and were subsequently cursed until they instituted ritual honors for their victims.
elea: A Greek city in southern Italy (in the region of Oenotria) founded by Phocaean refugees from Asia Minor after their defeat by Carthaginians and Tyrrhenians, formerly called Hyele.
lucania: A Greek colonial city in the Oenotrian region of southern Italy (modern Campania), founded by Phocaean refugees from Asia Minor after their defeat by Carthaginians and Tyrrhenians.
posidonia: A Greek city in the Oenotrian (southern Italian) region, whose resident informed the Phocaean refugees that "Cyrnus" in the Delphic oracle referred to a hero rather than the island Corsica.
velia: A Greek city in southern Italy (Oenotrian country, now called Hyele) founded by Phocaean refugees from their failed settlement at Corsica.
leleges: An ancient Aegean people who, according to Cretan tradition, were islanders under Minos before being driven to the mainland by Dorians and Ionians, later becoming known as Carians.
calynda: A town on the border of Caunus in southwest Asia Minor.
ionian-phocaea: An Ionian Greek city in Asia Minor whose inhabitants fled en masse by sea when the Persian general Harpagus besieged it, eventually settling in Thrace.
ceramicus: A gulf (or bay) on the north coast of the Cnidian peninsula in Caria, marking the boundary of Cnidian territory as they attempted to fortify themselves against the Persian general Harpagus.
xanthians: Lycian inhabitants of the city of Xanthus in southwest Asia Minor, who chose mass suicide rather than surrender to Harpagus and the Persian army in the sixth century BC.
bubassus: A peninsula in southwestern Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey), south of Caria, whose territory lay adjacent to the Cnidian isthmus that the Cnidians attempted to fortify against Harpagus' conquest.
caunian: An Anatolian people of Caria who claimed Cretan origins, spoke a language akin to Carian, and once expelled foreign gods to restore worship of their ancestral deities.
lide: A hill in Caria near Halicarnassus, fortified by the Pedaseans during their resistance against the Persian general Harpagus.
hit: A city eight days' journey from Babylon on the little river Is (a tributary of the Euphrates), from which bitumen was extracted and transported to build Babylon's walls.
is: A city eight days' journey from Babylon on a tributary river of the Euphrates, from which bitumen was extracted and transported for use in building Babylon's walls.
solymi: An ancient people of Asia Minor whom Herodotus identifies as the original inhabitants of the region later called Lycia, before they were renamed Termilae and subsequently Lycians.
patara: A sanctuary in Lycia where a prophetess of Apollo was occasionally appointed to deliver oracles by spending the night shut in the temple.
ait: A city eight days' journey from Babylon on the little river Is, a tributary of the Euphrates, from whose source bitumen was brought for Babylon's wall.
dardanean: A people of Asia Minor through whose territory the Gyndes river flowed toward the Tigris on Cyrus's march to Babylon.
euphrates-river: A major river of western Asia flowing through Mesopotamia and Babylon.
kerkha: A river of Mesopotamia forming part of the boundary between Assyria and Media, mentioned in Cyrus's campaign against Labynetus.
gyndes-river: A tributary of the Tigris rising in the Matieni mountains and flowing through Dardaene, whose drowning of Cyrus' sacred horse during his Babylonian campaign caused him to divert his army to dissect it into 180 canals.
oxus: A great river flowing from the Matieni mountains eastward into the Caspian Sea, forming the boundary between Persian and Scythian territories and notable for its many mouths and island peoples.
jaxartes: A river flowing from the Matieni mountains eastward through multiple channels into the Caspian Sea, whose islands and delta regions Herodotus describes as inhabited by unusual peoples.
plinthinete-gulf: A gulf on the Mediterranean coast of northern Egypt, marking the western boundary of Egypt proper as Herodotus defines it.
atlantic: The sea beyond the Pillars of Heracles, which Herodotus says is one and the same as the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, unlike the separate, landlocked Caspian.
serbonian-marsh: A coastal swamp on Egypt's Mediterranean shore, located near Mount Casian in the eastern Nile Delta, marking the eastern boundary of Egypt proper.
aras: A river flowing from the country of the Matieni eastward through multiple mouths into the Caspian Sea, notable for its islands and the peculiar customs of peoples inhabiting its banks and delta.
upper-egypt: The southern region of Egypt, beginning south of the marshy delta and extending upriver, which the Egyptians claimed was the only part not flooded in the time of their earliest kings.
thebaic: The Thebaic district, a region of Egypt centered on Thebes in Upper Egypt, which alone remained above water before Min drained the marshland to found Egypt.
echinades-islands: An island group off the coast of Acarnania in northwestern Greece, partially formed by silt deposits from the Achelous River, cited by Herodotus as an example of land-building by river action.
fayyum: A natural lake in Lower Egypt, located seven days' journey upriver from the Mediterranean, which in antiquity bordered the northern limit of habitable land during the earliest period of Egyptian civilization.
watchtower-of-perseus: A coastal landmark near Pelusium marking the eastern boundary of the Nile Delta's seaboard, forty schoeni east of the Salters' at Pelusium.
saitic: A branch of the Nile Delta in Lower Egypt, one of the channels formed where the river divides before reaching the sea.
sebennytic: The middle and greatest mouth of the Nile, flowing straight through the Delta to the sea.
mendesian: One of the seven mouths of the Nile in the Delta region of northern Egypt, flowing into the Mediterranean Sea.
sebennytic-mouth: The natural channel of the Nile that flows straight through the middle of the Delta into the sea, carrying the greatest volume of its waters.
bucolic: An artificial channel of the Nile Delta in Egypt, branching off near the Sebennytic mouth, not a natural distributary of the river.
crophi: One of two sharp-peaked hills located between Syene and Elephantine in Upper Egypt, traditionally identified as a source of the Nile's waters.
mophi: One of two sharp-peaked hills between Syene and Elephantine in Upper Egypt, said (by the priests of Saïs) to mark the bottomless sources of the Nile.
takhompso: An island in the Nile River beyond Elephantine, inhabited half by Egyptians and half by Ethiopians, marking the boundary between Egyptian and Ethiopian territory.
thebaid: A region of Upper (southern) Egypt between the cities of Syene and Elephantine, traditionally associated with the southernmost part of Egypt proper.
soloeis: A promontory marking the western extremity of the North African coast inhabited by Libyans, forming the boundary of Libya proper.
assuan-dam: A series of cataracts and rocky rapids on the Nile south of Elephantine, requiring boats to be hauled by ropes and impassable without disembarkation, marking the boundary of Ethiopian territory.
cynesii: A western European people living beyond the Pillars of Heracles, neighbours of the Celts and the westernmost inhabitants of Europe known to Herodotus.
asmakh: Egyptian soldiers who revolted during Psammetichus' reign after three years of unrelieved guard duty at Elephantine, fled to Ethiopia, and settled there as a garrison people for the Ethiopian king.
pyrene: A city of the Celts located beyond the Pillars of Heracles (Strait of Gibraltar) in western Europe, mentioned by Herodotus as a reference point for the source of the Danube (Ister) river.
danube: A major river flowing eastward through the middle of Europe from the land of the Celts to the Euxine Sea, where it terminates at Istria; Herodotus uses it as a geographical reference point for reasoning about the Nile's course and distance.
atarbekhis: A town on the island of Prosopitis in the Nile Delta, where boats originate to collect the bones of dead bulls for communal burial, and which houses a notably sacred temple of Aphrodite.
parthenius: A river in the region of the Black Sea's southern coast, near Colchis, whose valley inhabitants adopted circumcision from the Colchians.
dodonaean: Inhabitants of Dodona in Epirus, site of the oracle of Zeus.
egyptian-delta: The fertile alluvial region of northern Egypt where the Nile divides into multiple branches before reaching the Mediterranean, home to several major religious sanctuaries including Busiris (temple of Isis) and Bubastis.
new-city: A city in the Theban district of Egypt, near which Khemmis, the site of Perseus-worship, was located.
pelasgia: A region in what is now Greece, formerly called Pelasgia, identified with Thesprotia and the site where Herodotus imagines an abducted priestess established the oracle of Zeus at Dodona.
aegean-sea: The sea separating Greece from Asia Minor and containing numerous islands, used here as a comparison for how Egyptian towns appear above the Nile flood waters.
karabel: A rock carving in Ionia on the road between Sardis and Smyrna, attributed by Herodotus to the Egyptian king Sesostris but identified by modern scholars with a Hittite relief.
red-clay: A town in Egypt where King Pheros confined and burned the women he had tested during his blindness, except for the one whose urine restored his sight.
semitic: A Semitic-speaking people inhabiting the Levantine coast (Phoenicia and Cyprus mentioned here), known to Herodotus through their shared musical traditions with Egypt and Greece.
egyptian-sea: The body of water along Egypt's Mediterranean coast, where winds drove Paris (Alexandrus) to the Nile Delta during his flight with Helen.
tyrians: Phoenician maritime traders from the city of Tyre who maintained a settlement (the Camp of the Tyrians) at Memphis in Egypt, where Herodotus notes they had a temple to the Foreign Aphrodite associated with Helen.
great-pyramid: A monumental stone tomb built by King Kheops (Khufu) in Egypt over twenty years, with a square base of 800 feet on each side and equal height, constructed by rotating gangs of 100,000 workers to serve as his burial-place.
