gizeh: A place in Lower Egypt near Memphis, site of the great pyramids, whose construction methods and costs Herodotus describes in detail.
canopic-mouth: One of the seven mouths of the Nile delta in northern Egypt, where Paris was driven ashore and where a temple of Heracles afforded sanctuary to his fleeing servants.
telemachus: Son of Odysseus and Penelope, to whom Menelaus recounts his wanderings in Egypt in the Odyssey.
hyksos: A foreign people who ruled Egypt for 106 years during a period of temple closure and national hardship, remembered by Egyptians with such hostility that they called the pyramids after a shepherd rather than honor the "shepherd kings'" names.
lower-egypt: The northern region of Egypt, comprising the Nile Delta and the valley north of Memphis.
elbo: An island in the Nile marshes where an Egyptian king lived in hiding for fifty years, built of ashes and earth, and remained undiscovered until the reign of Amyrtaeus.
hawara: An ancient Egyptian structure near Lake Moeris and the City of Crocodiles, consisting of a vast maze of twelve roofed courts and three thousand chambers (both above and below ground) built as a common memorial by multiple rulers, and surpassing even the pyramids in Herodotus' judgment.
egyptian-lake: A large artificial lake in Egypt near Memphis, said to drain underground toward the Libyan Syrtis, created by redirecting excavated earth to the Nile River.
patumus: An Arabian town on the Nile canal route from above Bubastis toward the Red Sea, through which Necho's canal was carried.
suez: A canal region in Egypt connecting the Nile to the Red Sea, begun by Necos and completed by Darius the Persian, running from near Bubastis southeastward through the Arabian foothills toward the Arabian Gulf.
tel-basta: The modern name for the site of ancient Bubastis in the Nile Delta of Egypt, near which Necos began his canal to the Red Sea.
the-camps: Two settlements on opposite banks of the Nile's Pelusian mouth, below Bubastis, where Psammetichus settled Ionian and Carian mercenaries who helped him gain Egypt, later relocated to Memphis by Amasis.
sebennytic-arm: One of the seven mouths of the Nile delta in Lower Egypt, where the city of Buto and its famous oracle of Leto are located.
city-of-crocodiles: A city in Upper Egypt near Lake Moeris, named for the sacred crocodiles kept there and famous as the site of the great labyrinth built by early Egyptian kings.
libyan-syrtis: A large gulf or bay on the coast of Libya (North Africa), notorious for its dangerous shallows and shifting sands, into which an Egyptian lake was said by local sources to drain underground.
mogdol: A fortified town in northern Egypt or the Sinai peninsula, site of Pharaoh Necos II's victory over the Syrians.
natho: A district in Egypt, half of which was inhabited by the Hermotubies, a warrior class exempt from other trades.
sebennys: An Egyptian district in the Nile Delta, one of the regions from which the Kalasiries (the warrior caste) were recruited.
thmuis: A district in the Nile Delta region of Egypt, one of the home territories of the Kalasiries (Egyptian warrior caste).
athribis: An Egyptian city in the Nile Delta, one of the districts from which the Kalasiries (Egyptian warrior caste) were drawn.
pharbaithis: An Egyptian district in the Nile Delta, one of the regions from which the Kalasiries (a warrior class) were drawn.
aphthis: A district of Lower Egypt, one of several regions from which the Kalasiries (Egyptian warrior caste) were recruited.
onuphis: A district in the Nile Delta whose inhabitants were enrolled as Kalasiries (a warrior class) under the Egyptian military system.
anytis: A district of Lower Egypt, among the nomes from which the Kalasiries (warrior caste) were recruited.
myecphoris: An Egyptian district or nome in the Nile Delta, located on an island opposite Bubastis, home to part of the Kalasiries warrior class.
siuph: A town in the Saïs district of Egypt, birthplace of King Amasis (r. 570–526 BC).
hellenion: A joint sanctuary in Naucratis founded by nine Greek cities (four Ionian, four Dorian, and one Aeolian) where Greek traders worshipped their gods in Egypt under King Amasis.
round-pond: A circular artificially-constructed lake at Sais in Egypt, comparable in size to the sacred lake at Delos known as the Round Pond.
corcyreans: Greek inhabitants of the island of Corcyra (Corfu) in the Ionian Sea, whose friendship Amasis of Egypt sought partly through his marriage to Ladice.
aeolian-greeks: Greeks from Aeolia (a region of western Asia Minor) who served as soldiers in Cambyses' Persian army during his invasion of Egypt.
corys: A river in Arabia that flows into the Red Sea, mentioned in a legendary account of how the Arabian king supposedly supplied water to the desert during Cambyses' campaign.
mytileneans: Greeks from the island of Lesbos whose deaths at Memphis during Cambyses' conquest of Egypt were avenged by the Persian king through the execution of ten Egyptian nobles for each Mytilenean lost.
khargeh: An oasis settlement in the Egyptian desert, seven days' march southwest of Thebes across sand, where a Persian expeditionary force under Cambyses is said to have disappeared en route to attack the Ammonians.
luxor: A city in Upper Egypt on the Nile, where Herodotus reports an unprecedented rainfall occurred during the reign of Psammenitus as a portent before the Persian conquest.
mytilenean: Inhabitants of Mytilene, a Greek island city in the Aegean, whose ship Cambyses commandeered as a herald's vessel to the besieged Egyptians at Memphis.
carpathus: An island in the Aegean Sea between Rhodes and Crete, where Samian exiles paused during their voyage to or from Egypt before seeking aid from Sparta against the tyrant Polycrates.
islands-of-the-blest: An oasis settlement in the Libyan desert seven days' march south-west of Thebes, identified by Greeks with a mythical blessed land, where a Persian army under Cambyses vanished while marching against the Ammonians.
aeschrionian: A Samian tribe, some of whom inhabited the Oasis city (called Islands of the Blest by Greeks), seven days' march from Thebes.
callatiae: An Indian people who practice ritual consumption of their deceased parents, cited by Herodotus as evidence that all nations regard their own customs as superior to others.
megarian: A Greek people from Megara, a city-state in the Corinthiad; Eupalinus the renowned engineer of the tunnel under the hill at Samos was born among them.
corcyraean: Greeks living on the island of Corcyra off the northwest coast of Greece, whose young men were once sent by the Corinthian tyrant Periander to be castrated but were rescued by the Samians, creating lasting enmity between Corinth and Samos that motivated Corinthian support for the expedition against Samos.
hydrea: An island near the Peloponnesus, taken by the Samians from Hermione and left in the keeping of Troezen as a temporary deposit.
gaubaruwa: A Persian of unknown rank who joined the seven conspirators against the Magus and became one of the seven who later drew lots to choose Persia's king.
asiatics: A collective term for the subject peoples of the Persian empire, who under the usurper Magus enjoyed tax and military exemptions and regretted his death, unlike the Persians themselves.
lasonians: An Anatolian people of western Asia Minor who, together with the Mysians, Lydians, Cabalians, and Hytennians, formed the second satrapy under Darius and paid five hundred talents of annual tribute.
utana: A Persian noble who first suspected the false Smerdis and organized the conspiracy of seven against the Magi usurper at Susa.
posideion: A city on the Cilician and Syrian border, founded by Amphilochus son of Amphiaraus, marking the northwestern boundary of the Persian fifth tax-province.
cabalians: A people of Asia Minor who, together with the Mysians, Lydians, Lasonians, and Hytennians, formed the second satrapy under Darius and paid five hundred talents of annual tribute.
sattagydae: A people of the Persian Empire who, together with the Gandarii, Dadicae, and Aparytae, formed the seventh taxation province and paid one hundred and seventy talents collectively.
hellespontians: The Hellespontians were inhabitants of the region on the right (north) side of the Hellespont (Dardanelles strait), grouped in Darius's third Persian satrapy and liable for tribute.
white-wall: A Persian garrison and supply depot at Memphis in Egypt, provisioned with grain for troops stationed there under Achaemenid rule.
hytennians: An Anatolian people subject to the Persian Empire under Darius, grouped with the Mysians, Lydians, Lasonians, and Cabalians in the second satrapy and assessed at five hundred talents of tribute.
gandarii: A people of the eastern Persian empire who, together with the Sattagydae, Dadicae, and Aparytae, paid a collective tribute of one hundred and seventy talents as the seventh satrapy.
aparytae: A people of the seventh Persian satrapy who, together with the Sattagydae, Gandarii, and Dadicae, paid one hundred and seventy talents in tribute.
pausicae: A people of inland Asia, located east of the Caspian region, who paid tribute to the Persian king Darius as part of the eleventh satrapial province.
sarangeis: A people of the Persian Empire's fourteenth satrapy, grouped with the Sagartii, Thamanaei, Utii, and Myci in paying six hundred talents of tribute.
pantimathi: A people of the Caspian region who, together with the Caspii, Pausicae, and Daritae, formed the eleventh satrapy under Darius and paid two hundred talents in tribute.
daritae: A people of the eleventh Persian satrapy who, together with the Caspii, Pausicae, and Pantimathi, contributed two hundred talents to Darius' provincial tax system.
aegli: A people dwelling east of Bactria in the Persian tribute system, forming the eastern boundary of the twelfth satrapy.
utii: An Iranian tribe included in the fourteenth satrapy of the Persian empire under Darius I, grouped with the Sagartii, Sarangeis, Thamanaei, and Myci, contributing to a collective tribute of six hundred talents.
orthocorybantians: A people of Media who, together with the Paricanians, formed part of the tenth satrapy under Darius and contributed four hundred and fifty talents of silver to the Persian crown.
myci: A people included in the fourteenth Persian satrapy along with the Sagartii and others, contributing to a tribute of six hundred talents.
sogdi: A people of Central Asia, grouped with Parthians, Chorasmians, and Arii in the sixteenth Persian satrapy, contributing three hundred talents to Darius' tribute.
arii: A people of the Persian Empire grouped with Parthians, Chorasmians, and Sogdi in the sixteenth satrapy, paying three hundred talents in tribute.
saspiri: A people of Asia Minor, grouped in the eighteenth tribute province of Persia along with the Matieni and Alarodii, required to pay two hundred talents annually.
caucasus-mountains: A mountain range forming the northern boundary of the Persian Empire's dominion, beyond which lay peoples independent of Persian rule.
nubia: A region south of Egypt inhabited by Ethiopians who, after Cambyses' conquest, paid the Persian king biennial gifts of gold, ebony, and ivory rather than tribute.
padaei: A nomadic, raw-flesh-eating Indian tribe who ritually killed and ate their sick and elderly.
paricanii: A people of Asia Minor included in the seventeenth satrapy of the Persian empire, who paid four hundred talents in tribute.
indian-callantiae: An Indian people who cultivated the same crops as certain Ethiopians and lived underground, required to send gifts rather than tribute to the Persian king.
alarodii: A people of Asia Minor grouped with the Matieni and Saspiri in the eighteenth Persian tax province, contributing two hundred talents of tribute.
caspapyrus: A town in northernmost India near the Pactyic country, where warlike Indians dwell and venture into sandy deserts to collect gold-dust excavated by giant ants.
tin-islands: An island or islands located at the far western or northern edge of the known world, source of tin for the Mediterranean, whose precise location Herodotus acknowledges he cannot verify.
afghanistan: Northern region beyond the Indus valley, inhabited by Caspatyrians and Pactyae who resemble Bactrians in warfare and are sent to extract gold from giant ants' sand in the arid wastes.
cnidos: A Greek city whose inhabitants enjoyed friendly relations with Tarentum in Italy, chosen by the exiled Tarentine Gillus as his escort back home on Darius' orders.
cnossus: A major city on Crete, legendary home of King Minos, whom Herodotus calls the first to rule the sea among what may be called the human race.
cabul: A town in the territory of the Caspatyrians in northern India, near the Pactyic country, from which gold-digging Indians venture into the desert.
sarangians: A people inhabiting a mountainous plain in Asia bounded by the Chorasmians, Hyrcanians, Parthians, and Thamanaei, who depended on the river Aces for irrigation until Persian kings blocked its flow and controlled water access as a form of taxation.
chaldean: A Babylonian priestly caste of astrologers and diviners, after whom a gate of Babylon was named.
ninevites: Inhabitants of Nineveh, whose name designated a gate of Babylon through which Zopyrus arranged for Darius's forces to gain entry.
belian: Belian is a gate of Babylon, opened by Zopyrus to admit the Persians during Darius' siege; it is misclassified as a people rather than a place.
babylons: A major city of Mesopotamia, conquered by Darius with the aid of the self-disfigured general Zopyrus, whom Darius valued so highly that he declared he would not trade it for twenty additional Babylons.
tauric-mountains: A mountain range in Scythia, forming part of the southeastern boundary of Scythian territory near the Maeetian lake, used by the sons of Scythian slaves and their masters' wives to dig a defensive trench against returning Scythian warriors.
katiari: A Scythian clan descended from the legendary Arpoxaïs, one of three brothers in the mythical origin-account of the Scythian people.
auchatae: A Scythian clan descended from the legendary Lipoxaïs and considered one of the four main Scythian peoples in their own genealogical traditions.
traspians: A Scythian clan, said to descend from Arpoxaïs and dwelling in the steppes north of the Black Sea, counted among the Skoloti peoples.
paralatae: A Scythian clan descended from Kolaxais, the youngest of three brothers, named after their eponymous ancestor Paralatae.
cimmeria: A region north of the Black Sea in Scythia, vacated by the Cimmerians when they fled southward before Scythian invasion into Asia Minor and Media.
metapontum: A city in southern Italy where, according to local tradition, the spirit of Aristeas the Proconnesian appeared and instructed the inhabitants to erect an altar and statue to Apollo, which they maintained in the marketplace.
scythian-greeks: Greeks living in Scythia north of the Borysthenites who adopted Scythian ways but also cultivated grain and other crops.
erythea: An island in the far western Ocean near Gadira beyond the Pillars of Heracles, legendary home of the giant Geryones whose cattle Heracles drove away.
proconnesian: Inhabitants of Proconnesus, an island in the Sea of Marmara, home of the prophet Aristeas.
olbia: A Greek trading post on the northern coast of the Black Sea (in modern Ukraine), located at the mouth of the Borysthenes river and serving as a port for commerce with the Scythian interior.
skoloti: A Scythian people named after their king, comprising three clans (Auchatae, Katiari, Traspians, and Paralatae) who inhabited the steppes north of the Black Sea and were known to Greeks as Scythians.
panticapes-river: A river in Scythia that forms the boundary between the agricultural Scythians to the west and the nomadic Scythians to the east.
iyrkae: A hunting people living east of the Thyssagetae in the steppes north of the Black Sea, who pursue game from trees while riding trained horses and using dogs.
olbiopolitae: Greek colonists settled on the Hypanis River in the region of the Borysthenes (modern Dnieper), who named themselves after their city Olbia and distinguished the neighboring Scythian farming peoples from true Scythians.
argippeans: A bald, snub-nosed people dwelling in the foothills of mountains beyond Scythia, subsisting on the fruit of the Pontic tree, revered as sacred arbiters of disputes among neighboring tribes and sanctuary for the exiled.
cossacks: Not in Herodotus; the people described at 4.23 are the Argippeans, not Cossacks.
pontic: The tree, called "Pontic," whose fruit sustains the bald, sacred Argippeans dwelling beyond the Scythian foothills.
the-cliffs: A port on the Maeetian (Sea of Azov) lake, marking the eastern boundary of the territory of the Royal Scythians.
gerrus-river: A river in Scythia marking the eastern boundary of nomadic Scythian territory, fourteen days' journey east of the Panticapes.
gerrus: A river in Scythia north of the Black Sea, marking the western boundary of the territory of the Royal Scythians.
syrian-palestine: A coastal region stretching from Phoenicia southward along the Mediterranean toward Egypt, forming part of the broad peninsula between Persia and the sea.
myriandric-gulf: A gulf near Phoenicia forming the southern starting point of the peninsula stretching west to the Triopian headland.
solois: A promontory on the Libyan coast west of the Pillars of Heracles, rounded by Sataspes in his attempted circumnavigation of Libya.
melian: Inhabitants of the region on the Melian Gulf in Greece, between Thessaly and Euboea, through which sacred offerings from the Hyperboreans were said to travel en route to Delos.
caryanda: A Greek coastal city in Caria (southwest Asia Minor), home to the explorer Scylax whom Darius commissioned to navigate the Indus River and sail to Egypt.
ocean-river: A river Herodotus regarded as a mistaken invention of mapmakers who pictured it encircling a perfectly round earth.
araxes-river: A river flowing eastward that forms the northern boundary of inhabited Asia beyond Persia, between the Caspian Sea and the lands toward India.
sindi: A people dwelling east of the Cimmerian Bosporus, accessible to Scythians by crossing the frozen sea in winter.
cape-cantin: A promontory on the Libyan coast west of the Pillars of Heracles, rounded by Sataspes during his incomplete circumnavigation of Libya.
colchian-phasis-river: A river in Colchis (in the Caucasus region east of the Black Sea) that Herodotus cites as one traditional boundary between Europe and Asia, though he expresses skepticism about such divisions.
maeetian-tanais-river: A river of the Scythian region north of the Black Sea, sometimes proposed as a boundary between Europe and Asia.
egyptian-nile-river: The great river of Egypt, forming the boundary between Africa and Asia in Herodotus' geographical scheme of the world.
cimmerian-ferries: A strait or passage in the Cimmerian Bosporus region (between the Black Sea and Sea of Azov), proposed by some as a boundary between Europe and Asia.
porata: A river of Scythia (called Pyretus by Greeks), flowing east to join the Ister and one of five major tributaries that make the Ister the greatest river known.
asiad: An aristocratic clan at Sardis in Lydia, said by Lydians to descend from Asies son of Cotys, and invoked to support their claim that Asia was named after this ancestor rather than Prometheus' wife.
maris-river: A river flowing from the Agathyrsi that mingles with the Danube (Ister) in the region north of the Balkans.
pyretus: A river in Scythia, known to the Scythians as Porata and to the Greeks as Pyretus, flowing eastward into the Ister (Danube) and reckoned among the five great tributaries that make the Ister the mightiest river known to Herodotus.
auras: A river flowing northward from the heights of Haemus into the Ister (Danube), in the region north of Thrace.
tibisis: A river flowing north from the heights of Haemus into the Danube (Ister), one of three major tributaries originating from that mountain range.
scythian-river: A major river system of Scythia, specifically the Ister (Danube) and its five Scythian tributaries (Porata/Pyretus, Tiarantus, Ararus, Naparis, Ordessus), which together form the greatest river known to Herodotus and flow eastward through the Scythian country into the Black Sea region.
balkan: A mountain range in Thrace and the Balkans from which several tributaries of the Danube flow northward into the Ister.
athrys: A river in Thrace flowing into the Ister (Danube) from the territory of the Crobyzi.
alps: A mountain range in northern Europe from which the Alpis river flows northward to join the Danube (Ister), marking the western extent of Herodotus' knowledge of the continent's interior geography.
angrus-river: A river flowing north from Illyria into the Triballic plain, where it joins the Brongus before emptying into the Danube (Ister).
carpathians: A mountain range in Europe north of the Danube (Ister), located in the territory north of the Ombrici, from which rivers flow northward into the Danube.
crobyzi: A Thracian people whose territory lay north of the Danube, from which three rivers (Athrys, Noes, and Artanes) flowed into the Ister.
noes: A river flowing into the Danube (Ister) from Thrace, in the country of the Crobyzi.
cius-river: A river flowing through the middle of Haemus mountain from the territory of the Paeonians and the Rhodope range, tributary to the Danube (Ister).
carpis: A river flowing north from the region north of the Ombrici into the Danube (Ister).
alpis: A river flowing north from the country of the Ombrici into the Ister (Danube), situated in the region north of the Ombrici in central Europe.
neurian: A northern people dwelling beyond Scythia, whose territory bordered Scythia along the Tyras river and a great lake.
brongus: A river flowing northward from the Triballic plain into the Danube (Ister), receiving the Angrus river.
sacred-ways: A spring in Scythia on the border between the farming Scythians and Alazones, whose bitter waters contaminate the Hypanis River; also the name of the place where it rises.
brongus-river: A river flowing northward into the Danube (Ister) from the Triballic plain in what is now the Balkans.
gerrhan: A Scythian people after whose land the Borysthenes is named known, marking the limit of forty days' navigable travel upstream from the river's mouth.
dniester: A river of Scythia flowing from the north out of a great lake that marks the boundary between Scythian and Neurian lands, with a Greek settlement called Tyritae at its mouth.
tyritae: Greek inhabitants of a settlement at the mouth of the Tyras river on the northern coast of the Black Sea, near the boundary between Scythian and Neurian lands.
cynetes: A people of the far southwestern Iberian Peninsula, said to be the westernmost dwellers in Europe.
panticapas: A river of Scythia flowing from the north into a lake, running south through territory of the farming Scythians before joining the Borysthenes.
hypacuris-river: A river of Scythia rising from a lake, flowing through nomadic Scythian territory and emptying near Carcine, with the Woodland and the Racecourse of Achilles bordering its right bank.
lesbian: A Greek island people of the Aegean, known for a distinctive type of bowl that Herodotus uses as a point of comparison for Scythian cooking vessels.
nomads: Nomadic peoples dwelling in the steppes north of the Black Sea, whose territory was divided from that of the Royal Scythians by the river Gerrhus.
don: A river of Scythia that rises from a great lake and flows into the Maeetian Lake, forming a boundary between the Royal Scythians and the Sauromatae.
enarees: Hermaphrodites among the Scythians who practiced divination using braided lime-tree bark, which they attributed to a gift from Aphrodite.
hyrgis: A river tributary of the Tanaïs in the region north of the Black Sea, flowing through Scythian territory.
dobrudja: A region in the northwestern Black Sea area, north of Thrace and the Danube, inhabited by the Getae.
sindic: A people dwelling in the region east of the Black Sea (Pontus), used here as a geographical reference point for measuring the sea's width.
donetz: A river in the Scythian region that flows from a great lake into the Maeetian Lake, separating the Royal Scythians from the Sauromatae.
borysthenite: Greeks inhabiting the city of Borysthenes on the north coast of the Black Sea, known for their practice of Dionysian rites which scandalized the neighboring Scythians.
themiscura: A town on the Thermodon river in Pontus (Black Sea region), marking the greatest width of the sea eastward from the Sindic coast, which Herodotus uses as a reference point for measuring the Pontus.
ister-river: The great river flowing into the Black Sea from the north (modern Danube), where Darius commanded his Ionian fleet to construct a bridge during his Scythian campaign.
tearus-river: A river in Thrace whose sources Darius reached during his campaign across Europe after crossing the Bosporus (4.89).
thermodon-river: A river on the southern coast of the Pontus (Black Sea), at Themiscura, marking the greatest width of that sea according to Herodotus' measurements.
contadesdus-river: A river of Thrace, tributary of the Agrianes (itself a tributary of the Hebrus, which empties into the sea near Aenus), and which receives the Tearus.
artescus: A river flowing through the country of the Odrysae in Thrace, where Darius I ordered his army to deposit stones as they crossed during his Scythian campaign.
odrysae: A Thracian people whose territory lay east of the Artescus river, through which Darius passed during his Scythian campaign.
cyrmianae: A Thracian people living around Salmydessus and above Apollonia and Mesambria on the Black Sea coast, who submitted without resistance to Darius' invasion.
carcinitis: A city marking the southern boundary of ancient Scythia along the Black Sea coast, west of the Tauric Peninsula.
orthosian: A people or tribe whose identity is not specified in the passage, known only from an epithet applied to Artemis at Byzantium (Orthosian Artemis), to whose altar the Byzantines repurposed two marble pillars set up by Darius.
thoricus: A deme of Attica on the coast of the Sunium peninsula, used by Herodotus as a geographic reference point for comparing the scale and projection of the Tauric peninsula into the Pontus.
salmydessus: A coastal Thracian region on the Black Sea, located between Apollonia and Mesambria, whose inhabitants surrendered to Darius without resistance during his Scythian campaign.
rough-peninsula: A promontory jutting into the eastern sea at the southeasternmost extremity of the Tauric peninsula in Scythia.
anaphlystus: A deme or town in Attica on the southern coast of the Sunium peninsula, used by Herodotus as a geographical reference point to help readers visualize the shape and position of the Tauric territory on the northern shore of the Pontus.
nipsaei: A Thracian people inhabiting the coast and inland regions above Apollonia and Mesambria who submitted without resistance to Darius during his Scythian campaign.
calabria: A promontory in southern Italy, located between the harbors of Brundisium and Tarentum, used by Herodotus as an analogical example for the shape and position of the Tauric peninsula.
brindisi: Brindisi (Brundisium), a harbor city in Calabria, southern Italy, cited by Herodotus in a comparison illustrating the shape of the Tauric peninsula.
tauris: A mountainous peninsula in the northern Black Sea (modern Crimea), inhabited by the Tauric people and projecting into the sea like Attica's Sunium.
taranto: A promontory in southern Italy (Calabria) that Herodotus uses as a geographical analogy for the projection of the Tauric Peninsula into the Pontus.
sauromatic: A people inhabiting territory east of the Scythians in the steppes north of the Black Sea and the Caucasus, through which Darius' Persian army marched during the Scythian campaign.
oiorpata: A warlike people whom the Scythians called by this name (meaning "killers of men" in Scythian), identified by Greeks as Amazons, who after being captured by Greeks in a war at the Thermodon seized ships and eventually reached Scythian territory.
calabrian: An Italian region (the heel of the peninsula) used here as a geographical analogy for understanding the Tauric peninsula's position relative to Scythia.
lake-maeetis: A shallow inland sea north of the Black Sea and east of the Tanaïs river, serving as a boundary marker for the lands of the Sauromatae.
amazon: A legendary nation of warrior women dwelling east of the Scythians, whom they encountered during the Scythians' wars with the Massagetae and subsequently interbred with, eventually settling near the Tanais river.
chersonesites: Greeks inhabiting the Chersonese (Gallipoli peninsula) on the Hellespont, ruled by Miltiades in the Ionian Revolt of c. 500 BC.
maeetians: A people inhabiting the region around the Maeetian Lake (Sea of Azov), through whose land four great rivers—the Lycus, Oarus, Tanaïs, and Syrgis—flowed from the country of the Thyssagetae.
oarus: A river flowing from the country of the Thyssagetae through the land of the Maeetians into the Maeetian lake (modern Sea of Azov).
oarus-river: A river in Scythia where Darius halted his pursuit of the Scythians and established a line of forts during his campaign in the region.
pyrgus: A city in the region of Elis in the northwestern Peloponnese, founded by the Minyae after they were driven out of Lacedaemon and subsequently conquered by the Eleans.
macistus: A city in the territory of the Paroreatae and Caucones in southern Greece, founded by Minyae refugees and later sacked by the Eleans.
cymae: An Aeolian city whose representative Aristagoras was among those who opposed Miltiades' plan to bridge the Danube under Darius.
pagasaean: Greeks from Thessaly (specifically the region around Pagasae, a port city) who were among the Argonauts' descendants and later settled in Lacedaemon after being expelled from Lemnos by the Pelasgians.
epium: A city established by Minyae refugees in the territory of the Paroreatae and Caucones, subsequently captured by the Eleans.
lacedamonians: The Spartans (Lacedaemonians) of southern Greece, who imprisoned and attempted to execute the Minyae, a group of colonists who had demanded a share of kingship and committed sacrilege.
phrixae: A city in the region of Elis in the western Peloponnese, founded by Minyae refugees who drove out the Paroreatae and Caucones, later sacked by the Eleans.
nudium: A city in Elis established by Minyae refugees who migrated to the western Peloponnese after escaping Lacedaemonian captivity, later captured by the Eleans.
triphylia: A region in the northwestern Peloponnese, seized from the Paroreatae and Caucones by Minyae who founded six cities there, most later taken and sacked by the Eleans.
itanus: A town on the island of Crete where Theraean messengers met the murex fisherman Corobius, who had knowledge of Libya.
thestes: A spring in Libya near Irasa, where Cyrenaeans defeated an Egyptian army sent by Apries.
leucon: A place in Libya where Cyrenaean soldiers under Arcesilaus were decisively defeated by eastern Libyans, with seven thousand Cyrenaean troops killed.
bomba: An island off the Libyan coast where Theraean colonists were initially guided by the fisherman Corobius before establishing their permanent settlement.
minyan: A Greek clan whose members included Euphemus and his descendant Battus, who founded Cyrene in Libya under Delphi's command.
plynus: A harbor on the Libyan coast marking the western boundary of Adyrmachidae territory, west of Egypt.
argolic: Argolic denotes people of the Argolid region of Greece, here describing a style of bronze cauldron made there.
tauchira: A coastal town in the Barcaean region of Libya, situated in the territory of the Bacales tribe.
aphrodisias: An island off the Libyan coast west of Cyrene, marking the western boundary of the Giligamae territory and lying near the Cyrenaean colonial settlements of Platea and Aziris.
psylli: A Libyan people who occupied territory on the borders of the Nasamones near the Syrtis, said to have been entirely destroyed when a south wind dried their water sources and buried them in the desert.
maraphian: A general of the Egyptian forces whom Aryandes appointed to lead an expedition supporting Pheretime against Barce; his tribal origin is otherwise unidentified in the text.
phla: An island in the Tritonian lake of Libya, where according to oracle the Lacedaemonians were instructed to establish a colony.
aseans: A Libyan people living near the Triton river, with the Maxyes located west of them.
bacales: A small Libyan tribe dwelling inland in the territory between Barce and Cyrene, with coastal access at Tauchira, whose customs resembled those of the inland peoples west of Cyrene.
cyrauis: An island off the coast of Libya near Carthage, said to be twenty-five miles long and rich in olives and vines, noted for a lake from which gold-dust was allegedly extracted.
sigynnae: A people north of the Danube wearing Median dress and claiming Median origin, said to breed small shaggy long-haired horses unfit for riding but swift at drawing chariots.
caucasian: The Sigynnae, wrongly indexed under "Caucasian," are a people dwelling north of the Ister who claim descent from Median colonists and are noted for their small, shaggy horses used to draw chariots.
zauekes: A Libyan people, neighbors of the Maxyes, whose women drove chariots to war.
sigynni: A people living north of the Danube beyond Scythia, wearing Median dress and claiming Median origin, known for small shaggy-haired horses unfit for riding but swift in harness, with territory said to reach nearly to the Eneti on the Adriatic.
massalia: A Greek coastal city on the Mediterranean coast of southern Gaul (modern France), mentioned as a reference point for the inland Ligurian peoples.
euhesperitae: A Libyan people dwelling in a fertile coastal region west of the Cinyps, whose land produced grain yields of up to a hundredfold.
mytilenaean: Inhabitants of Mytilene, the principal city of the island of Lesbos, whose representative Coes served Darius as a counselor and was rewarded with a tyranny.
gyzantes: A Libyan people living in the mountains west of Egypt, known for honey production and for painting themselves with vermilion and hunting the apes abundant in their region.
pangaeaneast-of-the-strymon-mountains: A mountain range east of the Strymon river in Thrace, whose inhabitants near the Prasiad lake resisted Persian conquest under Megabazus.
siriopaeones: A Paeonian tribe living in the region toward the Prasiad lake, deported to Asia by Megabazus' Persian army.
orbelus: A mountain in Thrace north of the Prasiad lake, from which the lake-dwellers obtain piles for building their platform settlements.
cyclades: A group of islands in the Aegean Sea near Ionia, including Naxos, Paros, and Andros, that Aristagoras proposed as a Persian military objective as a springboard for attacking Euboea.
cycladic-islands: A group of Aegean islands (including Naxos) lying southeast of mainland Greece, at this time independent of Persian rule and wealthy enough to attract the attention of ambitious Ionian Greeks seeking military support to restore exiled factions.
myndian: A people whose territory included the city of Myndus in Caria (southwestern Asia Minor), represented here by the ship captain Scylax in the failed Persian expedition against Naxos.
lamponium: A town in the Troad (northwestern Asia Minor) captured by the Persian general Otanes in his campaign to extend Persian control over Thracian and Aegean territories.
caucasa: A harbor on the island of Chios where Megabates anchored the Persian fleet before its attempted assault on Naxos, but where a quarrel between Megabates and Aristagoras led to the Naxians being warned of the expedition.
dysorum: A mountain range forming the natural border between Thrace and Macedonia, which travelers crossing from the Prasiad lake region must traverse to enter Macedonia.
myndus: A city in Caria (southwestern Asia Minor) whose ship participated in Aristagoras' expedition against Naxos, notable when its captain Scylax was brutally punished by Megabates for negligent watch-duty.
eleon: A town in Boeotia, Greece, home of Antichares who advised the Spartan Dorieus to found a colony at Heraclea in Sicily based on oracles of Laius.
heraclea: A coastal settlement in Sicily near Mount Eryx in the west, where Dorieus attempted to establish a colony on the advice of an oracle but was prevented by Carthaginian and Phoenician opposition.
minoa: A colony founded by Selinus on the coast of Sicily, which Euryleon captured after the destruction of Dorieus' expedition.
mt-eryx: A mountain in Sicily associated with Heracles, whose territory Dorieus sought to claim by founding a colony at nearby Heraclea.
erycine: A region in southern Italy near Sybaris and Croton, contested between those cities and site of Dorieus' fatal attempt at colonization.
cilica: A region in Asia Minor between Cappadocia and Armenia, traversable in three stages along the Persian royal road, with the Euphrates as its boundary toward Armenia.
encheleis: A region in Illyria to which the Cadmeans of Thebes fled after being expelled by the Argives during the reign of Laodamas.
matienian: A people inhabiting a region east of Armenia through which the Persian Royal Road passed, crossed by the Tigris and other navigable rivers, on the way to Susa.
gephyrae: A clan/people of Phoenician origin claiming Eretrian descent who settled in Boeotia then migrated to Athens as restricted citizens, including the assassins of Hipparchus.
heracleum: A sanctuary of Heracles in Attica near Athens, serving as a landmark to identify the location of Anchimolius' tomb.
gephyreans: A family of Athenian origin to which the assassins of the tyrant Hipparchus belonged, later prominent in efforts to overthrow Peisistratid rule.
archelaoi: A Sicyonian tribe renamed by Cleisthenes (tyrant of Sicyon) after himself, meaning "rulers of the people," to distinguish it from the mockingly-named Dorian tribes he imposed on the city.
swinites: One of four Doric tribes established by Cleisthenes of Sicyon, named mockingly after swine (the name derived from a word for 'pig' with a modified ending).
lipsydrium: A fortified stronghold north of Paeonia in Attica, where the Alcmeonidae and exiled Athenians made a failed attempt to overthrow the Pisistratid tyrants.
conium: A city in Thessaly, home of King Cineas who led a thousand horsemen sent by the Thessalians to aid the Pisistratidae against a Spartan invasion of Attica.
hylleis: One of three Dorian tribal names that the Sicyonians adopted after abandoning the derisive names imposed by Cleisthenes, replacing the former "Swinites."
dymanatae: One of four Sicyonian tribes, named after Dymas, adopted to replace Cleisthenes' derogatory tribal names after his death.
pamphyli: A Dorian tribe that the Sicyonians adopted as one of their official tribal names after abandoning the insulting designations imposed by Cleisthenes.
assites: One of the mocking Dorian tribe-names ('ass-people') given by Cleisthenes at Sicyon, used for sixty years after his death until replaced along with the others.
oenoe: A border district of Attica that the Boeotians seized during Cleomenes' invasion of Attica around 510 BC.
sicyonian: A Greek people inhabiting Sicyon, a city-state in the Peloponnese whose tyrant Cleisthenes (grandfather of the Athenian reformer) reorganized tribal divisions, influencing later Athenian political reform.
porkites: A Sicyonian tribe named 'swine' by Cleisthenes, used for sixty years after his death until it was renamed along with the other tribes.
propylon: The entrance portico to the Athenian acropolis, on the left side of which stood a four-horse chariot dedicated from the ransom of captives taken from the Chalcidians and Boeotians.
aegialeis: An Ionic tribe of Sicyon named after Aegialeus son of Adrastus, adopted by the Sicyonians after they abandoned the mocking tribal names imposed by Cleisthenes.
lacedaimonians: A Greek people inhabiting the Peloponnese, whose representatives are addressed by Corinthian envoys warning against supporting tyranny and the restoration of Hippias to Athens.
phaleron: An Athenian coastal settlement that the Aeginetans raided by sea during their war against Athens in support of Thebes.
acheron: A river in Thesprotia (northwestern Greece) where an Oracle of the Dead allowed the living to communicate with deceased spirits, consulted by Periander concerning a lost deposit.
propylaea: The monumental gateway to the Athenian acropolis, situated at its entrance, where a bronze four-horse chariot dedicated from ransom money taken in the Boeotian and Chalcidian wars was displayed.
achilleum: A settlement held by the Mytilenaeans on the Troad coast, opposite Sigeum, over which they and the Athenians fought for control during the tyranny of Pisistratus.
coresus: A harbor or anchorage in the territory of Ephesus where the Ionian fleet landed before marching inland to attack Sardis during the Ionian Revolt.
pirene: A spring at Corinth, mentioned in an oracle warning the Bacchiadae of coming danger.
cayster: A river in western Asia Minor (modern Turkey) near Ephesus, mentioned as a geographical reference point in the Ionians' inland march during their revolt against Persian rule.
carpass: A headland at the eastern extremity of Cyprus, around which the Phoenician fleet sailed while the Persian land army marched toward Salamis during the Ionian revolt.
cap-st-andre: A headland in Cyprus through which Phoenician ships sailed while marching to aid the Persians against the Ionians during the Ionian Revolt.
abydus: A city on the Hellespont (modern Turkey), captured by the Persian general Daurises during the Ionian Revolt.
curium: A city on the island of Cyprus, reportedly founded by Argives, whose ruler Stesenor betrayed the Cypriot rebels to the Persians during the Ionian Revolt.
percote: A city on the Hellespont (Dardanelles strait) in the region of the Troad, captured by the Persian general Daurises in a single day during his suppression of the Ionian Revolt.
soli: A Cyprian city that resisted Persian siege longer than any other Cypriot settlement during the Ionian Revolt, finally falling in the fifth month when the Persians tunneled under its walls.
pedasus: A city in Caria (southwestern Asia Minor) where the Carians ambushed and destroyed a Persian army under Daurises, killing the generals and inflicting a major defeat during the Ionian Revolt.
samnians: An Ionian people whose warriors distinguished themselves for bravery in the naval battle against the Phoenicians during the Ionian revolt.
cius: A city in Mysia on the Propontis, captured by the Persian general Hymaees during his campaign against the Ionians and their allies.
cindya: A Carian city in the southwestern region of Asia Minor, home to Pixodarus who advised the Carians before their battle against the Persians at the White Pillars.
labraunda: A sanctuary of Zeus of Armies in Caria (inland from the coast of Asia Minor), famous for its sacred grove of plane-trees where the defeated Carians took refuge after their battle against the Persians at the Marsyas river.
idria: A region in Caria (southwestern Asia Minor) from which the river Marsyas flows into the Maeander, mentioned as a geographical reference point during the Carian revolt against Persian rule.
parius: A city on the Hellespont (Dardanelles strait) in the Troad region of northwestern Asia Minor, which Daurises besieged during the Ionian Revolt but abandoned when news of Carian revolt reached him.
edonia: A region in Thrace where Myrcinus, a fortified settlement given to Histiaeus by Darius, was located and considered by Aristagoras as a potential refuge during the Ionian Revolt.
gergithae: A remnant of the ancient Trojans dwelling in the territory of Ilium in the Troad, conquered by the Persian general Hymaees during his campaigns in Asia Minor.
panionium: A sanctuary and meeting-place of the Ionians, where their representatives gathered to deliberate on common defense against Persian attack.
didyman: A Milesian tribe or people; the passage refers to the shrine and temple at Didyma, not to an ethnic or tribal group named Didyman.
laus: A city in southern Italy where Sybarite refugees settled after their city's destruction by Crotoniates.
ampe: A city on the Persian Gulf near the mouth of the Tigris River, where King Darius settled captive Milesians after their defeat.
prieneans: Ionic Greeks inhabiting Priene on the coast of Asia Minor who contributed twelve ships to the Ionian fleet against the Persians at the battle of Lade.
scidrus: A city in southern Italy where Sybarite refugees settled after their city was destroyed by Croton.
crotoniates: The people of Croton, a Greek city in southern Italy, who destroyed Sybaris, Miletus's close ally.
italiot: Greek term for the Greek inhabitants of southern Italy.
sicilian: Inhabitants of Sicily, generally referring to the island's native and Greek populations rather than a specific event.
mysian: A people inhabiting the region around the Caicus plain in northwest Asia Minor (modern Turkey), whose grain-producing lands were targeted by Histiaeus during his flight from Thasos.
epizephyrian: A Greek people of Sicily living in the region west of the Strait of Messina, through whose territory the Samians passed on their way to seize Zancle.
thracian-dolonci: A Thracian tribe holding the Chersonese (Gallipoli peninsula) who, defeated in war by the Apsinthians, consulted the Delphic oracle and were directed to seek a Greek founder, eventually receiving Miltiades son of Cypselus as their leader.
messina: A coastal region in Sicily facing Tyrrhenia (the Tyrrhenian Sea), where Zancle invited displaced Ionians to establish a settlement after the Persian Wars.
chaeronea: A city in Boeotia (central Greece) through which the Dolonci passed on their journey from Delphi to Athens seeking a founder for their Thracian settlement.
dascyleum: A city and seat of a Persian provincial governor near the Hellespont (Propontis), mentioned as the seat of Oebares son of Megabazus, before whom Cyzicus submitted to Persian rule.
pactye: A coastal settlement on the Thracian Chersonese opposite Cardia, marking the southern terminus of the isthmus that Miltiades fortified against Thracian raids.
bulair: A narrow isthmus in the Chersonese (Gallipoli peninsula) connecting the peninsula to the mainland, which Miltiades fortified by building a wall across its thirty-six-stadia width to protect the Greek settlers from Thracian raids.
coenyra: A location on the island of Thasos between which and Aenyra the Phoenicians worked gold and silver mines in a great hill, opposite Samothrace.
aenyra: A place on the island of Thasos between which and Coenyra the Phoenicians discovered famous gold and silver mines.
dug-forest: A gold-mining region on the Thasian mainland (in Thrace) that yielded approximately eighty talents annually and was a major source of the island of Thasos's wealth.
mr-ram: Crius son of Polycritus was an Aeginetan who defied King Cleomenes of Sparta's attempt to arrest Aeginetans, prompting Cleomenes to pun grimly on his name (Crius = ram).
phoenician-thasos: An island in the northern Aegean (off Thrace, opposite Samothrace) originally colonized by Phoenicians from the Levant, famous for its gold and silver mines worked by the Phoenician settlers.
stymphalian-lake: A freshwater lake in the Peloponnese (Arcadia) from which the river Erasinus flows underground before resurfacing near Argos.
stymphalian: A tribe of the Peloponnese whose territory contained the lake from which the river Erasinus flowed toward Argos.
hesipeia: A location near Tiryns in the Argolid where the Argives encamped opposite the Lacedaemonians during a military confrontation.
pheneus: A city of Arcadia in the Peloponnese, near which lay Nonacris, where the legendary water of the Styx was said to spring from a cliff.
chelmos: A mountain or high region in Arcadia where the waters of the Styx allegedly originate and flow down near the city of Nonacris, serving as a sacred oath-swearing site used by Cleomenes to bind Arcadian leaders.
old-city: A fortified position on Aegina where an anti-tyrant faction under Nicodromus was to seize power with Athenian support, but Athenian naval delays prevented timely intervention.
phigalea: A town in Arcadia in the Peloponnese, birthplace of the prophet Cleander who stirred up slaves in Tiryns against their masters.
argolid: A region in the southeastern Peloponnese that forms the territory of Argos, where Cleomenes and the Lacedaemonians landed with captured Aeginetan ships before attacking Aegina.
carystos: A city on the island of Euboea in the Aegean Sea, which initially resisted Persian demands for hostages and military support during Xerxes' invasion but was compelled to submit after siege and devastation of its territory.
rhenaea: An island lying across the water from Delos in the Aegean Sea, where Datis anchored his Persian fleet during his expedition to avoid desecrating the sacred island of Delos itself.
temenos: A coastal landing place in Eretrian territory on Euboea, where the Persian invasion force under Darius disembarked horses during their assault on the city of Eretria in 490 BC.
choereae: A settlement in Eretrian territory on Euboea where the Persians landed and disembarked horses during their attack on Eretria in 490 BC.
parthenian-mountain: A mountain above Tegea in Arcadia where the runner Philippides encountered the god Pan and received a message for Athens before the Battle of Marathon.
aegilea: A coastal settlement in Eretrian territory on Euboea where the Persian fleet landed to prepare their assault on Eretria during the campaign of 490 BC.
oropus: A town on the Boeotian coast opposite Euboea where Eretrians fled to escape the Persian invasion force attacking Eretria in 490 BC.
myconos: An Aegean island where the returning Persian commander Datis had a vision leading him to find and later return a stolen image of Apollo to Delos.
aegilia: An island belonging to the Styrians, used by the Persians to deposit enslaved Eretrians during the approach to Marathon in 490 BC.
theban-delium: A sanctuary of Apollo on the Theban coast facing Chalcis, to which a gilded image of Apollo stolen from Delos was eventually brought by oracle's command.
delium: A sanctuary of Apollo on the Boeotian coast opposite Chalcis, where a gilded Apollo statue taken by Datis was later brought by the Thebans on oracular command.
aetolian: A Greek people inhabiting the region of northwestern Greece (in the area later called Aetolia), from which the suitor Males came to compete for the hand of Agariste at Athens.
aetolia: A region of central Greece north of the Gulf of Corinth, from which Males, brother of the exceptionally strong Titormus, came as a suitor to the wedding-contest of Agariste.
paeus: A town in Azenia, Arcadia, homeland of the suitor Laphanes.
epidamnian: A Greek people inhabiting Epidamnus on the Ionian Gulf (in what is now Albania), represented here by Amphimnestus, a suitor competing for the hand of Agariste of Sicyon.
azenian: An Arcadian people inhabiting the town of Paeus in the Peloponnese, represented here by Laphanes son of Euphorion.
scopad: A Thessalian noble house; Diactorides of Crannon, a member of this family, competed for the hand of Agariste, daughter of the Athenian Cleisthenes.
crannon: A city in Thessaly, home of the Scopad family, from which Diactorides came as a suitor to Agariste of Athens.
nine-wells: A water source near Athens where Athenian children went to fetch water and were maltreated by the Pelasgians, prompting their expulsion from Attica.
hephaestians: Inhabitants of Hephaestia, a city on the island of Lemnos in the Aegean Sea, who submitted peacefully to Miltiades' Athenian expedition when ordered to leave the island, unlike the more resistant Myrinaeans.
olophyxus: A Greek town on the isthmus of Athos, intended by the Persians to become an island through the canal-cutting project.
thyssus: A Greek town on the isthmus of Athos, intended by Xerxes' Persians to be converted into an island through canal-digging.
myrinaeans: An Athenian-hostile Pelasgian community on Lemnos who resisted Miltiades' claim that the Chersonese was Athenian territory and were forced to submit by siege.
tyrodiza: A depot-city in the Perinthian region of Thrace where Xerxes' army stockpiled provisions during the Persian invasion of Greece.
critalla: A city in Cappadocia designated as the mustering point for Xerxes' invasion army before it marched westward toward Sardis and the Hellespont.
white-headland: A coastal promontory in Thrace where Xerxes' army stockpiled provisions during preparations for the invasion of Greece.
acrothoum: A Greek town in the Chalcidice on the isthmus of Mount Athos, one of several the Persians under Xerxes intended to isolate as an island by cutting a canal across the isthmus.
cydrara: A city in Phrygia on the border with Lydia, marked by a boundary pillar erected by Croesus.
perinthian: A Thracian people inhabiting the region around the city of Perinthus on the Propontis, mentioned as a supply depot location for Xerxes' invasion of Greece.
callatebus: A city in Lydia where the road from Phrygia to Sardis passes, notable for craftsmen who produce honey from wheat and tamarisks.
hermes-valley: A valley in Phrygia through which Xerxes' army marched en route to Sardis during the Persian invasion of Greece.
zemenik: A headland on the Chersonese in the Hellespont region, between Sestus and Madytus, opposite Abydos, where Xanthippus later captured and crucified the Persian governor Artayctes.
carene: A city in Mysia in northwestern Asia Minor, located inland between Atarneus and the plain of Thebe, through which Xerxes' army passed on its march to the Hellespont.
cane: A mountain in northwestern Anatolia (near Mysia and the Troad), passed on the left by Xerxes' army during its march toward the Hellespont.
rhoetium: A city on the Hellespont coast in the Troad, passed on the left by Xerxes' army as it marched from the Scamander toward Abydos.
adramytteum: A city in northwestern Asia Minor (Mysia) on the route of Xerxes' invasion army from Lydia toward the Hellespont.
ophryneum: A city in the Troad (northwestern Asia Minor) near the Hellespont, which Xerxes' army passed, keeping it on their left, between Rhoetium and Dardanus.
serreum: A headland in Thrace near the beach where Xerxes beached his fleet during his invasion of Greece, marking the eastern end of the strand near Doriscus.
stentor: A marsh in coastal Thrace near Aenus, which Xerxes' army passed on their westward march toward Doriscus.
teucrian-gergithae: A people inhabiting the region southeast of the Troad, dwelling on the right (south) of Xerxes' line of march as his army approached the Hellespont.
cephenes: An ancient people of western Asia, formerly called Cephenes by the Greeks but known as Artaei to themselves and their neighbors, later renamed Persians after the legendary Perses.
amyrgian-scythians: Scythian people dwelling in the region of the Amyrgia (in Central Asia), who fought in Xerxes' army under the Persian name Sacae, armed with bows, daggers, and sagaris axes.
artaei: A people of the Near East who called themselves by this name (though Greeks knew them as Cephenes), serving under Otanes in Xerxes' invasion force and equipped with characteristic Persian arms and armor.
sarangae: An Iranian people of central Asia who wore dyed garments and knee-high boots, armed with bows and Median spears, and served under Pherendates son of Megabazus in Xerxes' invasion army.
sogdians: An Iranian people of Central Asia who served in Xerxes' invading army of 480 BC under the commander Azanes, equipped like the Bactrians with Median bows and javelins.
paphlagonian: Inhabitants of Paphlagonia (on the Black Sea coast of Asia Minor), who served in Xerxes' invasion force with equipment similar to the Phrygians, under the command of Artochmes.
aryan: An ancient people of the Iranian plateau formerly called by this name, whom Herodotus identifies with the Medes and who, according to their own account, adopted the name Medes after Medea the Colchian came from Athens to their land.
briges: A people who dwelt in Europe as neighbors of Macedonia before migrating to Asia, where they became known as Phrygians.
persians-cappadocians: Syrians (Cappadocians) called so by the Persians; a people of Asia Minor equipped like the Paphlagonians with woven helmets, small shields, short spears, javelins, daggers, and native knee-high shoes, serving in Xerxes' army under Gobryas.
strymonians: A Thracian people who dwelt along the Strymon river and later migrated to Asia Minor, where they became known as Bithynians after being displaced by Teucrians and Mysians.
cabelees: A Meionian people also called Lasonii, equipped like the Cilicians, who served in Xerxes' invasion force under Badres.
pisidians: A people of inland Asia Minor who served in Xerxes' invasion force, armed with raw-hide shields, wolf-hunters' spears, and bronze helmets adorned with ox-horns, and among whom lay a sanctuary of Ares.
pisidia: A region in south-central Asia Minor, inland from Cilicia, whose peoples (Cabelees, Milyae, and others) supplied troops to Xerxes' invasion force of Greece.
olympieni: Mysians dwelling on or near Mount Olympus in northwestern Asia Minor, named after that mountain, who served under Artaphrenes in Xerxes' invasion of Greece.
lasonii: Anatolian people dwelling in the region of Meonia, also called Cabelees, who fought in Xerxes' invasion force with equipment identical to the Cilicians.
mares: An Anatolian people who wore native woven helmets and carried javelins and small hide shields, commanded by Pharandates son of Teaspis in Xerxes' invasion army.
milyae: A people of Lycia in southwestern Asia Minor, equipped with short spears, brooches, Lycian bows, and skin caps, who served under Badres in Xerxes' invasion force.
sagartian: Persian-speaking nomads dwelling in the region between Persian and Pactyan lands, notable for fighting with lassoes of twisted leather rather than bronze weapons, who contributed eight thousand horsemen to Xerxes' invasion force.
phoenice: Phoenicia, the Levantine coastal region claimed by some Cyprians as the origin of one of their tribal groups.
aegialian-pelasgians: An ancient pre-Greek people who dwelt in what is now Achaia in the Peloponnese before being called Ionians after Ion son of Xuthus arrived.
aradus: An island city off the Phoenician coast, whose captain Merbalus served in Xerxes' fleet during the invasion of Greece.
alarodians: A people of the Caucasus region, armed with wooden helmets, small oxhide shields, and short spears, who served under Masistius in Xerxes' invading army.
hypachaei: The former name of the Cilicians before they took the name of their legendary founder Cilix, son of Agenor.
sidonians: Phoenician seafarers from Sidon whose ships were the most seaworthy in Xerxes' invasion fleet of 480 BC.
pactyan: A people of the Persian empire (from the region called Pactyica) whose fighting gear resembled that of the Sagartians.
nisyrus: A Dorian island in the Aegean Sea near Cos and Halicarnassus, which contributed ships to Xerxes' invasion fleet under Artemisia's command.
calydnos: An island in the southeast Aegean, part of the Dorian territories under Artemisia of Halicarnassus that contributed ships to Xerxes' invasion fleet against Greece.
thasian: Greeks inhabiting the island of Thasos in the northern Aegean, who controlled the mainland city of Stryme and were subject to the Persian king during Xerxes' invasion of Greece.
briantic: A region of Thrace (formerly called Gallaic) lying between the Lisus river and the Samothracian fortresses, rightly belonging to the Ciconians, through which Xerxes' army marched.
gallaic: The former name of the Thracian region later called Briantic, west of the Samothracian fortresses, through which Xerxes' army passed.
ciconians: A Thracian people whose territory lay in the region between the Thasian settlements and the river Lisus, formerly called Gallaic but in Herodotus' time known as Briantic.
compsantus: A river in Thrace that discharges into the Bistonian lake near the Greek city of Dicaea.
bistonian-lake: A lake near the Greek city of Dicaea in Thrace, into which the rivers Travus and Compsantus flow, passed by Xerxes' army during its march into Greece.
ismarid-lake: A lake situated between the Greek cities of Maronea and Stryme in Thrace, which Xerxes' army passed along during the invasion of Greece in 480 BC.
travus: A river of Thrace that discharged into the Bistonian lake near the city of Dicaea, which Xerxes' army crossed during the Persian invasion of Greece.
pergamus: A fortress of the Pierians in Thrace, situated beneath Mount Pangaeus, which Xerxes' army passed during the invasion of Greece.
pistyrus: A Thracian city near the Nestus river, notable for a nearby salt lake that Xerxes' army drained dry watering their pack animals during the Persian invasion.
paeti: A Thracian tribe dwelling in the coastal region of Thrace whose members joined Xerxes' invasion force by sea during his march toward Greece.
bistones: A Thracian tribe dwelling inland whose territory Xerxes' army traversed during the invasion of Greece, compelled to join his land forces.
edoni: A Thracian tribe dwelling inland in northern Greece whose territory Xerxes' army traversed during the Persian invasion, and who were compelled to join his land forces.
phyllis: A region in northern Greece north of the Pangaean mountains, bounded by the rivers Strymon and Angites, through which Xerxes' army marched en route to Greece.
sapaei: A Thracian tribe of inland regions whose territory lay along Xerxes' route to Greece during his invasion; they were compelled to join his land army.
pangaean-mountains: A mountain range in Thrace, north of the Strymon river, forming the boundary of a region called Phyllis that Xerxes' army traversed during his northwestward march into Greece.
dersaei: A Thracian tribe of the inland regions whose territory lay along Xerxes' route of invasion into Greece; they were compelled to join his land army during the Persian invasion.
argilus: A Greek coastal town in Thrace on the Aegean, situated west of the Strymon River, through which Xerxes' invading army passed en route to Greece.
angites: A river in northern Greece that flows into the Strymon, forming the southern boundary of the region Phyllis and marking the western limit of the territory near Mount Pangaeum.
bisaltia: A region of Thrace in northern Greece, lying inland and coastal around Argilus, whose inhabitants were incorporated into Xerxes' invading force during his march westward toward Acanthus.
syleus: A plain in Thrace between the Strymon and Acanthus, through which Xerxes' invading army marched during the Persian Wars.
singus: A Greek town on the Chalcidic peninsula in the Thermaic gulf region, which supplied ships and troops to Xerxes' fleet during the Persian invasion of Greece.
pilorus: A town on the coast of Chalcidice near the Athos canal, which supplied ships and troops to Xerxes' invading fleet.
galepsus: A Greek town on the coast of Macedonia (Chalcidice peninsula) that contributed ships and troops to Xerxes' invasion fleet.
stagirus: A Greek town in Thrace on the coast between Poseideion and Acanthus, which lay on Xerxes' route during his invasion of Greece.
sermyle: A Greek coastal town in the Thermaic gulf region of Macedonia, which supplied ships and troops to Xerxes' Persian fleet during the invasion of Greece.
assa: A coastal town in Thrace on the gulf beyond the Athos canal, which supplied ships and men to Xerxes' fleet during the Persian invasion.
phlegra: A peninsula in northern Greece (modern Pallene in Chalcidice) formerly called Phlegra, which supplied ships and troops to Xerxes' fleet during his invasion of Greece.
canastraean-headland: The southernmost promontory of the Pallene peninsula in northern Greece, marking the point where Pallene extends farthest into the sea and serving as a reference point for Xerxes' fleet's course along the Thermaic coast.
mecyberna: A Greek coastal town on the Thermaic gulf in Macedonia that provided ships and troops to Xerxes' fleet during the Persian invasion.
lipaxus: A town in the region of Crossaea near the Thermaic gulf in northern Greece, which supplied ships and men to Xerxes' fleet during the Persian invasion.
aege: A town of Pallene (formerly called Phlegra) in northern Greece near the Thermaic gulf, which contributed ships and men to Xerxes' fleet during the Persian invasion.
aesa: A town of Crossaea near the Thermaic gulf in northern Greece, from which Persian forces took troops during Xerxes' invasion.
therambus: A town in the region formerly called Phlegra (later Pallene) in northern Greece, from which ships and men were contributed to Xerxes' fleet during the Persian invasion.
combrea: A town in the region called Crossaea near the Thermaic gulf in northern Greece, from which Xerxes' fleet received troops during its advance toward Therma.
smila: A town in the region of Crossaea near the Thermaic gulf in northern Greece, from which Xerxes' fleet received ships and men during the invasion of Greece.
gigonus: A town in Crossaea, a district adjacent to Pallene near the Thermaic Gulf in northern Greece, from which Xerxes' fleet received ships and men during the Persian invasion.
campsa: A town near the Thermaic gulf in the region called Crossaea, from which Persian forces gathered ships and troops during Xerxes' invasion.
ichnae: A town in Bottiaean territory near the river Axius, on the narrow coastal strip between Mygdonian and Bottiaean lands, which Xerxes' fleet passed during its advance into Greece.
crossaea: A coastal region near the Thermaic Gulf in Macedonia, comprising seven towns (Lipaxus, Combrea, Aesa, Gigonus, Campsa, Smila, Aenea) from which Xerxes' fleet drew supplies during his invasion of Greece.
chalestra: A town in Mygdonia near the mouth of the river Axius, where Xerxes' fleet assembled during the invasion of Greece.
othrys: A mountain forming the southern boundary of the Thessalian plain, part of the ring of mountains that once allegedly enclosed it as a lake.
sindus: A town of Mygdonia near the mouth of the river Axius in northern Greece, where Xerxes' fleet gathered during the invasion of 480 BC.
pamisus: A river of Thessaly that flows from the surrounding mountains into the vale and merges with the Peneus before reaching the sea.
edessa: A city in Macedonia through which the Haliacmon and Lydias rivers were said to flow before their confluence.
thessalian-mountains: A range of mountains in northern Greece (including Olympus and Ossa) through which the Peneus river flows in a narrow pass that serves as the traditional gateway into Thessaly from the north.
macedonian-mountains: A mountain range in northern Greece through which Xerxes' army cut a road to reach the Perrhaebian plain on their invasion of Greece.
perrhaebian: A Greek people of Thessaly, through whose territory Xerxes' army passed during his invasion of Greece.
lydias: A river in northern Greece that joins the Haliacmon to form the boundary between Bottiaean and Macedonian lands, delimiting Xerxes' encampment near Therma.
perrhaebians: A Thessalian tribe inhabiting the region around Mount Olympus who submitted to Persian tribute during the invasion of Greece.
tirynthian: A Greek people of the Peloponnese, whose settlement of Halia was attacked and seized by Aneristus son of Sperthias during a merchant voyage.
boebean-lake: A lake that formerly covered the Thessalian plain until earthquakes (attributed by locals to Poseidon) created the Peneus river gorge to drain it into the sea.
lindians: Greeks from the island of Rhodes who, together with Antiphemus, founded the colony of Gela in Sicily.
argolis: A region of the Peloponnese in southern Greece containing the city of Argos and the Tirynthian settlement of Halia.
geloans: Greek settlers of Gela in Sicily, whose ancestor Telines gained priestly power over the cult of the underworld goddesses and used it to restore exiled Geloans to their city.
mactorium: An inland town near Gela in Sicily, to which exiled Geloans were banished before being restored by Telines through religious authority.
triopium: A promontory of Caria in southwestern Asia Minor, off which lay the island of Telos, homeland of Gelon's ancestor who later settled at Gela in Sicily.
callipolis: A city in Sicily that was conquered by the tyrant Hippocrates of Gela during Gelon's service as cavalry captain.
elorus: A river near Syracuse in Sicily, where Hippocrates defeated the Syracusans in battle but was prevented from fully conquering the city by Corinthian and Corcyraean intervention.
sicels: An indigenous people of Sicily against whom the tyrant Hippocrates was campaigning when he died near Hybla.
cyllyrians: A slave population of Syracuse, originally from Casmena, whom Gelon restored to the city along with the Syracusan aristocrats they served.
casmena: A Sicilian town from which Gelon recruited aristocratic exiles (the landed gentry) and their slaves to repopulate Syracuse in the early fifth century BC.
coans: Inhabitants of the island of Cos in the Aegean.
egesta: A city in Sicily where the Carthaginians defeated and killed Dorieus, son of Anaxandrides, in an earlier conflict to which the Greek city-states refused to send aid.
sardinians: An island people off the coast of Italy and Gaul who were brought by the Carthaginian king Amilcas to attack Sicily in support of the tyrant Terillus of Himera.
semites: A Semitic-speaking people of the Levantine coast and interior, whose interactions with Greek traders and armies figure in Mediterranean conflicts of the archaic period.
iberian: A people of the Iberian peninsula who, according to Herodotus, were among the forces recruited by Amilcar of Carthage to invade Sicily around 480 BC on behalf of the deposed tyrant Terillus of Himera.
iberians: A people inhabiting the Iberian Peninsula who were enlisted by Carthage under Amilcas to support Terillus' invasion of Sicily in 480 BC.
sicilians: The inhabitants of Sicily, whose tyrant Gelon was invited by Terillus to support a Carthaginian invasion against the Greeks during the Persian Wars, but instead sent money to Delphi.
corsicans: An island people dwelling off the western coast of Italy, who supplied troops to the Carthaginian general Amilcas in his invasion of Sicily c. 480 BC.
messapians: Descendants of Cretans who, shipwrecked off Iapygia after a failed siege in Sicily, settled at Hyria and spread across the region, later clashing disastrously with the Tarentines.
ligureians: A people from Liguria in northwestern Italy, listed among the forces brought by Carthaginian king Amilcas to aid Terillus against Gelon in Sicily.
rhone: A river of southern Gaul (modern France), Herodotus' westernmost reference point, near which he mistakenly places the source of the Danube.
praesus: A city in eastern Crete that, along with Polichne, did not send settlers to Sicily with the other Cretans in pursuit of Daedalus.
carthaginian: A Phoenician people dwelling in North Africa whose king Amilcas led a massive invasion force into Sicily at the behest of the exiled tyrant Terillus around 480 BC, preventing Gelon of Syracuse from aiding the Greeks against Xerxes.
praesians: Inhabitants of Praesus, a city in eastern Crete, who claimed descent from Greeks repopulating Crete after the Trojan War and preserved a tradition that famine and plague had devastated their island.
tarentine: Greeks who inhabited Tarentum in Iapygia (southern Italy) and suffered catastrophic defeat when they attempted to destroy settlements founded by Messapians descended from shipwrecked Cretans.
oeta: A high mountain forming the western boundary of the pass of Thermopylae in central Greece, significant as a natural fortification in the Persian War narrative.
sepias: A beach in Magnesia on the coast of Thessaly where the Persian fleet anchored after sailing from Therma, and where a great storm subsequently destroyed many ships.
troezenian: Greeks from Troezen in the Peloponnese who provided a ship to the advance guard stationed at Sciathus before the Persian invasion of Greece.
thracian-sea: The sea north of Euboea and south of Thessaly and Magnesia, between the mainland and islands like Sciathus, which narrows at the strait leading to Artemisium.
eordi: A people of Macedonia who furnished troops to Xerxes' invasion of Greece.
meliboea: A city of Magnesia in Thessaly (northern Greece), where Persian ships were wrecked during a storm while the fleet lay at anchor off the coast before Salamis.
bottiaei: A people of northern Greece who contributed troops to Xerxes' invasion force in 480 BC.
ilissus-river: A river near Athens where the Athenians established a sacred precinct to Boreas after crediting the north wind with destroying the Persian fleet.
scyros: An island in the Aegean Sea north of Euboea, whose inhabitant Pammon guided the Persian fleet through the strait to avoid a reef.
magnesian: Greeks inhabiting the coast of Thessaly in northern Greece, whose land between Casthanaea and Cape Sepia was the site where a Persian fleet was destroyed by storm during Xerxes' invasion.
sepian: A headland on the Magnesian coast (not a people) where much of the Persian invasion fleet was wrecked in a violent storm.
pagasae: A coastal town in Magnesia (Thessaly) at the head of a gulf where Xerxes' fleet anchored during the invasion of Greece; legendary site of the Argonauts' departure.
sepia: A cape or coastal locality in Magnesia (northeastern Thessaly) where Persian ships were wrecked during Xerxes' invasion, providing windfall riches to the landowner Ameinocles.
paphian: The Paphians were inhabitants of Paphos on Cyprus who contributed ships to Xerxes' fleet during his invasion of Greece.
peoples-house: A communal meeting-house in Alus, Achaea, where the Achaeans confined the eldest descendant of Phrixus' son Cytissorus to prevent him from leaving alive, as part of a sacrificial ritual prescribed by an oracle.
aridolis: A coastal city in Caria (southwestern Asia Minor) ruled by the tyrant Alabanda, from which Greek forces captured the ruler Aridolis during the naval campaign at Artemisium.
hot-gates: A narrow mountain pass in Malis (central Greece) where hot springs give it its name, and where the Greek forces made their stand against Xerxes' invading Persian army.
enieni: An inland people of central Greece whose territory lay in the region of the upper Spercheus river valley, in the mountainous country of Malis.
dyras: A river in Malis near the gulf where Xerxes' army marched, said in local legend to have emerged from the ground to aid Heracles during his death by fire.
spercheus: A river flowing from the country of the Enieni into the sea in Malis, near the town of Anticyra on the gulf where Xerxes' army advanced during the invasion of Greece.
locrian: Greeks inhabiting the region of Locris in central Greece, whose territory lay near the pass of Thermopylae and included the city of Alpenus.
alpenus: A Locrian city in the region of Malis, situated at the terminus of the Anopaea mountain path that allowed the Persians to outflank the Greek forces at Thermopylae.
carystian: Inhabitants of Carystus, a city on the island of Euboea, one of whom (Onetes son of Phanagoras) was rumored but ultimately rejected by Herodotus as the guide who betrayed the Greeks at Thermopylae.
caphereus: A promontory on the southeastern coast of Euboea, around which Persian ships attempted to sail to cut off the Greek retreat during the naval campaign of 480 BC.
spercheius-river: A river in Thessaly in central Greece that the Persian army crossed during its invasion in 480 BC, mentioned in the epitaph of the seer Megistias who died at Thermopylae.
euboean: Greeks inhabiting the island of Euboea, whose livestock Themistocles advised the Greek fleet to slaughter to provision themselves before the battle of Salamis.
ozolian-locrians: A Greek people inhabiting the region west of Phocis along the coast, near the town of Amphissa, where Phocian refugees fled during the Persian invasion.
histiaeans: Greeks inhabiting the northernmost part of Euboea whose coastal territory was occupied by the Persian fleet after the Greek withdrawal from Artemisium.
ellopian: The inhabitants of Ellopia, a coastal district of Histiaea in Euboea overrun by the Persian fleet after the Greek withdrawal from Artemisium.
drymus: A town in Phocis (central Greece) destroyed by the Persian army during their advance down the Cephisus River in 480 BC.
oetaean-mountains: A mountain range forming the northern boundary of the Thermopylae pass in central Greece, which the Persians used to outflank the Greek defenders in 480 BC.
crisaean: A people inhabiting the plain inland from the Gulf of Corinth in central Greece, whose territory lay near the town of Amphissa in the region of Ozolian Locris.
charadra: A town in Phocis, central Greece, destroyed by the Persian army during their march down the Cephisus river in 480 BC.
amphicaea: A town in Phocis (central Greece), burned by the Persians during Xerxes' invasion in 480 BC while they advanced down the Cephisus valley.
neon: A town in Phocis (central Greece), destroyed by the Persians during their advance down the Cephisus river in the invasion of Greece.
tethronium: A town in Phocis (central Greece), burned by the Persian army during their advance down the Cephisus River in 480 BC.
pediea: A town of Phocis in central Greece, destroyed by the Persian army during Xerxes' invasion while advancing down the Cephisus river valley.
erochus: A town in Phocis (central Greece), destroyed by the Persians during their invasion of Greece in 480 BC while marching down the river Cephisus.
elatea: A town in Phocis in central Greece, burned and plundered by the Persian army under Xerxes as it advanced down the Cephisus river valley in 480 BC.
panopeans: A Phocian people inhabiting a town in central Greece that was burned by Xerxes' army during its march toward Delphi in 480 BC.
panopea: A town in Boeotia, central Greece, where Xerxes' invading army divided into two companies during the campaign against Athens.
tritea: A town in Phocis in central Greece, destroyed and burnt by the Persian army under Xerxes during their advance down the Cephisus river valley in 480 BC.
daulii: A Phocian people whose town in central Greece was burned by Xerxes' army during the invasion of 480 BC.
hyarapean-peak: A peak near Delphi in central Greece, located above the Castalian spring and associated with the shrine of the hero Autonous.
cythnians: A Dryopian people from the Cycladic islands who contributed one trireme and a fifty-oared boat to the Greek fleet at Salamis, being among the few islanders who refused submission to Persia.
cranai: An early name for the Athenians when Pelasgians ruled the land that became Greece, before they were called Cecropidae under King Cecrops.
oenone: The former name of the island of Aegina.
aeolidae: A people of Phocis in central Greece whose town was burned by Xerxes' army during the Persian invasion while a detachment marched toward Delphi.
corycian: A cave on Mount Parnassus above Delphi where the Delphians stored their valuables when fleeing the Persian advance in 480 BC.
