cecropidae: An ancient Athenian people named after their early king Cecrops, before they adopted the name Athenians under Erechtheus.
acheron-river: A river in northwestern Greece (Epirus) forming the boundary of Thesprotia, beyond which peoples to the west did not participate in the Greek defense against Persia.
erineus: A town in Doris, part of the region (with Pindus) from which Dorian peoples migrated south into the Peloponnese.
thespia: A city in Boeotia whose inhabitants fled to the Peloponnese before Xerxes' army burned it in 480 BC for refusing to submit to Persia.
hellene: Greek; a member of the Greek-speaking peoples, some of whom fought against Xerxes' Persian invasion in 480 BC.
laconian-cardamyle: A town in Laconia (southern Greece) near which the Dryopians settled, mentioned as a geographical point of reference in the Peloponnese.
scironian: "Scironian" refers to the Scironian road along the Isthmus of Corinth, which the Peloponnesians demolished to hinder the Persian advance after Thermopylae, not a distinct people.
thesprotians: A Greek people inhabiting the region bordering the Ampraciots and Leucadians in northwestern Greece, who contributed forces to the Greek resistance against the Persian invasion.
munychia: A coastal promontory on the Athenian peninsula, forming part of the harbor of Piraeus, used by the Persian fleet as a reference point for blockading the Greeks during the Battle of Salamis.
orneatae: One of two divisions of the Cynurians (the aboriginal Ionians of the Peloponnese), inhabiting the region around Orneae and subject to Argive rule, who remained neutral during the Persian Wars.
teneans: An Aegean island people who joined Xerxes' invasion force after initially remaining absent from his army at Sepias and Thermopylae.
tenian: An Aegean island people whose trireme deserted from Xerxes' fleet to the Greeks at Salamis, bringing news of the Persian approach, and were honored at Delphi for aiding the Greek victory.
aegaleos: A mountain on the northern shore of the Salamis strait opposite the island, where Xerxes positioned himself to observe the naval battle of 480 BC.
anagyrus: A deme of Attica, home of the Athenian Eumenes, who distinguished himself for courage in the naval battle at Salamis.
colian: The people of Colias, a shore of Attica where a west wind drove Persian wrecks after the Battle of Salamis, fulfilling an old oracle about women cooking with oars.
colias: A shore in Attica where wreckage from the Battle of Salamis was driven by westerly winds, fulfilling an ancient oracle about "Colian women" cooking with oars from the destroyed Persian fleet.
bottiaeans: A people displaced from the Thermaic gulf region by the Macedonians who subsequently settled at Olynthus, where they were massacred by Artabazus during his siege of the town.
scionaeans: A Greek people dwelling in Scione on the Pallene peninsula in Thrace, whose general Timoxenus attempted to betray Potidaea to the Persian commander Artabazus during the invasion of 479 BC.
crestonian: A Thracian people whose territory was ruled by a king who blinded his six sons for disobeying his order to avoid Xerxes' invasion of Greece.
bisaltae: A Thracian people whose king, having refused to serve Xerxes, blinded his six sons for joining the Persian invasion of Greece against his orders.
strymonian: Not a people but a strong wind off the Strymon river in Thrace that nearly capsized Xerxes' ship as he fled Greece.
lebadea: A town in Boeotia with an oracular cave of Trophonius, which Mys visited via a bribed local diviner rather than descending himself.
ptoum: A sanctuary of Apollo in Boeotia near Acraephia, overlooking Lake Copais, famous for an oracle that once spoke in the Carian language.
copais: A lake in Boeotia near Acraephia, where the shrine of Ptoan Apollo stands on a hill above it.
acraephia: A town in Boeotia, near Lake Copais and the temple of Ptoan Apollo, where Mys of Europus received a foreign-language oracle during the Persian wars.
lebaea: A town in the Macedonian highlands where the young Perdiccas worked as a hired laborer and received an omen of his future power.
hercules: A legendary hero of Greek mythology, son of Zeus, whose descendants (the Heraclidae) contested the return to the Peloponnese against the allied Greeks, leading to the single combat between Hyllus and Echemus cited as precedent for Tegean military honor.
cephallenia: An island in the Ionian Sea west of Greece, whose town of Pale sent two hundred men to fight in the Greek line at Plataea.
scolus: A town in Boeotia near the Asopus river, where Mardonius established a fortified camp for his army before the battle of Plataea.
hermotybies: One of two main classes of Egyptian fighting men, serving as marines in Mardonius' army at Platea until disembarked at Phalerum.
calasiries: Egyptian warrior caste who served as marines and were unique among Egyptians as professional soldiers; Mardonius disembarked them from ships to fight on land at Plataea.
sphendalae: A settlement in Attica on the route from Decelea to Tanagra, used as a waypoint by Mardonius' Persian army in 479 BC.
leucas: An island off the coast of northwestern Greece (Ionian Sea), home to the diviner Hippomachus who served with the Persian forces.
styreans: A Greek people who provided six hundred hoplites to the Greek army assembled against the Persians at Plataea, stationed in the line between the Eretrians and the Chalcidians.
illyrians: A barbarian people dwelling in the region northwest of Greece, mentioned as subjects of a prophecy that Mardonius mistakenly applied to the Persians at the Battle of Plataea.
paleans: A Greek people of Pale on the island of Cephallenia who fought with the Greek allies against the Persians at Plataea.
oaks-heads: A mountain pass through Cithaeron between the Peloponnese and Plataea, called by Athenians the Oak's Heads and by Boeotians the Three Heads, where Mardonius' cavalry successfully ambushed Greek supply convoys during the campaign of 479 BC.
molois: A stream in Boeotia near Plataea, where Pausanias halted his Greek forces during their retreat in 479 BC to wait for Amompharetus' lagging battalion before being attacked by Persian cavalry.
three-heads: A mountain pass over Cithaeron leading from the Peloponnese toward Plataea, known to Boeotians as the Three Heads and to Athenians as the Oak's Heads, through which supply convoys passed during the Persian invasion of 479 BC.
stenyclerus: A place in the Peloponnese where a Spartan named Aeimnestus and three hundred men were killed in battle against the Messenians, long after the Persian Wars.
edonians: A Thracian people dwelling near Datus who controlled gold-mines and killed the Athenian general Sophanes in battle.
lacmon: A mountain in Epirus from which the river Chon flows through the territory of Apollonia toward the sea.
coan: An Aegean island people; the woman in this passage identifies herself as Coan, daughter of Hegetorides of Cos, seized by the Persians and rescued by Pausanias after Plataea.
plataeae: A city in Boeotia in central Greece, site of the decisive hoplite battle (479 BC) where Greek forces defeated the Persian army under Mardonius, ending the Persian Wars.
enchelees: An Illyrian people whose territory lay in the region that Herodotus associates with the Thermodon river valley, invoked by the historian as the true subjects of an oracle that Mardonius wrongly applied to the Persians.
calamisa: A coastal locality in Samian territory near a temple of Hera, where the Greek fleet anchored before engaging the Persian navy in the campaign following Xerxes' invasion.
argiopium: A locality in Boeotia near the stream Molois, marked by a shrine of Eleusinian Demeter, where the Greek forces under Pausanias regrouped during the Battle of Plataea.
chon: A river in northwestern Greece flowing from Mount Lacmon through the territory of Apollonia and emptying into the sea at the harbor of Oricum, sacred to the people of Apollonia as the daytime pasture of a flock dedicated to the Sun.
lectum: A promontory on the Asiatic coast near the Hellespont where the Greek fleet from Mykale anchored, driven there by contrary winds, before proceeding to Abydos.
oricum: A harbor on the coast of Apollonia in Epirus, where the river Chon empties into the sea.
